Before Hour 1

Intro Introduction

What the book sets out to teach, who it was written for, what you should bring with you, and how its 24 one-hour lessons fit together. It closes with a short guide to reading this companion.

In this introduction

  • What data structures and algorithms are, and why the book treats them together
  • The four features that set the book apart, starting with its Workshop applets
  • Who the book is for and what you should know before you begin
  • The software you needed in 1999, and what you need today
  • How the five parts and 24 hours are organized, and the conventions used along the way

What This Book Is About

Almost every program keeps some information and does something with it. A data structure is a way of arranging that information in the computer's memory. The book covers the classic ones: arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, several kinds of trees, and hash tables.

An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that works on a structure. Typical jobs are putting a new item in, looking an item up, taking one out, and sorting everything into order.

The two ideas belong together. A structure is only useful because of the operations you can run on it, and the speed of each operation depends on how the data is arranged. Looking up one name can take a single step or a million steps, depending on the structure underneath.

Lafore's aim is practical. He wants programmers and students to know these tools well enough to pick the right one, so their programs run faster and are better organized. The book stays light on mathematics and skips formal proofs. To show that one method beats another, it counts steps and draws pictures.

What's Different About This Book

Four features shape the way the book teaches.

Workshop applets. For each major topic, the book's CD carried a small interactive program, a Workshop applet, that draws the structure on screen. You press buttons to insert, delete, search or sort, and watch the data change. Seeing a structure move teaches more than pages of description, which is the old point about a picture being worth a thousand words.

An easy-to-understand approach. Where many textbooks rely on proofs and formulas, this one leans on intuition, everyday analogies and plenty of figures.

C++ sample programs. Every important idea comes with a complete, short program that you can compile, run, and read in one sitting.

Hour-sized chapters. Each chapter is designed to be learned in about an hour, with a quiz at the end to check that it stuck.

Who This Book Is For

Students taking a data structures course can use the book as a friendly companion to a heavier textbook. Programmers who never took such a course, self-taught developers, and anyone who wants a quick, practical grounding will find it a good place to start. It is not written for experts, since it explains everything from the ground up.

What You Need to Know Before You Read This Book

You should have written some programs before. C++ experience is ideal, but a reader who knows C or Java will follow the code easily because the syntax is so similar. You should be comfortable with variables, loops, functions and arrays, and have a rough idea of what a class is. Hour 1 includes a quick refresher on object-oriented programming.

You don't need to know anything about data structures. The mathematics stops at simple algebra, and the one tool beyond it, the logarithm, gets a plain explanation in Hour 3.

The Software You Need to Use This Book

To run the sample programs you need a C++ compiler. The programs are standard console-mode C++, reading and writing plain text with no graphics, so any standard compiler of the day would do, such as Microsoft Visual C++, Borland C++ or the GNU compiler, g++.

To run the Workshop applets you needed a Java-enabled web browser, or the appletviewer program from Sun's Java Development Kit (JDK). Appendix B of the book explained how to set up both.

Web browsers dropped support for Java applets years ago, so the original Workshop applets no longer run. This companion re-creates each one in JavaScript, and they work right in the page. The C++ programs still compile with any modern compiler. For example, g++ -std=c++17 highArray.cpp -o highArray builds one of the programs from Hour 2.

How This Book Is Organized

The 24 hours are grouped into five parts, followed by three appendixes. Each part builds on the ones before it, so the structures grow more capable as you go.

Part I, Introducing Data Structures and Algorithms (Hours 1 to 5). Hour 1 surveys the field and refreshes your C++. Hour 2 covers arrays and wraps one in a class. Hour 3 keeps the array in order for binary search, which leads to logarithms and Big O notation. Hours 4 and 5 teach two simple sorts, the bubble sort and the insertion sort.

Part II, Abstract Data Types (Hours 6 to 10). Hour 6 introduces stacks and Hour 7 queues and priority queues, structures that limit which item you can reach. Hour 8 brings in linked lists, Hour 9 rebuilds stacks and queues from lists and explains abstract data types, and Hour 10 covers sorted and doubly linked lists.

Part III, Recursion and Quicksort (Hours 11 to 14). Hour 11 explains recursion, a function calling itself. Hour 12 applies it to the Towers of Hanoi and to mergesort. Hour 13 presents quicksort, and Hour 14 keeps it fast on awkward data.

Part IV, Trees (Hours 15 to 20). Hours 15 and 16 cover binary search trees. Hours 17 and 18 explain red-black trees, which keep themselves balanced. Hours 19 and 20 describe 2-3-4 trees, whose nodes hold several items, and their close tie to red-black trees.

Part V, Hash Tables (Hours 21 to 24). Hour 21 introduces hashing and linear probing, Hour 22 adds quadratic probing and double hashing, and Hour 23 covers separate chaining and hash functions. Hour 24, "When to Use What," turns the whole book into advice for choosing a structure.

Part VI, Appendixes. Appendix A answers every quiz, Appendix B explains how to run the applets and sample programs, and Appendix C suggests further reading.

Enjoy Yourself!

Data structures have a reputation as a dry and difficult subject, and Lafore sets out to prove otherwise. He invites you to treat the book as a place to play, where you run the applets, feed them odd inputs, and see what happens.

There is real satisfaction in watching a tree rebalance itself or a quicksort carve an array into pieces. Once the pictures make sense, the code usually does too.

Conventions Used in This Book

The book sets code, such as class and function names, in a monospace font. New terms are flagged and defined where they first appear. Short notes, tips and cautions sit in boxes beside the main text, and "To Do" boxes give numbered steps for working with the applets.

Every hour ends the same way, with a summary, a Q&A section, and a Workshop quiz whose answers are in Appendix A. This companion keeps the same habits, with a few changes for the web. Its boxes carry these labels:

The note boxes in this companion
LabelWhat the box holds
New termThe definition of a term, where it first appears
Just a minuteA remark to pause on, or a clarification
Time saverA shortcut or rule of thumb
CautionA common mistake or trap
To doNumbered steps to try in a Workshop panel
Beyond the bookExtra context that is not in the book, such as modern C++ practice

Quiz answers are hidden under an "Answer" toggle at the end of each hour, so you can test yourself before you look. The Workshop panels are JavaScript re-creations of the book's applets, with similar buttons and displays.

How to Use This Companion

Read the hours in order, because later hours lean on earlier ones. Big O notation from Hour 3, for example, appears in every hour after it.

When a Workshop panel appears, stop and use it. Follow the To do steps, then try inputs of your own; watching the counts of comparisons and moves is the quickest way to feel why one structure beats another. At the end of each hour, answer the quiz before opening the answers, then press the button at the end of the hour to mark it as read.

The C++ listings keep the book's class and function names, so you can match them to the original. The code itself is written fresh for this companion in the book's style, and it compiles with a modern compiler.

Part I · Introducing Data Structures and Algorithms

Hour 1 Overview of Data Structures and Algorithms

Before studying any single structure, it helps to survey the whole toolbox. This hour covers what data structures are for, what each one is good and bad at, which jobs algorithms perform, and the C++ you'll use to build them.

In this hour you'll learn

  • The three kinds of jobs that data structures and algorithms do
  • The strengths and weaknesses of each structure in the book
  • The basic operations: insertion, searching, deletion, iteration and sorting
  • What databases, records, fields and keys are
  • How C++ classes, objects, constructors and access control work
  • The newer C++ features the book relies on, and where all this fits in software engineering

Some Uses for Data Structures and Algorithms

Nearly every serious program has to hold data and work with it. The way that data is arranged can make the difference between a program that answers instantly and one that grinds away for minutes. The situations where data structures help fall roughly into three groups.

Real-World Data Storage

Many structures store information about things outside the computer, such as employees in a personnel file, parts in an inventory, or stamps in a collector's catalog.

Lafore's example is an address book kept on 3×5 index cards, each holding one person's name, address and phone number. Imagine moving the card box into a computer, with 1,000 cards in it. You'd have to arrange the cards in memory, and you'd need ways to add a card, find the card for a given name, and remove a card, all without wading through every card each time.

Those three jobs, insert, find and delete, come up again and again. For ten cards any arrangement is fast enough, but for thousands or millions the arrangement decides everything. Most of the structures in this book are different answers to this storage problem.

Programmer's Tools

Some structures never hold the user's data. The program uses them internally as scaffolding, and the user never knows they exist. Stacks, queues and priority queues, the subject of Part II, are often used this way. In Hour 6, for example, a stack checks that every opening bracket in an expression has a matching closing one.

Modeling

A few structures mirror a real situation directly. A queue behaves just like customers waiting for a bank teller or cars lined up at a toll booth, where whoever arrived first is served first, so a program that simulates the bank can use a queue to stand for the line. Graphs, which this book doesn't cover, model networks such as airline routes or city roads.

Overview of Data Structures

The book covers nine structures. Each one makes some operations fast at the cost of making others slow or complicated, and no structure wins at everything. The table below previews the trade-offs, and every row gets one or more hours of its own later on.

Characteristics of data structures
StructureAdvantagesDisadvantagesCovered in
ArrayQuick insertion; very fast access if you know the indexSlow search; slow deletion; fixed sizeHour 2
Ordered arrayQuicker search than an unsorted arraySlow insertion and deletion; fixed sizeHour 3
StackLast-in, first-out accessSlow access to other itemsHour 6
QueueFirst-in, first-out accessSlow access to other itemsHour 7
Linked listQuick insertion; quick deletionSlow searchHours 8 to 10
Binary treeQuick search, insertion and deletion, if the tree stays balancedDeletion algorithm is complexHours 15 and 16
Red-black treeQuick search, insertion and deletion; always balancedComplexHours 17 and 18
2-3-4 treeQuick search, insertion and deletion; always balanced; similar trees suit disk storageComplexHours 19 and 20
Hash tableVery fast access if the key is known; fast insertionSlow deletion; slow access if the key is not known; inefficient use of memoryHours 21 to 23

Read the table as a map of what lies ahead. The array is quick to add to but slow to search, and keeping it sorted trades faster searching for slower insertion. Stacks and queues deliberately let you reach only one item at a time.

Linked lists make insertion and deletion quick. Trees make nearly everything quick while they stay balanced, and red-black and 2-3-4 trees guarantee that balance at the price of more complex code. Hash tables are fastest of all when you know the key, and Hour 24 returns to every structure to help you choose.

"Quick" and "slow" in this table are relative. They describe how the time for an operation grows as the number of items grows. Hour 3 makes these words precise with Big O notation.

Overview of Algorithms

Most algorithms in the book belong to one particular structure, since finding an item in an array has little in common with finding one in a tree. Across all the structures, though, the same basic jobs keep coming up.

  • Insertion puts a new data item into the structure.
  • Searching finds a specified item, usually by its key.
  • Deletion removes a specified item.

You'll also need to iterate through a structure, visiting each item in turn, for example to display them all. And you'll need to sort items into order, a job that earns several hours of its own (Hours 4, 5 and 12 to 14).

Recursion, in which a function calls itself, is a technique for writing algorithms rather than an operation. It is the key to the fastest sorts and to working with trees, and Part III is devoted to it.

For every algorithm, the book asks how much work it takes. Work is usually counted in comparisons (checking one key against another) and moves (copying an item from one place to another), and it almost always depends on N, the number of items.

Some Initial Definitions

A few words appear so often in the rest of the book that it pays to define them now. The address book makes a good running example.

Database

A database is all the data you are working with in a particular situation. The box of address cards is a database, and so is a company's file of employee records. In this book the word simply means the collection of data, with no suggestion of a special database program.

Record

A database is divided into records, the units you store and retrieve. Each index card is one record, holding everything the address book knows about one person. In an employee file, each record describes one employee.

Field

Each record is divided into fields, one for each kind of information. An address card has a name field, an address field and a phone number field. In a C++ program a record is usually an object, and each field is one of its data members, such as a string lastName or an int age.

Key

To find a record, or to sort a set of them, you pick one field to work with, and that field is the key. For the address book the natural key is the last name, since that's how you look people up and how you would file the cards.

The particular value you're looking for, such as "Smith," is the search key. A search compares the search key with the key field of each record it examines until it finds a match or runs out of records.

A Quick Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming

Every program in the book is built from classes, so this section reviews the object-oriented ideas you'll need. If you use C++ classes every day, you can skim it.

Problems with Procedural Languages

Object-oriented programming (OOP) was invented to fix two weaknesses of procedural languages such as C and Pascal, in which a program is a collection of functions and variables.

The first weakness is poor modeling of the real world. Picture a program that controls the heating in a house. It needs variables for the current and desired temperatures, and functions that switch the furnace on and off. In a procedural language these are separate items, possibly scattered through the program, and nothing says they belong together as one thermostat. With three thermostats, it's up to you to keep track of which function acts on which set of variables.

The second weakness is crude organizational units. A procedural program is built from only functions and global data, which is too little structure once a program grows to thousands of lines. Worse, any function can change global data, so a mistake in one corner can corrupt data used in another.

Objects in a Nutshell

An object bundles data together with the functions that act on that data. A thermostat object contains the data items currentTemp and desiredTemp along with the functions furnace_on() and furnace_off(). The data items are called data members, and the functions are called member functions. Now the language itself records that these things belong together.

A class is the specification for a kind of object, a blueprint that says what data and functions every object of that kind will have. Writing the class doesn't create any objects; it only describes them. Each object you later create from the class is an instance of it. Here is the outline of a thermostat class, with the furnace-control details left out.

The keyword class is followed by the class name and a pair of braces holding the members, and a semicolon ends the whole thing. The labels private and public control who may use each member, as you'll see shortly. Once the class exists, you create objects from it just as you create variables of a built-in type, and then you tell them what to do.

Each object gets its own copy of the data members, so therm1 and therm2 can hold different temperatures. To call a member function, you write the object's name, a dot, and the function. The dot operator ties the call to one object, so therm2.furnace_off() switches off the furnace that therm2 controls and leaves therm1 alone.

An object made with new is reached through a pointer, and the arrow operator, ->, replaces the dot. The book's pointer names start with a p, as in pTherm.

A Runnable Object-Oriented Program

The thermostat outline can't do anything, because its functions are empty. The book's first complete program, bank.cpp, models something just as familiar, a bank account. Its class, BankAccount, holds one data member, the balance, and offers three services: deposit money, withdraw money, and display the balance.

In main(), the statement BankAccount ba1(100.00); creates an account object named ba1 with an opening balance of $100. The program prints a label and calls ba1.display(). Then it deposits $74.35 and withdraws $20.00, each time by calling a member function of ba1, and displays the balance again. Since 100 + 74.35 − 20 = 154.35, the output is:

Before transactions, balance=100
After transactions, balance=154.35

(C++ prints 100 rather than 100.00 because its default format drops trailing zeros.) Notice that main() never touches balance directly. It asks the object to deposit, withdraw or display, and the object's own functions do the arithmetic.

Constructors

A constructor is a special member function that runs automatically when an object is created, to give the object's data sensible starting values. It has exactly the same name as its class, and it has no return type, not even void.

In bank.cpp the constructor takes the opening balance as an argument. The part after the colon, : balance(openingBalance), is an initializer list, which copies the argument into the data member, so the body has nothing left to do. You never call a constructor by name. Defining ba1 calls it for you, passing 100.00; without it, balance would start out holding whatever value happened to be in memory.

public and private

The data member balance sits in the class's private section. Private members can be read or changed only by the class's own member functions. If main() tried to write ba1.balance = 1000000;, the compiler would refuse. This protection is called data hiding, and it guards the data against careless or accidental changes from outside the class.

The member functions sit in the public section, so any code with a BankAccount object can call them. Together, the public functions form the class's interface, the services the outside world may use. The usual pattern, and the book's, is private data with public functions. Anyone who wants to change the balance must go through deposit() or withdraw(), which is where a real bank would add checks, such as refusing an overdraft.

Inheritance and Polymorphism

Two more OOP ideas complete the picture, though the book uses them very little. Inheritance lets you create a derived class from an existing base class. The derived class gets all the base class's data and functions and can add its own. You could derive a savings account class from BankAccount, for example, and add a function that pays interest.

Polymorphism lets you treat objects of different derived classes in the same way. You call the same function on each object, and each responds in the manner of its own class. In C++ this works through virtual functions, usually called through pointers to the base class.

New C++ Features

The book's programs rely on parts of Standard C++ that older courses and textbooks often skip. If you learned C++ from one of them, three features may be new to you.

The string Class

Older C++ code stores text in arrays of char and handles it with functions such as strcpy() and strcmp(), a clumsy style that makes it easy to write past the end of the array. Standard C++ offers a string class instead. After including <string>, you can write string s1 = "cat"; and treat the string much like a built-in type.

The + operator joins strings, so s1 + s2 glues the second onto the end of the first. The operators == and < compare them, with "less than" meaning "comes first alphabetically" (when both words use the same capitalization), and s1.length() reports the number of characters. A string grows as needed, and comparing strings with == is how the book's programs search by name.

The vector Class

The vector class belongs to the Standard Template Library (STL), a collection of ready-made containers and algorithms that is part of Standard C++. A vector behaves much like an array, and you reach its elements with square brackets, as in v[j]. Unlike an array, it knows its own size, which v.size() reports, it manages its own memory, and it can grow.

You include <vector> and name the element type in angle brackets. vector<double> v(100); creates 100 double values. You can also create an empty vector and size it later with v.resize(100);, as the book's classes do in their constructors, and v.push_back(value) adds an element at the end. Because of this, the array classes in Hour 2 and Hour 3 can take their size as a constructor argument while the program runs, which a plain C++ array can't do.

New-Style Headers and Namespaces

Standard C++ also renamed the library header files. You write #include <iostream> instead of the older #include <iostream.h>. Everything in the standard library now lives in a namespace called std.

The line using namespace std; near the top of a file lets you write cout, string and vector without putting std:: in front of each one, and every program in the book starts this way. Here is a short program that tries out both classes.

catfish has 7 letters
cat comes before fish
The vector now holds 6 numbers

The first half builds "catfish" by joining two strings, reports its seven letters, and confirms that "cat" sorts before "fish." The second half creates a five-cell vector, fills it with a loop exactly as you would fill an array, and then calls push_back() to add a sixth value, so size() reports 6.

Software Engineering

Software engineering is the study of how to create large programs. It covers a program's whole life cycle, from the first idea to years of later upkeep, and the stages are usually described like this:

  1. Specification, or analysis, works out what the program must do.
  2. Design decides how the program will be organized, including its classes and data structures.
  3. Coding writes the program.
  4. Testing finds and fixes errors.
  5. Maintenance keeps the program working and adapts it after release, often for years.

Data structures and algorithms matter most in design and coding. Choosing a structure that suits the job is a design decision, implementing it well is a coding task, and together they decide whether the finished program is fast or slow.

The benefits spread to the later stages too. Well-chosen, cleanly separated classes are easier to test, because each can be checked on its own, and easier to maintain, because a change inside one class doesn't ripple through the rest. Software engineering is a big subject with many books of its own, and this book deals only with the parts that concern data structures and algorithms.

Summary

  • Data structures and algorithms serve three purposes: storing real-world data, acting as tools inside programs, and modeling real situations.
  • Each structure makes some operations fast and others slow, and none is best for everything. Arrays, ordered arrays, stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees, red-black trees, 2-3-4 trees and hash tables each get hours of their own.
  • The basic operations are insertion, searching and deletion. Iterating through every item and sorting are also common.
  • A database is all the data in a situation. It is divided into records, and each record is divided into fields.
  • The key is the field you search or sort by. The search key is the particular value you're looking for.
  • An object bundles data members with the member functions that act on them. A class is the blueprint, and objects are its instances.
  • A constructor has the class's name and no return type, and it runs automatically to initialize each new object.
  • Private data can be reached only through the class's own functions. The public functions form the class's interface.
  • The book uses Standard C++: the string class, the STL's vector, and new-style headers with using namespace std;.
  • Software engineering covers a program's whole life cycle, and data structures and algorithms matter most in its design and coding stages.

Q&A

Standard C++ already provides containers such as vector. Why learn how data structures work inside?
Because you can't choose well among tools you don't understand. Knowing how each structure works tells you which library container fits a job, how to use it efficiently, and what each operation will cost. Sometimes no ready-made container fits your problem, and then you need to build your own.
Do I have to know C++ to get anything out of this book?
No. The structures and algorithms are the same in every language. A reader who knows Java or C will follow the code without trouble, and the pictures and applets need no language at all. C++ is simply the vehicle.
What if my compiler doesn't have the string and vector classes?
Then it predates Standard C++, and the best fix is a newer compiler, since every modern one includes both classes. If you're stuck with an old one, you can replace the vectors with ordinary arrays and the strings with char arrays, at the cost of messier code.
Is an algorithm the same thing as a program?
An algorithm is the procedure itself, the idea of how to do a job, and you can describe it in words, in a diagram or in any programming language. A program expresses one or more algorithms in a particular language. Binary search, for example, is one algorithm that appears in countless programs.

Quiz

  1. What are the three general kinds of uses for data structures and algorithms?

    Answer

    Storing real-world data (such as an address book or personnel records), serving as programmer's tools inside a program (such as stacks and queues), and modeling real situations (such as a queue of customers at a bank).

  2. In an address book database, what is the key, and what is a search key?

    Answer

    The key is the field used to search for or sort the records, usually the last name. A search key is the particular value you're looking for, such as "Smith."

  3. What is the difference between a class and an object?

    Answer

    A class is a specification, or blueprint, describing the data and functions that objects of its kind will have. An object is an actual instance created from the class, with its own copy of the data. One class can produce many objects.

  4. What does a constructor do, and how can you recognize one?

    Answer

    It initializes a new object's data, and it runs automatically when the object is created. It has the same name as its class and no return type.

  5. What does it mean for a data member to be private?

    Answer

    Only the class's own member functions can read or change it. Code outside the class must go through the public member functions, which protects the data from accidental changes.

  6. Why do the book's array classes use a vector instead of a plain C++ array?

    Answer

    A vector's size can be chosen while the program runs (with resize() in the constructor), it knows its own size, it manages its own memory, and it can grow with push_back(). A plain array's size is fixed when the program is compiled.

Part I · Introducing Data Structures and Algorithms

Hour 2 Arrays

The array is the simplest data structure and the one programmers use most. This hour measures how fast an unsorted array can insert, search and delete, then moves the array into a C++ class and shows why a well-designed interface matters.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How insertion, searching and deletion work in an unsorted array, and what each costs
  • What changes when duplicate keys are allowed
  • How to create, fill, search and shrink a plain C++ array
  • How to move an array into a class with a bare-bones interface
  • How a better interface puts the work inside the class, and why that abstraction pays off

The Array Workshop Applet

Suppose you coach a youth-league baseball team and want to take attendance at practice on a laptop. Players turn up one at a time. When a player arrives, you type in the number on the back of the player's jersey. When a parent asks whether a certain player made it, you check the list, and when a player leaves early, you take the number off.

This little program needs exactly the three basic operations from Hour 1: insertion, searching and deletion. The jersey number is the key, and each player is a record with just that one field.

The simplest structure for the job is an array, and the book's Array Workshop applet shows one on the screen. It draws the array as a row of cells, each labeled with its index number and able to hold one key. Buttons let you create a new array (New, which asks for a size and whether duplicate keys are allowed), fill it with random keys (Fill), and insert, find or delete a key typed into a number field (Ins, Find, Del).

Our re-creation below works the same way and counts the comparisons and moves that each operation makes. Try each button as you read the rest of this section.

Try it. Take attendance with the Array Workshop.

  1. Press Fill to put 10 random keys in the array.
  2. Type a new key and press Ins. It lands in the first empty cell with no comparisons at all.
  3. Type a key that is in the array and press Find. Count the comparisons as the search walks right from cell 0.
  4. Now Find a key that isn't there. The search checks every item before it gives up.
  5. Press Del for a key near the left end and watch each item above it shift down one cell.
  6. Tick Dups OK and insert a second copy of a key that's already there, so the array holds a duplicate.

Insertion

When a new player arrives, the applet puts the number into the first empty cell, just past the last item. It knows exactly where that is because it keeps a count of the items. If the array holds 10 items, they occupy cells 0 through 9, so the new item goes into cell 10 and the count becomes 11.

That makes insertion very fast. There is no searching and no comparing, just one move to copy the new item into place, and the time is the same whether the array holds 10 items or 10,000.

Searching

To check whether a player is present, you type the number and press Find. The algorithm has no idea where the number might be, so it starts at cell 0 and compares each key with the one you typed, moving right one cell at a time, until it finds a match or runs out of items.

Linear search. A search that examines items one after another, starting at the beginning, until it finds the one it wants or reaches the end.

If the player is there, the match could be in the first cell or the last, and every position is equally likely. On average the search looks at half the items before it succeeds, so for N items it needs about N/2 comparisons. With 20 players that's 10 comparisons on average; with 20,000 records it's 10,000.

If the player isn't there, the search can't stop early. It must compare all N items before it can report failure.

Deletion

Deleting a player takes two stages. First the algorithm must find the item, which costs about N/2 comparisons on average, just like a search. Then it has to deal with the empty cell the item leaves behind.

The applet's algorithms assume the array has no holes. The items sit in consecutive cells starting at 0, with no empty cells between them. That is what lets insertion go straight to the cell after the last item, and what lets a search stop at the last item instead of checking every cell in the array.

So after finding the item, deletion closes the gap. Every item above the deleted one moves down one cell, starting with the item just above the gap. If the deleted item was near the start, nearly everything moves; if it was near the end, hardly anything does.

On average about N/2 items move. Deletion therefore costs about N/2 comparisons plus about N/2 moves, which makes it the slowest of the three operations.

The Duplicates Issue

When you design a storage structure, you have to decide whether two items may share the same key. Jersey numbers are unique, so the attendance list never needs duplicates. If the key were a last name, though, two brothers named Garcia could easily be on the same team. The book's applet lets you choose when you press New, and allowing duplicates changes the costs.

  • Searching. Without duplicates, a search stops at the first match, after N/2 comparisons on average. With duplicates, finding every item with a given key means checking all N cells, since another match could be anywhere.
  • Insertion. This stays one move with no comparisons either way, because the new item always goes in the first empty cell. There is one catch. If duplicates are forbidden and a user might type a key that's already present, the program must search before inserting, which costs about N/2 comparisons when the key is found and all N to prove that it's absent.
  • Deletion. Deleting every copy of a key means examining all N cells, and each copy removed forces more items to shift, so the moves usually add up to more than N/2.
Duplicates allowed versus not allowed, for an array of N items
OperationNo duplicatesDuplicates OK
SearchN/2 comparisonsN comparisons
InsertionNo comparisons, one moveNo comparisons, one move
DeletionN/2 comparisons, N/2 movesN comparisons, more than N/2 moves

N/2 is an average. A single search might succeed at the very first cell or the very last. What matters when you compare algorithms is how that average grows as N grows, an idea that becomes Big O notation in Hour 3.

Not Too Swift

Playing with the applet makes the verdict clear. Insertion is fast, but searching and deletion are slow, because both have to plow through about half the array. For a team of 15 players nobody would notice. For a file of 100,000 customers, an average of 50,000 comparisons per lookup starts to hurt.

Much of the rest of the book is a hunt for structures that do better. An ordered array (Hour 3) makes searching far faster. Linked lists (Hour 8) do away with the shifting, trees (Hour 15) speed up all three operations, and hash tables (Hour 21) can find an item almost instantly.

An Array Example

Before wrapping an array in a class, it helps to see a plain C++ array doing the same jobs. First, a quick review of how C++ arrays work.

Creating an Array

You declare an array by giving the type of its elements, its name, and its size in square brackets. int arr[100]; sets aside room for 100 integers. The size must be a constant that is known when the program is compiled, and it can never change afterward. That fixed size is one of the array's big limitations, as you'll see at the end of Hour 3.

Accessing Array Elements

You reach an element by putting its index in square brackets, as in arr[j]. Indexes start at 0, so the 100 cells of arr are numbered 0 through 99. Asking for arr[100] is a mistake that the compiler won't catch, and the running program won't catch it either. It simply reads or overwrites whatever memory lies beyond the array, which can cause baffling bugs or a crash.

C++ never checks array indexes for you. Every loop that walks an array has to stop at the right place, and the most common array bug is an off-by-one error that touches one cell too many.

Initialization

You can fill an array when you create it by listing values in braces, as in int intArr[] = {0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15};. If you leave the brackets empty, the compiler makes the array just big enough for the list, six cells in this case.

The array.cpp Program

The program array.cpp puts all of this to work. It inserts ten items, displays them, searches for one, deletes another, and displays what's left, and everything happens inside main(). In our version the ten keys start out in an initialized array, and a loop inserts them one at a time into the working array, arr.

The variable nElems is the heart of the program. It counts the items, and it's also the index of the first empty cell, since the items fill cells 0 through nElems − 1. That's why insertion is just arr[nElems] = value followed by nElems++.

The search loop compares each item with searchKey and uses break to leave as soon as it finds a match. When the loop ends there are only two possibilities. Either it broke out early and j holds the index of the match, or it ran all the way to the end and j equals nElems. The test j == nElems tells the two apart.

Deletion begins with the same search, this time for 55, which it finds at index 3. The second loop then closes the gap by copying the item at k + 1 into cell k, for each k from the hole upward. It stops when k reaches nElems − 1, so its last copy moves the final item into the cell below it. Then nElems drops by one.

Our version also checks that the search succeeded before it shifts anything, so asking it to delete a missing key does no harm. Here is the output:

77 99 44 55 22 88 11 0 66 33
Found 66
77 99 44 22 88 11 0 66 33

The program shows the ten items, reports the successful search for 66, and then shows the array after 55 has gone. The items that followed 55 kept their order; each simply slid one cell to the left.

Dividing a Program into Classes

array.cpp works, but it's organized like a procedural program. The data (the array and its count) and every operation on it are mixed together in one long main(). In a program of ten thousand lines that used the array in dozens of places, search loops and shifting loops would be scattered everywhere, and any one of them could damage the array.

The object-oriented cure from Hour 1 is to put the data into a class, together with the functions that act on it. The book takes this in two steps. The first, lowArray.cpp, moves the array into a class called LowArray but gives that class only the most basic abilities.

The array is now a private vector<double> named v, so no code outside the class can reach it directly. The constructor takes the size you want and calls resize() to make the vector that big. After that there are just two member functions. setElem() stores a value at a given index, and getElem() returns the value at a given index.

Client. The code that uses a class, also called its user. Here the client of LowArray is main().

The client still does all the real work, as the main() function shows.

These are the loops from array.cpp, with arr[j] replaced by arr.getElem(j) and assignments replaced by setElem() calls. main() still keeps nElems, still decides where each item goes, still runs the linear search, and still does the shifting. Our version searches for 26, which isn't there:

77 99 44 55 22 88 11 0 66 33
Can't find 26
77 99 44 22 88 11 0 66 33

The one real gain is that the data is now hidden. The only way to touch the vector is through two member functions, which could later be changed to check every index, for example. But the interface is so primitive that LowArray is little more than an array with a clumsier syntax.

Class Interfaces

A class's interface is the set of public member functions its clients can call. The interface decides how easy the class is to use, and how much its clients need to know about its insides. LowArray shows what goes wrong when the interface is too thin.

Not So Convenient

With LowArray, every client must know that items are packed from index 0, keep its own count, write its own search loop, and remember to shift items after a deletion, in the right direction and stopping at the right place. Two clients might do these things in two different ways, and a client that forgot to shift would silently leave a hole. The interface hands over all of the responsibility and none of the help.

Who's Responsible for What?

A better division of labor asks the class to manage its own data. The client should only have to say what it wants, such as "insert this," "is this here?" or "remove that," and the class should work out how. That means the item count and all three algorithms move out of main() and into the class. The result is the book's HighArray class.

The highArray.cpp Example

The class now owns both the vector and the count, nElems, which the constructor sets to zero. Its four public functions do everything main() used to do.

  • insert() puts the new value in cell nElems and adds one to the count.
  • find() runs a linear search. It returns true from inside the loop the moment it sees a match, and if the loop finishes, the key wasn't there.
  • remove() searches for the value and returns false if it can't find it. Otherwise it shifts the higher items down, reduces the count, and returns true.
  • display() prints every item on one line.

Look closely at the shifting loop in remove(). It runs while k < nElems - 1, so its last pass copies v[nElems-1], the final item, into the cell below. If it ran while k < nElems, its last pass would read v[nElems], a cell beyond the last item. Usually that junk would land in a cell that no longer counts, so the mistake could go unnoticed, but when the array is full the read runs off the end of the vector.

insert() trusts its client not to overfill the array. Insert more items than the size given to the constructor and it writes past the end of the vector. A sturdier version would compare nElems with v.size() first, and refuse or grow the vector when the array is full.

Here is the new client:

77 99 44 55 22 88 11 0 66 33
Can't find 35
77 44 22 88 11 66 33

The search for 35 fails. After 0, 55 and 99 are removed, seven items remain, still in their original relative order.

The User's Life Made Easier

Compare the two versions of main(). The LowArray client was full of loops, index arithmetic and bookkeeping. The HighArray client reads almost like plain English: insert these numbers, display them, look for 35, remove three numbers, display again.

There's no nElems in sight, and main() has no way to leave a hole in the array, because it can reach the array only through functions that keep it tidy. The work didn't disappear, of course; the same loops still run. But they're written once, inside the class, where they can be tested once and trusted wherever the class is used.

Abstraction

The client of HighArray knows what the class does. It stores numbers and can insert, find, remove and display them. The client doesn't know how the class does these things, and doesn't need to. It can't tell whether the numbers live in a vector or somewhere else, or which search method find() uses.

Separating what from how is called abstraction, and it's one of the most useful ideas in programming. Because the client depends only on the interface, you could rewrite HighArray to store its data differently or to search faster, and every client would keep working unchanged. Hour 3 does something close to this when it keeps the items in order and switches to a much faster search, and the idea returns in full force in Hour 9, on abstract data types.

Summary

  • An unsorted array inserts a new item in one step, with no comparisons, by putting it in the first empty cell (index nElems).
  • Linear search takes about N/2 comparisons on average when the item is present, and N when it isn't.
  • Deletion takes about N/2 comparisons to find the item plus about N/2 moves to close the gap, because the array must not have holes.
  • If duplicates are allowed, searches and deletions must examine all N items. Insertion stays one step unless you must check for a duplicate first.
  • A C++ array has a fixed size set at compile time, indexes from 0 to size − 1, and no bounds checking.
  • Moving the array into a class (LowArray) hides the data, but a low-level interface leaves the client doing all the work.
  • HighArray moves the count and the algorithms into the class, so its client just calls insert(), find(), remove() and display().
  • Abstraction, separating what a class does from how it does it, lets you change a class's insides without touching its clients.

Q&A

Why not just mark a deleted cell as empty instead of shifting everything down?
You could, and some structures do. The hash tables of Hour 21 mark deleted cells with a special value. In an array, though, holes complicate everything else. Insertion would have to hunt for an empty cell, and every search would have to skip holes and could no longer stop at nElems. Shifting keeps the other operations simple, at the cost of slower deletion.
Why does HighArray use a vector rather than a plain array?
So the client can choose the size while the program runs, by passing it to the constructor. A plain array's size must be fixed when the program is compiled. The vector also knows its own size and could be grown if it filled up.
Is linear search ever the right choice?
Yes. For a small array, a few dozen items or so, it's fast enough and as simple as code gets. It's also the only choice when the data is in no particular order and you search too rarely to justify sorting it.
remove() deletes only the first match. How would I delete every copy of a key?
The simplest way is to call remove() in a loop until it returns false. Each call searches from the start again, so that's slow when there are many copies. A faster approach makes a single pass, copying each item that should stay down into the next free position.

Quiz

  1. In an unsorted array of N items with no duplicates, about how many comparisons does it take to find an item that is present? One that is absent?

    Answer

    About N/2 on average for an item that is present, and N for an item that is absent, because the search must check every item before it can give up.

  2. About how many comparisons and moves does it take to delete an item from an unsorted array of 1,000 items?

    Answer

    On average about 500 comparisons to find the item and about 500 moves to shift the items above it down one cell.

  3. Why do the array algorithms in this hour insist that there be no holes?

    Answer

    Because the other algorithms rely on the items filling cells 0 to nElems − 1. Insertion uses nElems as the index of the first empty cell, and searching stops at the last item. With holes, both would have to check for empty cells.

  4. What changes when duplicate keys are allowed?

    Answer

    Searching for every match takes N comparisons instead of N/2, and deleting every copy takes N comparisons and more than N/2 moves. Insertion is still one move with no comparisons.

  5. Why is HighArray a better class than LowArray?

    Answer

    HighArray keeps the item count and performs searching, insertion and deletion itself, so its clients only ask for what they want. The client code is shorter and clearer, can't corrupt the array, and keeps working if the class's inner workings change.

  6. In remove(), why does the shifting loop stop when k reaches nElems − 1?

    Answer

    The last copy it needs moves v[nElems-1], the final item, into v[nElems-2]. Going one step further would read v[nElems], which is past the last item, and past the end of the vector when the array is full.

Part I · Introducing Data Structures and Algorithms

Hour 3 Ordered Arrays

Keep an array's items in order and you can find any of them with binary search, which is far faster than checking cell by cell. This hour shows how binary search works, measures it with logarithms, stores whole objects in an array, introduces Big O notation, and explains why arrays still aren't enough.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How an ordered array keeps its items in key order, and what that costs on insertion
  • How binary search finds an item by halving the range, just like a guessing game
  • How logarithms tell you how many steps binary search needs
  • How to store objects with several fields in an array
  • How Big O notation describes the way running time grows with N
  • Why arrays can't be the answer to every storage problem

The Ordered Workshop Applet

An ordered array keeps its items sorted by key, with the smallest key in cell 0 and each cell holding a key at least as large as the one before it. The book's Ordered Workshop applet shows such an array. It looks and behaves much like the Array applet from Hour 2. The main difference is that pressing New to create an array also asks you to choose a search method, linear or binary.

Insertion

Order comes at a price, and insertion pays it. A new item must take its proper place among the others, so insertion finds the first item with a larger key, moves it and every item above it up one cell, and copies the new item into the gap. On average about N/2 items move, where an unsorted array needed a single move. Deletion works as in Hour 2, shifting the larger items down to close the hole.

Linear Search

If you choose linear search, the applet steps through the cells from the left, just as before, with one small advantage. Because the keys increase from left to right, the search can stop as soon as it reaches a key larger than the one it wants. A failed search therefore gives up about halfway on average, after roughly N/2 comparisons instead of N. A successful search still takes about N/2.

Binary Search

The real payoff of keeping things in order is binary search, which finds an item by repeatedly cutting the range of possible cells in half. The idea is easiest to see in a children's game.

The Guess-a-Number Game

A friend thinks of a number between 1 and 100 and asks you to guess it. After each guess, the friend tells you whether you're too high, too low, or right. You could start at 1 and work upward, but that might take 100 guesses.

The smart move is to guess the middle, 50. Whatever the answer, one guess throws away half the possibilities. Then you guess the middle of the half that's left, and keep going. Here is how the game goes when the secret number is 33.

Guessing the number 33 by always choosing the middle
StepGuessResultRange still possible
050Too high1–49
125Too low26–49
237Too high26–36
331Too low32–36
434Too high32–33
532Too low33–33
633CorrectFound it

It took seven guesses, numbered 0 through 6. Each guess is the middle of the remaining range, rounded down when the middle falls between two numbers. Starting from 100 possibilities, at most 50 remain after the first guess, then at most 25, 12, 6, 3 and finally 1, so this strategy never needs more than seven guesses for a number from 1 to 100.

Our Workshop panel turns the game around. You think of a number, and the computer finds it by binary search.

Try it. Let the computer guess your number.

  1. Press Demo with 33 to watch the computer replay the table above, guess by guess.
  2. Now think of your own whole number from 1 to 100 and press Start over.
  3. After each guess, press Too low, Too high or Correct.
  4. Watch the range shrink by about half with every answer.
  5. Try 1, then 100, then 64. The guess count never goes above 7.

Binary Search in the Ordered Applet

Binary search in an ordered array plays the same game with cell numbers. The applet shows a lower bound and an upper bound enclosing the cells where the key could still be, starting at the first and last cells. At each step it points at the cell halfway between them and compares that cell's key with the one you want.

If the middle key is too small, the lower bound jumps to just past the middle; if it's too large, the upper bound jumps to just before it. Half the remaining cells drop out each time, so while linear search plods from cell to cell, binary search finishes in a handful of steps.

Try it. Race the two searches and watch insertion make room.

  1. Press Fill to create an ordered array of random keys.
  2. Choose Linear, type a key near the right end, and press Find. Note the number of comparisons.
  3. Switch to Binary and find the same key. Watch the lower, upper and middle pointers close in.
  4. Search for a key that isn't there with each method. Linear search stops once it passes the spot where the key would be; binary search stops when the range is empty.
  5. Type a small key and press Ins. Count the moves as the larger items shift up to make room.

C++ Code for an Ordered Array

The book's program orderedArray.cpp defines a class called OrdArray. It resembles HighArray from Hour 2, with a private vector<double> v, a count nElems, and a small function getSize() that returns the count. The big changes are in find(), which now uses binary search, and in insert(), which keeps the items in order.

Binary Search with the find() Member Function

lowerBound and upperBound mark the ends of the range still in play. Each pass through the loop computes curIn, the index halfway between them; integer division drops any fraction, so the midpoint of 8 and 15 is 11.

If v[curIn] equals the search key, find() returns the index. If v[curIn] is smaller, the key can only lie to the right, so lowerBound moves to curIn + 1. Otherwise it can only lie to the left, and upperBound moves to curIn - 1. Either way, the middle cell and everything on the wrong side of it are ruled out.

If the key isn't there, the bounds eventually cross, with lowerBound greater than upperBound. The range is empty, the loop ends, and find() returns nElems, a value that can never be the index of a real item. The caller compares the result with getSize() to tell success from failure.

Here is a search for 57 in an array of 16 items. The first step examines cell 7.

Cell 7 holds 45, which is smaller than 57, so the lower half is discarded and lowerBound becomes 8.

Cell 11 holds 70, which is too large, so upperBound becomes 10. The third step examines cell 9 and finds the key.

Binary search found the key in three steps, each examining one cell. A linear search would have examined ten cells, 0 through 9.

The OrdArray Class

The rest of the class handles insertion, deletion and display.

insert() works in two stages. The first loop scans from the left for the first item larger than the new value, and when it stops, j is the cell where the value belongs (nElems if every item is smaller). The second loop opens a gap at j. It must start at the top and work down, so that each copy lands in a cell that is already free; starting at j would overwrite each item before it had been moved.

remove() calls find(), so deletion also benefits from binary search when it locates the item. The shifting afterward is the same as in HighArray.

The orderedArray.cpp Program

The main() function inserts the same ten numbers as in Hour 2, in the same scrambled order. It then searches for 55, displays the array, removes three items, and displays it again.

Found 55
0 11 22 33 44 55 66 77 88 99
11 22 33 44 66 77 88

Although the numbers went in scrambled, they come out sorted, because insert() put each one in its place. The last insertion, of 33, is the one pictured above.

Advantages of Ordered Arrays

The trade is easy to state. Searching becomes far faster, insertion becomes slow because half the items must move on average, and deletion is slow in both kinds of array.

So an ordered array pays off when searches are frequent and insertions and deletions are rare. The book's example is a database of company employees, where people are looked up constantly but hiring and firing happen far less often. A retail store's inventory is the opposite case. Items arrive and sell all day, and an ordered array would spend much of its time shifting data around.

Logarithms

Binary search is fast, and logarithms tell you exactly how fast. The word sounds intimidating, but here it has a very concrete meaning. Start with the numbers.

Comparisons needed to search N items
Range (N)Binary search, at mostLinear search, average (N/2)
1045
100750
1,00010500
10,000145,000
100,0001750,000
1,000,00020500,000
10,000,000245,000,000
100,000,0002750,000,000
1,000,000,00030500,000,000

For small arrays the difference hardly matters, since 4 comparisons against 5 is nothing. For a million items, though, binary search needs at most 20 comparisons where linear search averages 500,000, and for a billion items it needs just 30. Making the array ten times bigger adds only three or four steps to a binary search.

The Equation

To see where these numbers come from, think about the search backward. Each step cuts the range in half, so each extra step doubles the range you can handle. If some range takes s steps, a range twice as big takes s + 1, because its first step cuts it back down. Start from a range of 1, which needs no steps, and double it s times. The range r that s steps can cover is

r = 2s

Powers of two: the range r that s steps can cover
Steps s012345678910
Range r = 2s12481632641282565121,024

Seven steps cover 128 values, more than 100, which is why seven guesses are enough for the number game. Ten steps cover 1,024, so a thousand items need 10 comparisons.

The Opposite of Raising Two to a Power

The equation r = 2s tells you how big a range s steps can handle. A search needs the reverse, the number of steps s for a given range r. The operation that undoes raising 2 to a power is the base-2 logarithm, written log₂, so

s = log₂(r)

In words, log₂(r) is the power you must raise 2 to in order to get r. Since 210 = 1,024, log₂(1,024) = 10. When r isn't an exact power of 2, the logarithm has a fractional part, and you round up to get the number of steps. For example, log₂(100) is about 6.64, which rounds up to 7.

Many calculators only have a key for base-10 logarithms. To convert, multiply by 3.322, since log₂(x) = log₁₀(x) × 3.322. For a million items, log₁₀(1,000,000) is 6, and 6 × 3.322 = 19.93, which rounds up to 20, just as the table says.

Because 210 = 1,024 is close to 1,000, every factor of 1,000 in the size of an array adds about 10 steps to a binary search. A thousand items take about 10 steps, a million about 20, and a billion about 30.

Storing Objects

So far the arrays have held plain numbers. Real databases hold records with several fields, like the address cards in Hour 1. The book's next program, classDataArray.cpp, shows how an array can hold objects, using a simple record that describes a person.

The Person Class

A Person object has three fields: a last name, a first name, and an age. The constructor fills them in, displayPerson() prints them, and getLast() returns the last name so that other code can use it as the key.

The ClassDataArray Class

The array class, ClassDataArray, is HighArray adapted to hold people. Its vector doesn't contain Person objects themselves. It holds pointers to them, vector<Person*>, and each object is created with new when it is inserted.

The last name is the key field. find() takes a search key such as "Stimson" and compares it with v[j]->getLast() for each person, using the string class's == operator. When it finds a match it returns the pointer, which gives the caller the whole record. When it fails, it returns NULL, a pointer to nothing.

insert() receives the three field values, builds a new Person with new, and stores its address in the next free cell. remove() searches by last name, frees the object with delete, and shifts the remaining pointers down. Our version also adds a destructor, ~ClassDataArray(), which runs automatically when the array object is destroyed and frees the people still stored.

Storing pointers pays off whenever items move. When remove() closes a gap, each step copies one pointer, just a few bytes, however big the Person objects are.

The classDataArray.cpp Program

The main() function inserts ten people, searches for one, removes three, and displays the rest.

Found Stimson, Henry, age 29
Adams, Henry, age 63
Hashimoto, Sato, age 21
Stimson, Henry, age 29
Velasquez, Jose, age 72
Lamarque, Henry, age 54
Vang, Minh, age 22
Creswell, Lucinda, age 18

The search for Stimson succeeds and prints his whole record, and after Evans, Smith and Yee are removed, the other seven people remain in the order they were inserted. This array is unordered, so find() searches linearly. You could keep the pointers sorted by last name and use binary search instead, as OrdArray does with numbers.

Big O Notation

You need a compact way to describe an algorithm's efficiency that doesn't depend on a particular computer. A statement such as "binary search is 50 times faster than linear search" doesn't work, because the ratio changes with the size of the array. For 10 items the two are nearly even, and for a million items binary search wins by a factor of 25,000. What matters is how the running time grows as the number of items, N, grows, and Big O notation is the standard way to describe that growth.

Insertion in an Unordered Array: Constant

Inserting into an unsorted array takes the same time however many items the array holds, because the new item always goes into the next empty cell. The time T is a constant, K.

T = K

K depends on things like the speed of the processor and how well the compiler translates the code. It doesn't depend on N.

Linear Search: Proportional to N

A linear search examines about N/2 items on average, so its time is

T = K × N/2

The 1/2 is just another constant, so it can be folded into K. Calling the combined constant K again gives T = K × N. Double the array and the search takes twice as long.

Binary Search: Proportional to log(N)

Binary search takes about log₂N steps, so T = K × log₂N. Here there's a further simplification. Logarithms in different bases differ only by a constant factor (you saw that log₂N = 3.322 × log₁₀N), so the base can be folded into K as well and left out, giving T = K × log N.

Don't Need the Constant

Big O notation goes one step further and drops K altogether, because K says nothing about how the time grows. What remains is written with a capital O, read as "order of." Insertion into an unsorted array is O(1), linear search is O(N), and binary search is O(log N). The simple sorts in Hours 4 and 5 will turn out to be O(N²), which means that doubling the number of items makes them take four times as long.

Big O notation. A way of describing how an algorithm's running time grows with the number of items N, ignoring constant factors. O(N) means the time is proportional to N.

Running times in Big O notation
AlgorithmRunning time
Linear searchO(N)
Binary searchO(log N)
Insertion in an unordered arrayO(1)
Insertion in an ordered arrayO(N)
Deletion in an unordered arrayO(N)
Deletion in an ordered arrayO(N)

Big O can't predict how many microseconds a particular run will take, but it shows how the time changes as N grows, which is what you need when choosing between algorithms for large amounts of data. For small N the constants can matter more, and a simple O(N) method might even beat an O(log N) one. As N grows, the algorithm with the slower growth rate always pulls ahead.

To feel the gap, suppose each step takes one microsecond and N is a million. An O(1) operation takes a microsecond, and an O(log N) one takes about 20 microseconds. An O(N) operation takes a full second. An O(N²) operation takes 1012 microseconds, which is more than 11 days.

Try it. Watch the growth rates pull apart.

  1. Set the slider to N = 10 and compare the step counts. They are all small.
  2. Move to N = 1,000 and then to N = 1,000,000. Watch O(N²) explode while O(log N) barely moves.
  3. At N = 1,000,000, compare the times for O(N log N) and O(N²) at one microsecond per step.

Why Not Use Arrays for Everything?

Arrays are simple, and an ordered array with binary search finds things quickly. They still fall short in two ways, which is why the book has 21 more hours to go.

The first is speed. An unordered array inserts in O(1) time but searches in O(N). An ordered array searches in O(log N) time but inserts in O(N). Either way, deletion takes O(N), because items must shift to fill the gap. For data that is searched, inserted and deleted often, neither kind of array is good enough.

The second weakness is the fixed size. You must choose an array's size when you create it, usually without knowing how much data will arrive. Guess too small and the array overflows; guess too big and the unused cells waste memory. A vector can grow, but growing means allocating a bigger block of memory and copying every item into it, which is slow.

Modern vectors soften this by growing their capacity by a constant factor, such as doubling it, so that over many push_back() calls the copying averages out to a small, constant cost per item. Any single growth step still copies everything, and inserting or deleting in the middle still shifts items.

What's needed is a structure that is fast at insertion, deletion and searching, and that grows and shrinks with the data. The book builds toward that goal step by step, with linked lists in Hour 8, binary trees in Hour 15, and hash tables in Hour 21. First, though, Hour 4 takes up a question that ordered arrays raise, which is how to put data into order in the first place.

Summary

  • An ordered array keeps its items sorted by key, which lets binary search find any item in O(log N) steps.
  • Binary search checks the middle of the remaining range and discards the half that can't hold the key, like guessing a number from 1 to 100 in at most seven tries.
  • Insertion into an ordered array must shift larger items up to make room, so it takes O(N) time. Deletion is O(N) in both kinds of array.
  • Ordered arrays suit data that is searched often and changed rarely, such as an employee database, and not fast-changing data such as a store's inventory.
  • s steps can search a range of r = 2s items, so s = log₂(r), rounded up. To get log₂ from log₁₀, multiply by 3.322.
  • Binary search needs only 20 comparisons for a million items and 30 for a billion.
  • Arrays can hold objects with several fields. Storing pointers to the objects makes shifting cheap, and one field, such as the last name, serves as the key.
  • Big O notation describes how running time grows with N, ignoring constants. From best to worst, the common cases are O(1), O(log N), O(N) and O(N²).
  • Arrays have slow operations and a fixed size, which motivates the linked lists, trees and hash tables to come.

Q&A

If binary search is so fast, why does insert() find its spot with a linear scan?
Because the shifting that follows takes about N/2 moves anyway. A binary search would cut the comparisons to about log₂N, but insertion would still be O(N) overall, so the simple loop keeps the code short without changing the Big O.
Does it matter which base I use for logarithms?
Not in Big O notation. Logarithms in different bases differ only by a constant factor, such as the 3.322 between base 10 and base 2, and Big O ignores constants. When you want an actual count of binary search steps, use base 2.
Big O throws away the constants. Couldn't an O(N) algorithm beat an O(log N) one?
For small N, yes, if its constant is much smaller. Growth rates always win in the end, though. Beyond some size the O(log N) algorithm is faster, and its lead keeps growing with N.
Why does ClassDataArray store pointers instead of Person objects?
Shifting pointers is cheap, whatever the size of the objects they point to. Pointers also let find() hand back the actual record rather than a copy, with NULL as a natural signal for "not found."

Quiz

  1. Using binary search, what is the largest number of guesses needed to find a number between 1 and 1,000?

    Answer

    10, because 210 = 1,024 is the first power of 2 that reaches 1,000.

  2. What is log₂ of 1,024?

    Answer

    10, since 2 raised to the 10th power is 1,024.

  3. What is the Big O running time of binary search? Of insertion into an ordered array?

    Answer

    Binary search is O(log N). Insertion into an ordered array is O(N), because about half the items must shift.

  4. Why does Big O notation drop constants?

    Answer

    Constants depend on the computer, the compiler and the details of the code, and they don't change how the time grows as N grows. Big O compares growth rates, which decide the winner once N is large.

  5. When is an ordered array a good choice, and when is it a poor one?

    Answer

    It's good when searches are frequent and insertions and deletions are rare, as in an employee database. It's poor when the data changes constantly, as in a store's inventory, because every insertion or deletion shifts about half the items.

  6. In insert(), why must the shifting loop start at the top and work down?

    Answer

    Moving the highest item first means each copy goes into a cell that is already free. Working upward from j would overwrite each item before it had been copied, destroying data.

Part I · Introducing Data Structures and Algorithms

Hour 4 The Bubble Sort

Putting data in order is one of the jobs computers do most often. This hour builds the simplest sorting method there is, the bubble sort, and uses it to show that every sort is made of tiny steps whose cost you can count.

In this hour you'll learn

  • Why sorting matters and how it ties in with binary search
  • How a program that sees only two items at a time can still sort
  • How the bubble sort works, first with baseball players and then in the Workshop applet
  • How to write the bubble sort in C++, line by line
  • What an invariant is and how it helps you trust an algorithm
  • Why the bubble sort runs in O(N²) time

Sorting

As soon as a database holds more than a handful of records, someone wants to see them in order. You might list names alphabetically, students by grade, customers by zip code, home sales by price, cities by population, countries by gross national product, or stars by how bright they appear. Underneath, each of these is the same job. You arrange the items by the value of one field, the key.

Sorting. Rearranging a group of data items so that their keys run in order, usually from smallest to largest.

Order also pays off when you search. In Hour 3 you saw that binary search needs only about 20 comparisons to find an item among a million, while a linear search needs about 500,000 on average. Binary search works only on data that is already in order, so sorting is often the preliminary step that makes fast searching possible.

Because sorting is so useful, and can take so long, it has been studied as closely as any problem in computing. Lafore splits the subject into two groups. This hour and the next cover two simple sorts, the bubble sort and the insertion sort. Part III comes back with the fast ones, mergesort in Hour 12 and quicksort in Hours 13 and 14.

The simple sorts run in O(N²) time, which makes them slow for large amounts of data. They still earn their place. They are easy to understand and easy to code, they are quick enough when N is small, and their ideas return inside the advanced sorts. The insertion sort, for example, is often used to finish off the work of quicksort.

Inventing Your Own Sorting Algorithm

Before looking at any code, picture a kids' baseball team. Nine players have wandered onto the field and stand in a line in no particular order. You want them lined up by height, with the shortest player on the left. Think for a moment about how you would do it.

You would probably solve it without much thought. You can see the whole line at once, so you spot the shortest child and wave her to the left end, then spot the next shortest, and so on. If a couple of players are only slightly out of place, you notice that too and fix it with a quick shuffle.

A computer program has no such overview. At any moment it can look at just two items and compare them. Lafore likens this to being very nearsighted. You can make out the two players standing right in front of you, and everyone else is a blur. Whatever method you invent has to be built out of these close-up looks.

That limitation reduces every sorting algorithm to two basic operations, repeated many times.

  1. Compare two items to see which one is larger.
  2. Swap two items, or in some algorithms copy one item to a new place.

The sorts in this book differ in which pairs they compare and in when and how they move items. That is why each sort gets measured by counting its comparisons and its swaps or copies. Those two counts decide how fast it runs. In a program, each player becomes a number in an array cell, and "taller" becomes "holds the larger value."

Bubble-Sorting the Baseball Players

The bubble sort is famous for being slow, and just as famous for being simple. Here is how it works on the team. Stand at the left end of the line. Compare the players in positions 0 and 1. If the one on the left is taller, have them trade places. If not, leave them alone. Then move one position to the right and compare the players in positions 1 and 2, and keep going this way until you reach the right end. Each step follows three rules.

  1. Compare two players.
  2. If the one on the left is taller, swap them.
  3. Move one position to the right.

Follow the tallest player during this first trip down the line. Until you reach him, nothing happens to him. Once you do, he is compared with each player to his right in turn, and he is always the taller of the two, so he is swapped at every step. He gets carried all the way to the right end, the way a bubble rises through a glass of soda. That is where the name comes from. On each trip down the line, the largest remaining item bubbles up to the end.

A first pass through a line of N players makes N−1 comparisons (8 for our nine players) and some number of swaps that depends on how the players started out. In our line, 7 of the 8 comparisons led to a swap. After the pass, only one player is sure to be in his final place, the tallest.

Now go back to the left end and start a second pass. This time you can stop one position earlier, because the rightmost spot is settled. The second pass carries the second-tallest player to the second spot from the right. The third pass settles the third-tallest, and so on. Each pass puts one more player in his final place and makes the next pass one step shorter. So the rules get one more line: when you reach the first player who is already sorted, go back to the left end and start over. When there are no unsorted players left, you are done.

Here is the whole sort of our team, pass by pass.

Bubble-sorting the nine players
PassComparisonsSwapsHeights after the pass
1873 7 5 1 8 4 6 2 9
2753 5 1 7 4 6 2 8 9
3643 1 5 4 6 2 7 8 9
4531 3 4 5 2 6 7 8 9
5411 3 4 2 5 6 7 8 9
6311 3 2 4 5 6 7 8 9
7211 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9
8101 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9
Total3622

The table shows two patterns that matter later. First, the number of comparisons in each pass is fixed: 8, then 7, then 6, down to 1, however the players happened to stand. Second, tall players travel right quickly, but short players creep left slowly. Watch the player of height 2, who starts at the right end. A taller player passing him can push him one place to the left, but that happens at most once per pass, so he needs seven passes to reach position 1.

Notice also that the line was in order after pass 7, yet the rules still call for pass 8. The plain bubble sort has no way to notice that it has finished early. It simply makes all of its passes.

The bubbleSort Workshop Applet

The Workshop applet for this hour draws the data as a row of vertical bars with random heights, one bar per item. Five buttons control it.

  • Run animates the whole sort from start to finish, so you can watch the bars shuffle into order.
  • Step carries out a single comparison, plus the swap if one is needed, each time you press it.
  • Size switches between 10 bars and 100 bars.
  • New makes a fresh set of random bars. Pressed again, it produces an inversely sorted set, tallest bar on the left, which is the hardest case for the bubble sort.
  • Draw repaints the bars, in case some of them fail to appear properly during a fast run.

While the sort runs, two arrows labeled inner and inner+1 point at the pair of bars being compared. A third arrow, labeled outer, marks the right edge of the unsorted part, and the bars beyond it are finished. Counters show how many comparisons and swaps have been made so far.

With 10 bars you can step through the sort, predict each decision before the applet makes it, and see the tallest remaining bar ride to the right on every pass. With 100 bars the single steps blur together and you see the big picture instead. The tallest bars stack up at the right end in a staircase that grows leftward, while the left side stays a jumble almost until the end. You also get a feel for how slow the bubble sort is once there is a real amount of data.

Try it. Our re-creation uses the same bar display, pointers and counters.

  1. Press Size until there are 10 bars, then press New.
  2. Press Step again and again. Before each press, look at the two bars under the pointers and predict whether they will swap.
  3. Watch the outer pointer. After each pass it moves one bar to the left, and the bars to its right never move again.
  4. Switch to 100 bars and press Run. Watch the tall bars collect on the right, and write down the final comparison and swap counts.
  5. Press Reverse to get inversely sorted bars, run the sort again, and compare the swap count with the random case.

Implementing C++ Code for a Bubble Sort

The program bubbleSort.cpp keeps its data in a class named ArrayBub, built along the same lines as the array classes of Hour 2. The private data is a vector<double> called v and an int called nElems that counts how many cells are in use. The public interface offers a constructor, insert(), display() and the new member, bubbleSort(). A private helper, swap(), trades two items.
