Most of the class is familiar. The constructor sizes the vector to hold max items and sets nElems to zero. insert() places a new value in the first free cell, the one at index nElems, and then bumps the count. display() prints the items in order.

swap() needs the temporary variable temp. If you wrote v[one] = v[two] straight away, the old value of v[one] would be overwritten before you had a chance to move it. So the function parks one value in temp, copies the other value across, and then copies the parked value into the second cell. It is private because it is a tool for the class's own use. Code outside the class has no reason to call it.

The whole algorithm is two nested for loops. The outer loop's variable, out, starts at the last occupied cell, nElems-1, and moves one cell to the left after each pass. Think of it as the right edge of the unsorted part. Every cell with a higher index than out already holds its final item.

The inner loop's variable, in, starts at 0 on every pass and climbs toward out. At each position it compares the neighbors v[in] and v[in+1], and if the left one is larger it calls swap() to exchange them. The loop stops when in reaches out, so the last comparison of each pass is between v[out-1] and v[out]. That final comparison delivers the largest unsorted item into cell out, just before out moves left.

Watch the loop limits. The outer loop must keep going while out > 0, because its last pass, with out equal to 1, is the one that compares cells 0 and 1. Stop at out > 1 and the two smallest items may be left in the wrong order. The inner test must be in < out. If in were allowed to reach out, the program would compare v[out] with v[out+1], which on the first pass is a cell beyond the end of the data.

Lafore makes swap() a separate function so that bubbleSort() stays short and readable. A function call costs a little time, though, and this one sits in the innermost loop, where it may run millions of times. A program tuned for speed would put the three lines of the swap directly inside the if statement.

The main() function tests the class. It creates an ArrayBub with room for 100 items, inserts ten numbers in scrambled order, displays them, sorts them and displays them again.

The first line of output is the data in the order it went in. The second is the same data after bubbleSort() has put it in ascending order.

77 99 44 55 22 88 11 0 66 33
0 11 22 33 44 55 66 77 88 99

Invariants

Many algorithms have a condition that stays true for as long as they run. Such a condition is called an invariant. Spotting it helps you see why an algorithm works, and it gives you something concrete to check when a program misbehaves.

Invariant. A condition that remains true at every stage while an algorithm runs.

In bubbleSort() the invariant is that the items to the right of out are sorted and sit in their final positions. At the start this holds in a trivial way, because out is at the right end and nothing lies beyond it. Each pass of the inner loop carries the largest unsorted item into cell out, and then out steps one cell left. So the sorted zone on the right grows by exactly one item per pass. Nothing inside that zone is ever touched again, since the inner loop never looks past out.

The invariant also explains why the array must be sorted when the outer loop ends. The last pass runs with out equal to 1, and afterward out drops to 0. By the invariant, every cell from 1 to the end now holds its final item. The single item left over, in cell 0, can only be the smallest, so the whole array is in order.

As a debugging aid, an invariant gives you a precise test. Suppose a sort you wrote leaves the data slightly scrambled. You could add a temporary call to display() at the end of each outer pass and check that the right-hand zone is sorted and unchanged from one pass to the next. The first pass where the check fails is where the bug does its damage.

Efficiency of the Bubble Sort

Counting comparisons is easy, because their number doesn't depend on the data. Take the ten numbers in bubbleSort.cpp. The first pass makes 9 comparisons, the second makes 8, and so on down to a single comparison on the last pass. The total is 9+8+7+6+5+4+3+2+1 = 45.

For N items the sum is (N−1)+(N−2)+(N−3)+…+1, which works out to N×(N−1)/2. For N = 10 that gives 10×9/2 = 45, as expected. When N is large, subtracting 1 hardly changes anything, so the bubble sort makes roughly N²/2 comparisons.

Swaps are fewer, since a swap happens only when a pair is out of order, and their number depends on the data. If the data is random, a swap is needed about half the time, so there are about N²/4 swaps. In the worst case, when the data starts out inversely sorted, every comparison finds a pair out of order and triggers a swap, which gives about N²/2 swaps. Data that is already sorted needs no swaps at all, but the comparisons still run their full course.

There is a neat way to see where N²/4 comes from. Call two items an out-of-order pair if the larger one stands to the left of the smaller one. Swapping two neighbors fixes exactly one such pair and creates no new ones, so the number of swaps always equals the number of out-of-order pairs at the start. N items form N×(N−1)/2 pairs, and in random data each pair is as likely to be out of order as in order, so about N×(N−1)/4 of them need fixing. Our nine players started with 22 out-of-order pairs, which is exactly the 22 swaps in the table earlier.

How the bubble sort's work grows with N
NComparisons, N×(N−1)/2Swaps on random data, about N²/4
104525
1004,9502,500
1,000499,500250,000
10,00049,995,00025,000,000

Both columns grow in proportion to N². Multiply N by 10 and the work goes up about 100 times. Big O notation ignores constant factors such as the 2 and the 4, so the bubble sort runs in O(N²) time. With 10,000 items it makes about 50 million comparisons. At one microsecond per comparison, that is 50 seconds spent just comparing, before a single swap is counted. You can feel this slowness in the Workshop applet with 100 bars.

There's a quick way to recognize this kind of cost in any code. When one loop is nested inside another, and each loop runs about N times (or N divided by some constant), the body of the inner loop executes roughly N×N times. In the bubble sort the outer loop makes N−1 passes and the inner loop averages about N/2 steps per pass. Nested loops of this kind are a strong hint that an algorithm is O(N²).

How much this matters depends on N. For a few dozen items the whole sort finishes in a blink, and its simplicity is a real virtue. For thousands of items it becomes a nuisance. A million items would need about 500 billion comparisons, close to six days at a microsecond each. The next hour shows a simple sort that does about half the work, and Part III shows sorts that are far faster.

A common improvement, not part of the book's version, lets the bubble sort quit early. Keep a flag that records whether the current pass made any swaps. If a pass finishes without a single swap, every neighboring pair is in order, so the array is sorted and the outer loop can stop. On data that is already sorted, this version makes one pass of N−1 comparisons and quits. On random data it rarely saves much, because some small item near the right end usually keeps the passes busy almost to the end.

Summary

  • Sorting arranges data items by a key. People need it to read data comfortably, and binary search needs it before it can work.
  • A program can compare only two items at a time, so every sort is built from two operations: comparing items, and swapping or copying them.
  • The bubble sort compares neighbors from left to right and swaps them whenever the left one is larger. Each pass carries the largest remaining item to the end of the unsorted part.
  • In the C++ version, the outer loop variable out starts at the right end and moves left one cell per pass. The inner loop variable in runs from 0 up to out-1.
  • The bubble sort's invariant is that the items to the right of out are sorted and in their final places.
  • The bubble sort always makes N×(N−1)/2 comparisons, about N²/2. It makes about N²/4 swaps on random data and about N²/2 on inversely sorted data.
  • Both counts grow as N², so the bubble sort is O(N²). Two nested loops that each run about N times are a sign of O(N²).
  • The bubble sort is the slowest sort in the book and also the simplest. It is a reasonable choice only for small amounts of data.

Q&A

Why learn the bubble sort at all, if it's the slowest sort in the book?
It is the easiest sort to understand, which makes it a good place to learn the vocabulary of sorting: passes, comparisons, swaps, invariants and O(N²) analysis. It is also short enough to write from memory. With only a few dozen items, a faster sort would save too little time to notice, and simple code is less likely to hide a bug.
Does the bubble sort run faster when the data is already sorted?
A little, but it stays O(N²). The book's version makes all N×(N−1)/2 comparisons whatever the data looks like, because nothing in its loops checks whether the job is done. Sorted data does save every swap. The early-exit flag described in the last Beyond the book note removes most of the wasted comparisons.
Which costs more, a comparison or a swap?
A swap. A comparison only looks at two values, while a swap moves data three times: into temp, from one cell to the other, and out of temp. When the items are large objects, those moves add up. The insertion sort in Hour 5 gains part of its speed by moving items with single copies instead of swaps.

Quiz

  1. How many comparisons does the bubble sort make when it sorts 10 items?

    Answer

    45. The passes make 9, 8, 7 and so on down to 1 comparison, and 10×9/2 = 45.

  2. After the first pass, what do you know for certain about the item at the right end?

    Answer

    It is the largest item in the array, and it is already in its final position. It bubbled there because it won every comparison once the pass reached it.

  3. What is the invariant of bubbleSort()?

    Answer

    The items to the right of out are sorted and in their final positions.

  4. How many swaps does the bubble sort make on 10 items that start in inverse order?

    Answer

    45. With inversely sorted data every comparison finds a pair out of order, so every one of the 45 comparisons leads to a swap.

  5. What is the bubble sort's Big O efficiency, and why?

    Answer

    O(N²). It makes N×(N−1)/2 comparisons and, on random data, about N²/4 swaps. Both are proportional to N², and Big O ignores the constant factors.

  6. What does the inner loop do during one pass?

    Answer

    It moves in from 0 up to out-1, comparing v[in] with v[in+1] and swapping them when the left one is larger. This carries the largest unsorted item into cell out.

Part I · Introducing Data Structures and Algorithms

Hour 5 The Insertion Sort

The insertion sort belongs to the same O(N²) family as the bubble sort, yet it does about half the work on random data and very little work on data that is almost in order. This hour shows how it works, how to code it, and how it handles objects and items with equal keys.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How the insertion sort works on the baseball team, using the idea of partial sorting
  • What the insertSort Workshop applet shows
  • How to write the insertion sort in C++
  • Why it beats the bubble sort, and when it runs in nearly O(N) time
  • How to sort objects, such as people ordered by last name
  • What makes a sort stable, and how the two simple sorts compare

Of the two simple sorts in this book, the insertion sort is the one you would actually choose. It still runs in O(N²) time, but on random data it finishes in roughly half the time the bubble sort needs, and its code is only a little more involved. It is also a favorite finishing tool for faster algorithms. In Hour 14 you'll see quicksort hand its last small jobs to an insertion sort.

Insertion Sort on the Baseball Players

Take the baseball team from Hour 4 again, nine players to be lined up by height. The insertion sort is easiest to understand if you join it in the middle, when the job is already partly done.

Partial Sorting

Imagine a chalk mark on the ground somewhere in the middle of the line. The players to the left of the mark are in order among themselves: each one is taller than the player to his left. They are not necessarily in their final positions, though. Some shorter players are still waiting to the right of the mark, and when their turn comes they will be squeezed in among the sorted group, pushing some of its members to the right.

Partially sorted. A group of items that are in order among themselves but not yet in their final positions, because other items may still be inserted between them.

This differs from the bubble sort. There, the sorted players at the right end were finished and never moved again. Here, the sorted group on the left is only a draft that keeps getting revised as new players join it.

The Marked Player

The player standing just to the right of the mark is the marked player. He and everyone to his right are still unsorted. The next job is to insert him into the right place in the partially sorted group, and it goes like this.

  1. The marked player steps out of the line and waits nearby. In a program, this means copying him to a temporary variable. His old spot is now an empty gap.
  2. Look at the sorted player just left of the gap. If he is taller than the marked player, he shifts one place right into the gap, and the gap moves one place left.
  3. Repeat step 2 with the next player to the left, and keep shifting until the player left of the gap is shorter than the marked player, or until the gap reaches the left end of the line.
  4. The marked player steps into the gap.

Inserting this one player took four comparisons (with heights 9, 8, 6 and 4) and three shifts. Now the partially sorted group is one player bigger and the unsorted group one player smaller. Move the mark one place to the right, so the player with height 2 becomes the marked player, and do it all again. He is shorter than everyone in the group except the player of height 1, so five players shift right and he lands in position 1.

The process has to start somewhere, and it starts in the simplest possible way. A single player is always in order with himself, so the mark begins just after the first player. The first marked player is the one in position 1. The sort ends when the mark has passed the last player and everyone has been inserted. If you run the whole insertion sort on the nine players from Hour 4, it takes 28 comparisons and 22 shifts, where the bubble sort needed 36 comparisons and 22 swaps.

The insertSort Workshop Applet

The insertSort applet uses the same bar display and the same buttons as the bubbleSort applet. With 100 bars, press Run and watch the left end of the display. A sorted slope forms there and widens steadily to the right, while the unsorted bars wait on the right side. Each new bar gets slipped into its place somewhere in the slope, which is the partial sorting you just saw with the players.

With 10 bars, Step shows the details. An arrow labeled outer marks the marked bar, playing the role of the chalk mark. An arrow labeled inner shows where the shifting is happening, which is the position of the gap. At the start of each pass the marked bar is copied into temp and drawn off to one side, apart from the others, while the taller bars shift right one at a time. When the gap reaches the right spot, the bar in temp is copied into it. The counters report comparisons and copies. Copies take the place of the bubble sort's swaps, and they are cheaper, as you'll see shortly.

Try it. Our re-creation lets you run both simple sorts and compare their counters.

  1. Choose the insertion sort, press Size until there are 10 bars, press New, and then Step. Watch the marked bar go to temp, the taller bars shift right, and the marked bar drop into the gap.
  2. Switch to 100 bars and press Run. Write down the comparisons and copies.
  3. Choose the bubble sort, press New for a fresh set of 100 random bars, and press Run. Compare its counts with the insertion sort's.
  4. Press Reverse and run each sort on inversely sorted bars. Notice how much of the insertion sort's advantage disappears.

Implementing the Insertion Sort in C++

The program insertSort.cpp uses a class named ArrayIns. It is the ArrayBub class from Hour 4 with two changes. The swap() helper is gone, because the insertion sort never swaps, and bubbleSort() is replaced by insertionSort(). The data (a vector<double> named v and the count nElems), the constructor, insert() and display() are unchanged.

The outer for loop moves out, the marker, from 1 up to the last occupied cell. It starts at 1 because a single item in cell 0 counts as partially sorted already. At the start of each pass the marked item v[out] is copied into temp, and in is set equal to out. From then on, in is the position of the gap.

The inner while loop does the shifting. It keeps going as long as two things are true: in is greater than 0, so a cell still exists to the left of the gap, and the item in that cell, v[in-1], is larger than temp. Each time around, the loop copies v[in-1] one cell right into the gap and decrements in, which moves the gap one cell left. When either condition fails, the gap is exactly where temp belongs, and the last statement of the pass copies temp into v[in].

The order of the two tests in the while condition matters. When in reaches 0, the test in>0 fails first, and the && operator stops right there without evaluating v[in-1]. With the tests the other way around, the loop would try to read v[-1], a cell that doesn't exist.

The insertion sort has an invariant of its own. At the end of each pass, once temp has been dropped into place, the items in cells 0 through out are partially sorted. After out moves right for the next pass, the same fact reads this way: every item with an index less than out is partially sorted. When out finally moves past the last cell, "every item to its left" means the whole array, so the whole array is sorted.

The main() function is the same as in bubbleSort.cpp, except that it creates an ArrayIns and calls insertionSort(). It inserts the same ten numbers, displays them, sorts them and displays them again, with the same result.

77 99 44 55 22 88 11 0 66 33
0 11 22 33 44 55 66 77 88 99

On these ten numbers the insertion sort makes 36 comparisons and 31 shifts. The bubble sort makes 45 comparisons and 31 swaps on the same data. The number of moves comes out the same, but each of the insertion sort's shifts is a single copy, while each of the bubble sort's swaps is three copies.

Efficiency of the Insertion Sort

Count the comparisons pass by pass. On the first pass the marked item can be compared with at most one item, on the second with at most two, and so on, up to at most N−1 comparisons on the last pass. The largest possible total is 1+2+3+…+(N−1) = N×(N−1)/2, the same sum you met with the bubble sort.

The difference is that the insertion sort usually stops early. On each pass, the while loop quits as soon as it finds an item smaller than temp. In random data that happens, on average, about halfway through the partially sorted group, so a typical pass makes only about half of its possible comparisons. That brings the total down to about N×(N−1)/4, roughly N²/4.

The number of copies is roughly the same as the number of comparisons, since nearly every comparison leads to one shift. A copy is much cheaper than a swap, which needs three copies. So on random data the insertion sort makes about half the comparisons of the bubble sort and moves its data far more cheaply. In practice it runs about twice as fast. It is still an O(N²) algorithm, though, because N²/4 grows as N² and the 4 disappears in Big O notation.

Already Sorted and Almost Sorted Data

The insertion sort shines when the data is already in order, or nearly so. If the data is sorted, the condition in the while loop is false the first time it is tested on every pass, because the item left of the gap is always smaller than temp. No shifting ever happens. The inner loop shrinks to a single comparison, the outer loop makes N−1 passes, and the whole sort takes N−1 comparisons. That is O(N) time.

If the data is almost sorted, with only a few items out of place, most passes still end after one comparison, and only the few misplaced items trigger any shifting. The running time is close to O(N). That makes the insertion sort an excellent choice for data that is only slightly out of order, such as a sorted list with a few new items tacked onto the end.

Inversely Sorted Data

The worst case is data in inverse order. Every marked item is smaller than everything in the partially sorted group, so every pass compares and shifts all the way to the left end. The sort makes every possible comparison, all N×(N−1)/2 of them, and a shift for each one. Lafore's verdict is that in this case the insertion sort runs no faster than the bubble sort, since both make the maximum number of comparisons.

Work done sorting 100 items
Starting orderBubble comparisonsBubble swapsInsertion comparisonsInsertion copies
Random4,950about 2,475about 2,570about 2,670
Already sorted4,950099198
Inversely sorted4,9504,9504,9505,148

The insertion sort's copy count includes two copies per pass for the marked item itself, one into temp and one back out, which is why sorted data still costs 2×99 = 198 copies. The random rows are averages. They sit slightly above N²/4 = 2,500 because every pass that stops early spends one extra comparison discovering where to stop.

Counting copies adds a detail to the worst-case verdict. On inversely sorted data the comparisons tie, but each bubble-sort swap costs three copies, so the bubble sort moves data 14,850 times for 100 items against the insertion sort's 5,148. On a real machine the insertion sort usually stays ahead even here.

Sorting Objects

For simplicity, the sorts so far have worked on plain numbers. Real programs usually sort records, such as personnel files, parts lists or customer accounts. Each record is an object with several fields, and one field serves as the key. The program objectSort.cpp shows how little the insertion sort has to change to handle this.

Its data items are objects of a class named Person, with three fields: a last name, a first name and an age. The key is the last name. The array class, ArrayInOb, keeps its data in a vector<Person*>, a vector of pointers to Person objects. Its insert() member creates each new person with new and stores the object's address in the next free cell, and its destructor deletes the objects when the array goes away.

The only real change is the comparison. Because v[in-1] and temp are pointers, the code uses the -> operator to call getLast() on the objects they point to. The two strings that come back are compared with >, which the C++ string class defines to compare alphabetically. Everything else is as before, except that temp is now a Person* and each shift copies a pointer.

Storing pointers keeps the moves cheap. Copying a pointer copies a single address. Copying a whole Person on every shift would mean copying two strings and an int. The sort rearranges the vector's cells, and the Person objects themselves never move.

Lexicographical Comparisons

The string class compares strings lexicographically, a formal word for the way a dictionary orders words. It compares the first characters of the two strings. If they differ, the string whose character comes earlier in the alphabet comes first. If they match, it moves on to the second characters, and so on. If one string runs out while every character so far has matched, the shorter string comes first, which is why "Smith" sorts ahead of "Smithers."

So "Smith" comes before "Stimson": both start with S, and at the second letter m comes before t. "Vang" comes before "Velasquez" because a comes before e. Two copies of "Smith" are equal, so neither is greater than the other, and that fact becomes important in the next section. Here is the program's output for ten people.

Before sorting:
   Evans, Patty (24)
   Smith, Doc (59)
   Smith, Lorraine (37)
   Smith, Paul (37)
   Yee, Tom (43)
   Hashimoto, Sato (21)
   Stimson, Henry (29)
   Velasquez, Jose (72)
   Vang, Minh (22)
   Creswell, Lucinda (18)
After sorting:
   Creswell, Lucinda (18)
   Evans, Patty (24)
   Hashimoto, Sato (21)
   Smith, Doc (59)
   Smith, Lorraine (37)
   Smith, Paul (37)
   Stimson, Henry (29)
   Vang, Minh (22)
   Velasquez, Jose (72)
   Yee, Tom (43)

The people come out in alphabetical order of last name. Look at the three Smiths. They went in as Doc, Lorraine and Paul, and they come out in that same order.

Another Feature of Sorting Algorithms: Stability

Sometimes it matters what a sort does with items whose keys are equal. Suppose a company's employee records are already sorted alphabetically by last name. Now you want them sorted by zip code, and within each zip code you want the employees to stay in alphabetical order. You need a sort that leaves equal-key items in the order it found them. Such a sort is called stable.

Stable sort. A sort that keeps items with equal keys in the same relative order they had before the sort.

Six employees, before and after a stable sort by zip code
Before: sorted by nameZipAfter: sorted by zipZip
Arnold30303Arnold30303
Brooks98101Castillo30303
Castillo30303Fong30303
Dunn60601Dunn60601
Ellis98101Brooks98101
Fong30303Ellis98101

In the table, the three employees in zip code 30303 come out as Arnold, Castillo, Fong, still alphabetical. An unstable sort could legally produce Fong, Arnold, Castillo instead, because all three have the same key, and you would have to sort each zip code by name all over again.

The bubble sort and the insertion sort are both stable, and the reason lies in their comparisons. The bubble sort swaps two neighbors only when the left one is strictly greater, so two equal items never trade places. The insertion sort shifts an item only while it is strictly greater than temp. When the marked item meets an equal key, the shifting stops and the marked item lands just to the right of it, the same side it started on. The three Smiths in objectSort.cpp kept their order for exactly this reason.

Stability hangs on a single character. Change > to >= in either sort's comparison and equal items begin trading places, so the sort is no longer stable, and it also wastes time moving items that were fine where they were.

Comparing the Simple Sorts

There is seldom a reason to use the bubble sort. Its one strength is that it is so simple you can write it from memory without a mistake. That makes it tolerable for a small amount of data when you need something working in a hurry. For anything bigger it is too slow.

The insertion sort is the best of the simple sorts. It is about twice as fast as the bubble sort on random data, and it is very fast on data that is almost sorted, where it approaches O(N). For a small amount of data, or data that is nearly in order already, it is usually the right choice.

Both sorts work in place. Besides the original array they need only one extra variable, temp, to hold an item while it moves, and they never need a second array. So memory is no concern with either one. When the amount of data grows large, turn to the advanced sorts of Part III, which are much faster.

The two simple sorts side by side
PropertyBubble sortInsertion sort
Comparisons, random dataabout N²/2about N²/4
Data moves, random dataabout N²/4 swaps (3 copies each)about N²/4 copies
Already sorted dataN²/2 comparisons, no swaps, O(N²)N−1 comparisons, O(N)
Inversely sorted dataN²/2 comparisons, N²/2 swapsN²/2 comparisons, N²/2 copies
Overall efficiencyO(N²)O(N²)
StableYesYes
Extra memoryOne temporary variableOne temporary variable

Summary

  • The insertion sort splits the data into a partially sorted group on the left and unsorted items on the right. Partially sorted items are in order among themselves but not yet in their final places.
  • Each pass copies the marked item into temp, shifts the larger items of the sorted group one place right, and drops temp into the gap that opens up.
  • In C++, the outer loop moves out from 1 upward. The inner while loop shifts items while in>0 and v[in-1] is greater than temp.
  • The invariant is that at the start of every pass, the items to the left of out are partially sorted.
  • On random data the insertion sort makes about N²/4 comparisons and about as many copies. That is roughly twice as fast as the bubble sort, but still O(N²).
  • Already sorted data needs only N−1 comparisons, O(N), and almost sorted data is nearly as fast. Inversely sorted data is the worst case.
  • Objects are sorted the same way as numbers. Only the comparison changes, for example to compare last names with the string class's lexicographical > operator.
  • A stable sort keeps equal-key items in their original order. Both simple sorts are stable, and both sort in place with a single extra variable.

Q&A

If the insertion sort is better, why did the book start with the bubble sort?
The bubble sort is easier to follow, so it was the natural place to introduce comparisons, swaps, passes, invariants and O(N²) analysis. With those ideas in hand, the insertion sort's extra machinery (the marker, temp and the shifting loop) is much easier to absorb.
Is the insertion sort ever slower than the bubble sort?
Not by comparisons. Its largest possible count, N×(N−1)/2, is the count the bubble sort always makes, so the insertion sort can at worst tie. It ties only when every marked item has to travel to the far left end of the sorted group, or next to it, as happens with inversely sorted data. On typical data it makes far fewer comparisons.
Why does objectSort.cpp store pointers instead of Person objects?
So that every shift copies a small address instead of a whole object with two strings inside it. The people stay put in memory, and only the vector of pointers gets rearranged.
When does stability matter?
When you sort by one key after another, as in the zip code example, or when the existing order of equal items means something, such as the order in which they arrived. If ties never matter to anyone, stability is irrelevant.

Quiz

  1. Why does the insertion sort run about twice as fast as the bubble sort on random data?

    Answer

    It makes about half as many comparisons (about N²/4 against N²/2), and it moves data with single copies where the bubble sort uses swaps of three copies each.

  2. What is the insertion sort's Big O efficiency on data that is already sorted, and why?

    Answer

    O(N). The while test fails immediately on every pass, so each of the N−1 passes makes one comparison and no shifts.

  3. What does "partially sorted" mean?

    Answer

    The items are in order among themselves, but they are not necessarily in their final positions, because unsorted items may still be inserted between them.

  4. In insertionSort(), what does temp hold during a pass?

    Answer

    The marked item, copied from v[out] at the start of the pass. It waits there while larger items shift right, and then it is copied into the gap.

  5. What does it mean for a sort to be stable, and are the two simple sorts stable?

    Answer

    A stable sort keeps items with equal keys in their original relative order. Both the bubble sort and the insertion sort are stable, because each moves an item past another only when it is strictly greater.

  6. How many comparisons does insertionSort() make on 10 items that are already in order?

    Answer

    9, one for each pass, since every while test fails at once.

Part II · Abstract Data Types

Hour 6 Stacks

Part II turns from structures that store data to structures that help a program get work done. The stack is the simplest of them. It lets you reach only the item you added most recently, and that single restriction turns out to be remarkably useful.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How the structures of Part II differ from arrays
  • What a stack is, and what push, pop and peek do
  • How to build a stack class in C++ on top of a vector
  • How a stack reverses the letters of a word
  • How a stack checks that braces, brackets and parentheses match
  • Why stack operations take O(1) time

A Different Way to Think About Data Structure

The arrays of Part I are the kind of structure you would use in a database program. They hold records that matter in their own right, such as personnel files, inventory lists or financial data, and they let you insert, search for and delete those records. The linked lists and trees of later hours serve the same kind of purpose. The structures of Part II (stacks, queues and priority queues) are different in three ways.

Programmer's Tools

In a database program, the data is the point. The records exist before the program runs and are still there after it stops. Stacks and queues are more often working tools. A program sets one up to help it carry out some task, such as checking a line of code, and throws it away when the task is finished. Their lifetimes are short compared with those of database records.

Restricted Access

In an array you can reach any item directly if you know its index, or find it by searching. In a stack or a queue, access is restricted. Only one item can be read or removed at any given moment: the top item of a stack, or the front item of a queue. The other items are there, but the structure's interface gives you no way to get at them until the accessible item has been removed. This limit is deliberate. It is exactly what makes these structures fit the jobs they do.

More Abstract

Stacks, queues and priority queues are also more abstract than arrays. They are defined mainly by their interface, the set of operations a user can perform, such as putting an item on a stack or taking one off. The mechanism underneath is hidden from the user. In this hour the stack is built on a vector, but it could just as well be built on a linked list, and a program that uses the stack would work the same way. This separation of interface from mechanism leads to the idea of abstract data types, the subject of Hour 9.

Understanding Stacks

A stack allows access to only one data item, the last one inserted. To reach the item below it, you must first remove the top one. Remove that, and the next one down becomes accessible, and so on down to the bottom.

Stack. A data structure in which only the most recently inserted item can be read or removed.

That sounds limiting, yet a great many algorithms depend on it. Later in this hour a stack checks whether the parentheses, braces and brackets in a line of source code are properly matched. Stacks are also used to parse arithmetic expressions such as 3×(4+5) and to traverse the nodes of a tree. They even live inside the microprocessor. When a program calls a function, the address to return to and the function's arguments are pushed onto a stack, and when the function returns they are popped off again.

Three Everyday Stacks

Lafore gives three everyday pictures of a stack. The first is a pile of mail. In many households, letters get tossed onto a pile on the hall table as they arrive. When someone finally sits down to deal with the pile, they start at the top: open the top letter, pay the bill or throw away the ad, then pick up the next letter down, and so on until the table is bare. The letter on top is always the newest arrival. The weakness of this system shows when the pile never quite gets finished, because the letters at the bottom can sit untouched for weeks.

The second picture is a workday full of interruptions. You are deep in a long project, call it A, when a coworker asks for help with task B. While you are helping with B, someone from accounting calls about matter C. You deal with C first, then go back to B, and only when B is done do you return to A. Each interruption is placed on top of the work already in progress, and each finished job uncovers the one beneath it.

The third picture is the spring-loaded stack of plates in a cafeteria. Clean plates are pressed down onto the top of the pile, and a diner can take only the top plate. When one is lifted off, the spring pops the next one up into reach.

Push, Pop and Peek

Stacks come with their own vocabulary. Placing an item on the top of the stack is called pushing it. Removing the top item is called popping it. Reading the top item without removing it is called peeking. The top of the stack is the position of the most recently pushed item, and the bottom is the position of the first item pushed. Because the last item in is always the first item out, a stack is called a LIFO structure.

LIFO. Short for last-in, first-out, the rule that the most recently inserted item is the first one removed.

The Stack Workshop Applet

The Stack Workshop applet draws an array of cells stacked vertically, with the bottom of the stack at the bottom of the display. An arrow labeled top points at the highest occupied cell. Four buttons do the work. New creates a new, empty stack. Push asks you for a value and places it on top. Pop removes the top item and shows you its value. Peek shows you the top item and leaves it where it is. If you try to push onto a stack that is already full, or pop from one that is empty, the applet shows a warning instead of carrying out the operation.

Try it. Our re-creation has ten cells and a top pointer.

  1. Press New to start with an empty stack.
  2. Type 20 in the key field and press Push. Do the same with 40, 60 and 80, and watch the top pointer climb.
  3. Press Peek. The value 80 is reported, and the stack does not change.
  4. Press Pop four times. The items come out as 80, 60, 40, 20.
  5. Press Pop once more to see the empty-stack message. Then push more than ten items to see what happens when the stack is full.

Implementing a Stack in C++

The program stack.cpp builds a stack class named StackX on top of a vector. It has three data members: maxSize, the most items the stack can hold; stackVect, a vector<double> whose cells hold the items, with the bottom of the stack at index 0; and top, the index of the item currently on top.

The constructor sizes the vector and sets top to −1. Since top is the index of the top item, an empty stack has no valid value for it, and −1 is a natural choice because it is one below the first cell. It also makes push() work the same way every time. The very first push raises top from −1 to 0 and stores the item in cell 0, exactly as later pushes raise it from 0 to 1, from 1 to 2, and so on.

The two key members each fit on one line, and the position of the ++ and -- operators is what makes them work. In push(), the expression ++top increments top before its value is used, so top first moves up to the empty cell above the old top item, and then the new item is stored there. In pop(), the expression top-- uses the current value of top first, so the item on top is fetched, and only then does top drop by one to point at the item below. Swap the operators around and both functions break: push() would overwrite the current top item, and pop() would return the wrong one.

peek() returns the top item without changing top. isEmpty() reports whether top is −1, and isFull() reports whether it has reached the last cell, maxSize-1.

Popping doesn't erase anything. After pop() the old value is still sitting in its cell, but it is no longer part of the stack, because top has moved below it. The next push() simply writes over it.

The main() function creates a stack with room for ten items, pushes four numbers, and then pops and prints items until the stack is empty.

80 60 40 20

The numbers come out in the reverse of the order in which they went in. The last item pushed, 80, is the first one popped. That is LIFO in action.

Error Handling

Notice that main() calls isEmpty() before every pop. StackX leaves that responsibility to the code that uses it: you are expected to call isFull() before pushing and isEmpty() before popping. The class itself doesn't check.

Skipping those checks leads to trouble that the compiler won't catch. Pushing onto a full StackX writes past the end of the vector, and popping an empty one reads from stackVect[-1]. Either may corrupt memory, crash the program, or quietly return garbage.

A sturdier class would do the checking inside push() and pop(). It could print an error message and refuse the operation, as in the version of push() below, or it could throw an exception and let the calling code decide what to do.

Stack Example 1: Reversing a Word

The first real job for a stack is a tiny one, reversing the letters of a word. Push the letters one at a time, from first to last, and then pop them all. Because a stack hands items back in the opposite order, the letters come out backward. Push the letters of "part" and you pop "trap."

The program reverse.cpp uses the same StackX class with one change: its vector holds char values instead of double, so push() takes a char and pop() and peek() return one. The work is done by a class named Reverser. Its constructor stores the input string, and its doRev() member function produces the reversed output string.

doRev() first creates a stack exactly as big as the word, since it will never hold more letters than that. The for loop pushes every character of input. The while loop then pops characters until the stack is empty, appending each one to output with the string class's += operator. The finished output is returned to the caller.

In main(), a loop asks the user for a word, hands it to a new Reverser, and prints the result. Pressing Enter without typing anything ends the program. A short session looks like this.

Type a word (Enter alone quits): part
Backward: trap
Type a word (Enter alone quits): drawer
Backward: reward
Type a word (Enter alone quits):

Stack Example 2: Delimiter Matching

A more serious job for a stack is checking the delimiters in a line of text, the way a compiler checks a program's source code. The delimiters are braces { and }, brackets [ and ], and parentheses ( and ). Each opening delimiter must be matched by a closing delimiter of the same type. The matching also has to respect nesting, which means a delimiter opened later must be closed before any delimiter opened earlier. The book uses these examples.

Which strings have correctly matched delimiters
StringVerdict
c[d]Correct
a{b[c]d}eCorrect
a{b(c]d}eWrong. The ] arrives while ( is the delimiter waiting to be closed.
a[b{c}d]e}Wrong. Nothing matches the final }.
a{b(c)Wrong. Nothing matches the opening {.

Opening Delimiters on the Stack

The checking program reads the string one character at a time, from left to right, and follows three rules.

  • When it reads an opening delimiter, it pushes it onto a stack.
  • When it reads a closing delimiter, it pops the top item off the stack and checks that the two delimiters are the same type. A mismatch is an error. If the stack is empty, there is nothing to pop, which is also an error, because the closer has no partner.
  • Any other character is ignored.

When the whole string has been read, the stack should be empty. If an opening delimiter is still on it, that delimiter was never closed, and that is an error too. Here is the stack at every step of checking the correct string a{b(c[d]e)f}.

The stack while checking a{b(c[d]e)f}
Character readActionStack, bottom to top
aignore(empty)
{push{
bignore{
(push{ (
cignore{ (
[push{ ( [
dignore{ ( [
]pop [, a match{ (
eignore{ (
)pop (, a match{
fignore{
}pop {, a match(empty)

A stack suits this job because the delimiter that must close next is always the one opened most recently, and that is exactly the one on top. The stack remembers the open delimiters in the very order in which they have to be checked. Simply counting openers and closers of each type would not be enough. The string ([)] has one of each and is still wrong. With a stack the algorithm stays short and clear, which is what Lafore means by calling the stack a conceptual aid.

C++ Code for Delimiter Matching

The program brackets.cpp uses the char version of StackX again. The checking is done by a class named BracketChecker, which stores the input string. A small private helper, matches(), reports whether an opener and a closer are the same kind, and the check() member function does the rest.

check() creates a stack as long as the input string, because in the worst case every character could be an opener. The for loop reads the characters, and a switch statement sorts each one into one of three cases. Openers are pushed. For a closer, the code first checks for an empty stack, which means the closer has no partner. Otherwise it pops the most recent opener into chx and asks matches() whether the two belong together. Every other character falls through to the default case and is ignored.

After the loop, anything still on the stack is an opener that was never closed. The flag ok records whether any error turned up, so the function can announce success when none did. The error messages give the position of the offending character, counting from 0. As in reverse.cpp, main() repeatedly asks for a line of text and hands it to a new BracketChecker. Here is a session using the book's examples.

Type a string (Enter alone quits): a{b(c[d]e)f}
Delimiters match
Type a string (Enter alone quits): a{b(c]d}e
Error: ] at position 5 does not match (
Type a string (Enter alone quits): a[b{c}d]e}
Error: } at position 9 has no opener
Type a string (Enter alone quits): a{b(c)
Error: { is never closed
Type a string (Enter alone quits):

Try it. Our re-creation shows the stack after every character it reads.

  1. Type a{b(c[d]e)f} in the expression field and press Check. Compare the stack at each step with the table above.
  2. Press Reset, enter a{b(c]d}e, and use Step to move one character at a time. Before each press, predict what the stack will hold. Watch what happens at the ].
  3. Try a[b{c}d]e}. The final } arrives when the stack is already empty.
  4. Try a{b(c). The string runs out with { still on the stack.
  5. Try ([)] to see why counting delimiters is not enough.

Efficiency of Stacks

Items are pushed onto and popped off a StackX in constant time, O(1). Neither operation compares items or moves any other item. A push adds one to top and copies one item into a cell. A pop copies one item out and subtracts one from top. The time doesn't depend on how many items the stack holds, whether that is three or three million. peek(), isEmpty() and isFull() are O(1) as well.

That speed, together with the tiny interface, is why stacks turn up inside so many algorithms. The price is the restricted access, since you can never reach an arbitrary item. For a programmer's tool that is usually a good trade.

Summary

  • The structures of Part II are programmer's tools with short lives. They restrict access to one item at a time, and they are more abstract than arrays, being defined by their interface while the mechanism underneath stays hidden.
  • A stack allows access only to the most recently inserted item. It is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) structure.
  • Push places an item on top, pop removes the top item, and peek reads the top item without removing it.
  • StackX keeps its items in a vector. top holds the index of the top item and starts at −1. push() uses ++top and pop() uses top--.
  • StackX expects its user to call isFull() before pushing and isEmpty() before popping. A sturdier class would check inside push() and pop().
  • Pushing the letters of a word and then popping them reverses the word.
  • To check delimiters, push each opener, pop and compare on each closer, ignore everything else, and make sure the stack ends up empty.
  • Push and pop take O(1) time, no matter how many items the stack holds.

Q&A

Why use a stack when an array can do everything a stack can do, and more?
Because the restriction helps. A stack's interface states the intent of the code and makes it impossible to disturb items that should stay put. When a problem is LIFO by nature, as delimiter matching is, the stack version of the solution is shorter and easier to trust than one that juggles array indices.
What happens if I pop an empty StackX?
It reads the nonexistent cell stackVect[-1] and leaves top at −2. The result is unpredictable. Always call isEmpty() first, or build the check into pop().
Does a stack have to be built on an array?
No. A linked list works just as well, and the program using the stack can't tell the difference, because it sees only push, pop and peek. Hour 9 builds the same stack both ways.
Can a stack hold things other than numbers?
Yes. reverse.cpp and brackets.cpp simply change the vector's element type to char, and the same idea works for strings or objects. C++ templates can generalize a class like this to any type, although this hour's programs keep things simple by editing the type directly.

Quiz

  1. What does LIFO stand for, and what does it mean?

    Answer

    Last-in, first-out. The item inserted most recently is the first one removed.

  2. You push 1, 2 and 3 onto an empty stack and then pop until it is empty. In what order do the items come out?

    Answer

    3, 2, 1.

  3. What is the value of top in an empty StackX, and why that value?

    Answer

    −1. An empty stack has no top item, so top sits one below the first cell. The first push then raises it to 0 and stores the item in cell 0.

  4. While checking a{b(c, what is on the stack after the last character has been read?

    Answer

    { at the bottom and ( on top. The string ends with both still open, so the checker reports an error.

  5. What is the Big O efficiency of push and pop?

    Answer

    O(1). Each one changes top and copies a single item, whatever the size of the stack.

  6. What should the delimiter checker do when it reads a closing delimiter and the stack is empty?

    Answer

    Report an error. The closing delimiter has no opening delimiter to match.

Part II · Abstract Data Types

Hour 7 Queues and Priority Queues

In a queue the first item in is the first item out, just as in a line of people waiting their turn. A priority queue bends that rule so the most urgent item always leaves first. This hour builds both in C++ and shows the wraparound trick that keeps an array-based queue fast.

In this hour you'll learn

  • What a queue is and where queues turn up
  • Why an array-based queue needs to wrap around, and how a circular queue works
  • How to write a Queue class in C++
  • What a deque is
  • What a priority queue is, and how an ordered array implements one
  • How fast each of these structures is

Queues

In Britain, a queue is a line of people waiting for something. In computing, a queue is a data structure that works like such a line. It resembles a stack, except that the first item inserted is the first item removed. That rule is called FIFO, for first-in, first-out. A stack, as you saw in Hour 6, works the other way around, last-in, first-out.

Queue. A data structure in which items leave in the same order they arrived, so the first in is the first out (FIFO).

Think of the line at a movie theater. The first person to join it is the first to buy a ticket and go in, and the last person to join is the last one served. Nobody at the back gets served before the people ahead of them.

Queues turn up wherever things must wait their turn. Airplanes wait in a queue on the taxiway for their turn to take off. Data packets wait in queues for their turn to be sent across the Internet. A printer keeps a queue of print jobs and prints them in the order they arrived. Even your keyboard has one. A typeahead buffer holds your keystrokes when you type faster than a program can read them, so none are lost and they reach the program in the order you typed them.

Queues are also used to model real-world waiting lines in simulation programs, such as customers lining up at a bank teller's window or cars waiting at a toll booth. By watching how long the simulated lines grow, a planner can estimate, say, how many tellers are needed.

The names of the queue operations aren't standardized. Adding an item is called insert, put or enqueue, and the item goes in at the back of the queue, called the rear or tail. Taking an item out is called remove, get or dequeue, and the item comes from the front or head. Peek reads the front item without removing it. This hour uses insert, remove and peek, with front and rear.

The Queue Workshop Applet

The Queue Workshop applet shows a queue stored in an array, with one arrow labeled front and another labeled rear. Ins asks for a value and adds it at the rear. Rem removes the item at the front and shows its value. Peek shows the front item without removing it. New creates a new, empty queue.

Watch the arrows as you work. Each insertion moves rear up one cell, and each removal moves front up one cell and leaves an empty cell behind it. After a few insertions and removals, the whole group of items has crept up the array, with empty cells below front. Soon rear reaches the top cell, and the queue seems unable to take another item, even though there are empty cells at the bottom of the array.

One cure would be to shift all the remaining items down to the bottom of the array after every removal, the way a line of people shuffles forward when the person at the head leaves. That works, but it is slow, because every removal would have to move every item still waiting. The better cure is to let the arrows wrap around.

A Circular Queue

When rear reaches the last cell and another item arrives, rear jumps back to cell 0. As long as the queue isn't full, that cell is free, because its item has already left. In effect the two ends of the array are joined into a ring. This is called wraparound, and a queue that uses it is called a circular queue, or a ring buffer.

Circular queue. A queue stored in an array whose front and rear indices wrap around from the last cell to the first, so the space freed by removals gets reused.

After rear wraps around, it sits below front, the reverse of the usual arrangement. The items now form two broken sequences. One runs from front up to the top of the array, and the other continues from cell 0 up to rear. Front wraps around in the same way. When it moves past the last cell, it continues from cell 0, and the queue becomes one unbroken sequence again.

Try it. Our re-creation uses a ten-cell circular array.

  1. Press New. Type a key and press Ins, and repeat until all ten cells are full. Watch rear climb one cell at a time.
  2. Press Rem three times. Front moves up, leaving empty cells at the bottom.
  3. Insert two more items. Rear wraps around to cell 0 and then to cell 1.
  4. Keep removing items until front reaches the top cell, then remove one more and watch front wrap around as well.
  5. Press Peek at any point to read the front item without removing it.

C++ Code for a Queue

The program queue.cpp implements a circular queue in a class named Queue. Besides the vector queVect and its capacity maxSize, the class keeps three integers: front, the index of the item that will leave next; rear, the index of the item that arrived most recently; and nItems, the number of items waiting.

The constructor starts front at 0 and rear at −1, the same trick StackX used for top. The first insertion moves rear up to 0 and stores the item there, which is also where front is waiting.

insert() handles wraparound before it does anything else. If rear is already in the last cell, it is set back to −1, so the increment that follows carries it to cell 0. Then rear moves up one cell, the item is stored there, and nItems goes up by one. remove() works the other way around. It copies the item at front into temp and moves front up one cell. If that step has carried front past the last cell, it wraps back to 0. Then nItems goes down by one and the saved item is returned.

peekFront() returns the front item without changing anything, and isEmpty(), isFull() and size() simply consult nItems. Like StackX, the class trusts its user. It is up to the calling code to check isFull() before inserting and isEmpty() before removing.

The nItems field makes the full and empty tests trivial. A queue can be written without it, but then you must tell full from empty by comparing front and rear, and that is trickier than it looks. In a completely full array and in an empty one, rear ends up in the same place relative to front, one cell behind it once wraparound is allowed for. The usual fix is to make the array one cell bigger than the largest number of items the queue will ever hold, so a full queue always has one empty cell.

The main() function gives the wraparound code a workout. It creates a queue with only five cells and then runs this sequence.

The first four insertions fill cells 0 to 3. The three removals take out 10, 20 and 30, leaving only 40, with front at cell 3. Inserting 50 uses the last cell, cell 4. Then 60 arrives while rear is in the last cell, so rear wraps to cell 0, and 70 and 80 follow into cells 1 and 2. The queue is now completely full, with rear below front.

The final loop removes and prints items until the queue is empty. front takes 40 from cell 3 and 50 from cell 4, wraps to cell 0, and continues with 60, 70 and 80. The items leave in exactly the order they arrived.

40 50 60 70 80

Efficiency of Queues

As with a stack, items can be inserted into and removed from a queue in O(1) time. insert() and remove() each touch a single cell and adjust a couple of integers, and neither depends on how many items are waiting. The wraparound tests add only a constant amount of work. The circular arrangement is what makes this possible. The shift-everything-down cure mentioned earlier would have made every removal an O(N) operation.

Deques

A deque, pronounced "deck," is a double-ended queue. You can insert items at either end and delete them from either end. The operations might be called insertLeft() and insertRight(), and removeLeft() and removeRight().

Deque. A double-ended queue, which allows insertion and deletion at both ends.

A deque can stand in for either of the other two structures. If you use only insertLeft() and removeLeft(), or only the two right-hand operations, it behaves like a stack. If you insert at one end and remove at the other, it behaves like a queue. That makes the deque more versatile than either one, although in practice it is used less often than stacks and queues.

Priority Queues

A priority queue is a more specialized structure. Like an ordinary queue it has a front and a rear, and items are removed from the front. The difference is that the items are kept in order by key value, so the item with the lowest key is always at the front, ready to be removed next. Each new item is inserted at whatever position keeps the order, which may be anywhere from the rear to the front. In the book's version a lower key means a higher priority. Some implementations work the other way around and keep the highest key at the front, but the idea is the same.

Priority queue. A queue whose items are kept in order by key, so that the item with the highest priority (here, the lowest key) is always the next one removed.

Lafore's picture is a person who sorts incoming mail by urgency. As each letter arrives, it goes into the pile at the position its importance deserves, with the most urgent letters on top and the ones that can wait at the bottom. Whenever there is time to deal with mail, the top letter is taken first, so the most urgent matter always gets handled first. Compare that with the plain mail stack of Hour 6, where the newest letter was always on top regardless of what it said.

Priority queues are workhorses in system software. In a preemptive multitasking operating system, the programs waiting to run sit in a priority queue, so the highest-priority program is the one that gets the processor next. Priority queues also appear in many graph algorithms and simulation programs.

The PriorityQ Workshop Applet

The PriorityQ applet implements a priority queue with an ordered array. The item with the smallest key sits at the top of the array, in the highest occupied cell, and larger keys lie toward cell 0. Keeping the smallest item at the top makes removal fast, since Rem simply takes the top item and nothing else has to move.

Insertion is the slow part. When you press Ins with a new key, the applet must find the right place for it. Starting at the top, it shifts every item smaller than the new one up one cell to make room, and then puts the new item into the opening. This is the same shifting you saw in the insertion sort in Hour 5. Peek shows the front item without removing it, and New creates a new, empty priority queue.

No wraparound is needed. The front of the queue is always at cell nItems−1 and the rear is always at cell 0, so the items never creep along the array the way they do in an ordinary queue.

Try it. Our re-creation keeps the smallest key at the top, where it is removed first.

  1. Press New, then insert 30, 50, 10, 40 and 20 in that order. Watch where each key lands.
  2. Insert a key larger than all the others, then one smaller than all the others. Count how many items have to move each time to make room.
  3. Press Peek to see the front item, then press Rem repeatedly. The keys come out smallest first.

C++ Code for a Priority Queue

The program priorityQ.cpp defines a class named PriorityQ. It keeps its items in a vector named queVect in descending order, with the largest item in cell 0 and the smallest in the top occupied cell, nItems-1. There are no front and rear fields, because those positions never change.

insert() starts with j at the front of the queue, the top occupied cell. As long as the item in cell j is smaller than the newcomer, that item is copied up one cell and j moves down. When the loop meets an item that is not smaller, or runs off the bottom of the array, the opening is at cell j+1, and the new item goes there. If the queue is empty, j starts at −1, the loop never runs, and the item lands in cell 0. The book's listing treats the empty queue as a separate case, but the loop covers it naturally.

remove() could hardly be simpler. It reduces nItems by one and returns the item in cell nItems, which is the smallest one. The item stays in the cell, just as a popped item stays in a stack's vector, but it is no longer part of the queue. peekMin() returns the same item without removing it.

The main() function inserts 30, 50, 10, 40 and 20, in that scrambled order, and then removes and prints items until the queue is empty. Along the way the vector passes through the states [30], [50, 30], [50, 30, 10], [50, 40, 30, 10] and finally [50, 40, 30, 20, 10]. The items come out smallest first, whatever order they went in.

10 20 30 40 50

Efficiency of Priority Queues

In this implementation, insertion runs in O(N) time. On average a new item has to move past about half the items in the queue, and in the worst case past all of them. Deletion takes O(1) time, because the smallest item is always waiting in the top cell, and taking it needs no shifting at all.

The Part II structures so far, built on arrays
StructureInsertRemoveItem removed
StackO(1)O(1)The newest
Queue (circular array)O(1)O(1)The oldest
Priority queue (ordered array)O(N)O(1)The one with the lowest key

For a small priority queue, or one where items are inserted rarely, the ordered array is a perfectly good choice, and it is easy to write. When the queue holds many items and insertion speed matters, a different structure does better.

The standard choice for a large priority queue is a heap, a tree-shaped structure usually stored in an array, which this book does not cover. A heap performs both insertion and removal in O(log N) time. The C++ Standard Library's priority_queue container adapter is built on a heap.

Summary

  • A queue is a first-in, first-out (FIFO) structure, so items leave in the order they arrived. A stack, by contrast, is LIFO.
  • Queues model waiting lines of all kinds, from moviegoers and airplanes to print jobs, network packets, keystrokes and simulated bank customers.
  • Items are inserted at the rear of a queue and removed from its front. Peek reads the front item without removing it.
  • In an array, removals leave empty cells behind front. A circular queue lets front and rear wrap around to cell 0 so that space gets reused.
  • The Queue class tracks front, rear and nItems. The item count makes the full and empty tests simple.
  • Queue insertion and removal both take O(1) time.
  • A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends. Used one way it acts as a stack, and used another way it acts as a queue.
  • A priority queue keeps its items in order by key, so the item with the lowest key is always removed first. In the ordered-array version, insertion is O(N) and removal is O(1).

Q&A

Why would I ever use a deque?
When a problem needs to add or remove items at both ends, or when you want one general-purpose class that can serve as a stack in one part of a program and as a queue in another. Most problems need only one of the simpler behaviors, which is why deques are used less often than stacks and queues.
Why not shift the items down after each removal instead of wrapping around?
Because every removal would then move every item still in the queue, turning an O(1) operation into an O(N) one. Wraparound gets the same reuse of space for the price of an if statement.
What happens when two items in the priority queue have equal keys?
In PriorityQ, shifting stops at the first item that is not smaller than the newcomer, so a new item settles in front of any equal items and leaves before them. If items of equal priority should leave in arrival order, change the test to queVect[j] <= item, so the newcomer moves behind its equals.
Can a queue be built on something other than an array?
Yes. A linked list makes a natural queue, since items can be added at one end and removed from the other without any wraparound. Hour 9 returns to this when it looks at abstract data types.

Quiz

  1. What is the difference between FIFO and LIFO, and which structure uses each?

    Answer

    FIFO (first-in, first-out) removes items in the order they arrived; a queue works this way. LIFO (last-in, first-out) removes the newest item first; a stack works this way.

  2. Starting with an empty queue, you insert 1, 2 and 3, remove one item, insert 4, and then remove all the remaining items. In what order do the items come out?

    Answer

    1 comes out first, and then 2, 3 and 4.

  3. Why is a queue stored in an array usually made circular?

    Answer

    Removals leave empty cells at the bottom of the array. Letting front and rear wrap around to cell 0 reuses those cells, so rear doesn't get stuck at the top of the array while space is free, and no items ever have to be shifted.

  4. What can a deque do that a queue can't?

    Answer

    It can insert and remove items at both ends. That lets it act as a stack or as a queue, depending on which operations you use.

  5. What are the Big O efficiencies of insertion and removal in the ordered-array priority queue?

    Answer

    Insertion is O(N), because items must be shifted to make room. Removal is O(1), because the smallest item is always in the top occupied cell.

  6. In queue.cpp, why is 40 the first number printed?

    Answer

    Items 10, 20 and 30 were removed earlier, so 40 is the oldest item still in the queue when the final loop begins.

Part II · Abstract Data Types

Hour 8 Linked Lists

An array makes you pick its size up front, and it makes you shuffle items around whenever you insert or delete in the middle. A linked list ties its items together with pointers, so it grows and shrinks one item at a time and never has to move anything.

In this hour you'll learn

  • What a link is, and how pointers chain links into a list
  • How the LinkList Workshop applet inserts, finds and deletes links
  • How to write a simple linked list in C++ with insertFirst(), removeFirst() and displayList()
  • How to find a link with a given key and unhook it from the middle of the list
  • How linked lists compare with arrays in speed and in memory use

So far the array has done all the work in this book. It was a small database in Hour 2, an ordered array in Hour 3, and the storage inside the stacks and queues of Hours 6 and 7. Arrays have two built-in weaknesses. Inserting or deleting an item in the middle means shifting every item beyond it, which is slow. And you must fix an array's size when you create it, before you know how much data will turn up.

After the array, the linked list is probably the most widely used general-purpose storage structure, and it cures both problems. Items are added and removed by changing a pointer or two, so nothing ever shifts. The list is always exactly as long as the data it holds. You can use a linked list almost anywhere you would use an array. The main exception is a program that keeps asking for items by position number, as in "give me item 517". An array answers that in one step. A list can't.

This hour builds the basic machinery. In Hour 9 you'll use it to rebuild stacks and queues, and in Hour 10 you'll meet sorted lists and doubly linked lists.

Understanding Links

In a linked list, every data item is packed inside an object called a link. The link holds the data plus one extra member, a pointer to the next link in the list. The links can be scattered anywhere in memory. What turns them into a list is that each one knows the address of the link that follows it.

Link. An object that holds a data item together with a pointer to the next link. A linked list is a chain of links. (Many books call a link a node.)

The list as a whole is represented by a second, very small object of class LinkList. It holds a single pointer, pFirst, which points to the first link. The first link's pointer leads to the second link, the second link's pointer leads to the third, and so on down the chain. The last link's pointer holds NULL, the special value that means "points nowhere". That NULL is how code recognizes the end of the list.

A Class That Refers to Itself

Here is the declaration of a link that carries two pieces of data, an integer and a floating-point number.

The interesting member is pNext. Its type is Link*, a pointer to an object of the very class being declared. A class like this is called self-referential. That sounds like a riddle, but the compiler is perfectly happy with it, because pNext is only an address. The compiler knows how much room an address takes, so it can lay out a Link without knowing anything else about it. What a class can't do is contain a complete object of its own type, since that inner object would contain another one, and that one another, forever.

A link can hold any data at all: numbers, strings, a complete object such as the Person records of Hour 3, or a pointer to such an object. The list code never looks at the data except to compare keys. The part it cares about is pNext. The book keeps its links small, with one or two numbers, so the pointer logic stays easy to follow.

Relationships Instead of Positions

In an array, every item sits at a numbered position. If you want the item at index 7, the index takes you there in a single step, however big the array is. A linked list has no position numbers at all. An item belongs to the list only because the link in front of it points to it. So the one and only way to reach an item is to start at pFirst and follow the pointers, link by link, until you arrive.

Lafore compares this to tracking someone down through other people. Say you're looking for Bob. You ask Harry, who has no idea, though he thinks Jane might know. Jane remembers seeing Bob go off with Sally. Sally tells you she gave Bob a ride to Peter's office, and that is where you finally find him. You couldn't have gone straight to Peter's office, because you didn't know about it until Sally told you. Each person knew only the next step.

A linked list works the same way. To reach the fourth link, you must pass through the first, second and third, because only the third link knows where the fourth one is. Keep this picture in mind. It explains both the strengths and the weaknesses of lists that you'll see at the end of this hour.

The LinkList Workshop Applet

The book's LinkList Workshop applet draws each link as a small rectangle showing its key, with an arrow from each rectangle to the next. A long list won't fit across the screen, so the links wrap onto several rows, like words on a page. Four buttons drive it.

  • Ins asks for a key, makes a new link holding it, and puts that link at the beginning of the list. The new link's arrow points to the link that used to be first. In an unsorted list, inserting at the front is the fastest insertion there is, because there's nothing to search for and nothing to move.
  • Find asks for a key, then moves a red arrow from link to link, starting at the first one, until it reaches the link with that key. You can watch the cost of a list search directly. The farther along the key sits, the longer the arrow travels.
  • Del asks for a key, finds its link the same step-by-step way, and then removes it. On screen, the arrow leaving the link before the deleted one swings around to point at the link after it, so the chain simply skips over the deleted link.
  • New starts a fresh list. It asks how many links you want and whether the list should be sorted or unsorted. Sorted lists are the topic of Hour 10, so stay with unsorted lists for now.

Our re-creation below works the same way. It also labels the two pointers the C++ code uses while it walks the list, pCurrent and pPrevious. You'll meet both of them in the code later this hour.

Try it. Watch how each operation changes the chain.

  1. Press New for a fresh list.
  2. Type 33 in the Key field and press Ins. The new link appears at the front and points to the old first link.
  3. Type a key that sits near the end of the list and press Find. Count the steps pCurrent takes to get there.
  4. Press Del with the same key. Notice that pPrevious trails one link behind pCurrent, and that removing the link changes only one arrow.
  5. Try Find with a key that isn't in the list. The search visits every link before it gives up.

Implementing a Simple Linked List

The first program, linkList.cpp, supports only three operations: insert a link at the front of the list, remove the link at the front, and display the whole list. That sounds modest, but those three are exactly what a stack needs, as you'll see in Hour 9. The program has two classes, Link and LinkList, plus a main() that tries them out.

The Link Class

The complete Link class adds a constructor and a function that displays the link's data.

The constructor copies its two arguments into the data members and sets pNext to NULL. A brand-new link isn't part of any list yet, so it shouldn't point anywhere. The list code will set pNext when it hooks the link into the chain. displayLink() prints the two data items inside braces, such as {22, 2.99}. The members are public so the list class can reach them directly, which keeps the code short.

The LinkList Class

The LinkList class needs only one data member, the pointer to the first link. Here is the class with everything except displayList(), which comes a little later.

The constructor sets pFirst to NULL, so every new list starts out empty, and isEmpty() simply checks for that value. getFirst() hands out the address of the first link. As you'll see, main() uses it to look at a link before removing it.

The insertFirst() Member Function

insertFirst() is the heart of the class. It creates a new link with new, which returns the address of the new object, and keeps that address in pNewLink. Then it makes two pointer assignments.

  1. pNewLink->pNext = pFirst; The new link's pNext now points at whatever link used to be first. If the list was empty, pFirst was NULL, so the new link's pNext becomes NULL. That is correct, because in a one-link list the new link is also the last.
  2. pFirst = pNewLink; The list now begins at the new link.

The order of the two assignments matters. Suppose you did the second one first. pFirst would hold the new link's address, and nothing would remember where the old first link was. The other assignment would then make the new link point to itself, and the rest of the list would be adrift in memory with no pointer leading to it.

Before you overwrite a pointer in list code, make sure the address it holds is saved somewhere else, or is no longer needed. Otherwise the links it led to are lost for good.

However long the list is, insertFirst() does the same two assignments. Its running time doesn't depend on N at all, so it's O(1).

The removeFirst() Member Function

removeFirst() undoes what insertFirst() did. The first link's pNext holds the address of the second link, so the statement pFirst = pFirst->pNext; reroutes pFirst past the first link to the second. The old first link is now outside the chain.

In Java, an object that nothing points to is eventually cleaned up by the garbage collector. C++ has no garbage collector. Memory you get with new stays allocated until you hand it back with delete, so removeFirst() has to delete the old link itself. If it didn't, every removal would leave a dead link lying in memory, a problem called a memory leak. That's why the function starts by saving the old link's address in pTemp. Once pFirst moves on, pTemp is the only remaining record of where that link lives, and delete needs the address.

removeFirst() assumes the list has at least one link. On an empty list, pFirst->pNext follows a NULL pointer and the program crashes. Like pop() in the StackX class of Hour 6, it leaves the checking to the caller, who should call isEmpty() first.

The displayList() Member Function

To display the list, the program has to visit every link in turn, starting at the first.

Traverse. To visit every item of a data structure in order, usually to do something at each one, such as display it or add it to a total.

The function keeps a pointer called pCurrent that starts at pFirst. Each time around the loop, it displays the link that pCurrent points to and then moves on with pCurrent = pCurrent->pNext;. That statement is the basic step of all list code. It replaces the address in pCurrent with the address stored inside the current link, which is the address of the next link. When pCurrent steps past the last link it picks up that link's NULL, and the loop ends. For an empty list, pCurrent is NULL from the start, so the loop body never runs.

The main() Function

main() builds a list of four links, displays it, and then takes the links off the front one at a time until the list is empty.

List (first-->last): {88, 8.99} {66, 6.99} {44, 4.99} {22, 2.99}
Removed {88, 8.99}
Removed {66, 6.99}
Removed {44, 4.99}
Removed {22, 2.99}
List (first-->last):

The list comes out in the reverse of the order the links went in. Each insertFirst() puts its link in front of all the others, so the last one inserted (88) ends up first. The loop then removes links from the front until isEmpty() reports true, and the final display shows an empty list. A list used this way behaves like a stack, where the last item in is the first one out. Hour 9 builds on exactly that.
