main() displays each link before it calls removeFirst(). Once delete has run, pTemp still holds the old address, but that memory no longer belongs to the list. Using such a dangling pointer might print garbage or crash the program.

Finding and Removing Specified Links

The second program, linkList2.cpp, keeps everything from the first one and adds two member functions. find() searches the list for a link with a given key. remove() searches for a link with a given key and takes it out of the list, wherever it happens to be. Both treat iData as the key. Like displayList(), they are declared inside the class and defined after it.

The find() Member Function

find() is a traversal that can stop early. pCurrent starts at pFirst and steps along the chain, exactly as in displayList(). The loop keeps going as long as there is a current link and its key isn't the one wanted. It stops for one of two reasons: pCurrent points to a matching link, or pCurrent has become NULL because the search ran off the end of the list. Either way, returning pCurrent gives the caller the right answer, the address of the link or NULL for "not found".

The order of the two tests matters. C++ evaluates && from left to right and stops as soon as the result is known. When pCurrent is NULL, the left test fails and the right test, which reads pCurrent->iData, never runs. That is what you want, because following a NULL pointer crashes the program. Lafore's version checks for the end of the list in a slightly different way. Inside the loop, it looks at whether the current link's pNext is NULL before stepping forward, and returns NULL if it is. Both versions visit the same links. Ours also copes with an empty list, where pFirst itself is NULL.

Once find() has handed you a link, inserting a new link right after it takes just two assignments, the same pattern as insertFirst(). Point the new link's pNext at the found link's successor, then point the found link's pNext at the new link.

The remove() Member Function

Removing a link from the middle of a list is trickier than removing the first one. The pointer that has to change belongs to the link before the one being deleted. In a singly linked list you can only move forward, so once pCurrent has reached the target there's no way to step back. The fix is to carry a second pointer, pPrevious, that trails one link behind pCurrent all the way down the list.

Each time the loop advances, pPrevious takes over pCurrent's old value, and then pCurrent moves on to the next link. When the loop ends, one of three things is true.

  • pCurrent is NULL. No link holds the key, so remove() returns false and changes nothing.
  • pCurrent is the first link. There is no previous link to fix, so pFirst moves to the second link, just as in removeFirst().
  • pCurrent is somewhere further along. The assignment pPrevious->pNext = pCurrent->pNext; makes the previous link point to the link after pCurrent, so the chain now skips over it.

In the last two cases the link is out of the chain, and delete pCurrent returns its memory. Notice that the list never moves anything. However long the list is, removing a link changes exactly one pointer once the link has been found.

The main() Function of linkList2.cpp

This main() builds the same four-link list as before, displays it, and then tries the two new functions.

List (first-->last): {88, 8.99} {66, 6.99} {44, 4.99} {22, 2.99}
Found link with key 44
Removed link with key 66
List (first-->last): {88, 8.99} {44, 4.99} {22, 2.99}

The search for 44 compares three keys (88, 66 and 44) before it succeeds. The removal of 66 compares two keys and then changes a single pointer, the one inside the 88 link.

The Efficiency of Linked Lists

Speed

Insertion and deletion at the beginning of a linked list are about as fast as operations get. insertFirst() and removeFirst() each change a pointer or two, and the number of steps doesn't depend on how many links the list holds. Both are O(1).

Finding a particular link, deleting it, or inserting a new link next to it is another matter, because you have to find the link first, and that means walking from pFirst. On average the target is halfway down the list, so a search takes about N/2 comparisons. For a list of 10,000 links, that's around 5,000. Big O drops the constant, so these operations are O(N), the same as searching an unsorted array.

Even so, the list beats the array at deletions and at insertions in the middle, because once the spot is found, nothing has to move. To delete an item halfway through a 10,000-item array, you compare about 5,000 keys and then shift about 5,000 items down one cell to close the gap. In a list you compare about 5,000 keys and change one pointer. When the items are large objects, copying one takes much longer than comparing a key, and the list's advantage grows.

Unsorted array and linked list compared
OperationUnsorted arrayLinked list
Insert a new itemO(1), at the endO(1), at the front
Remove the first itemO(N), the rest shift downO(1)
Find an item by keyO(N), about N/2 comparisonsO(N), about N/2 comparisons
Delete an item by keyO(N), N/2 comparisons plus N/2 movesO(N), N/2 comparisons and no moves
Reach the item at position iO(1), use the indexO(N), walk i links
SizeFixed when createdGrows and shrinks one link at a time

Memory

A linked list uses exactly as much memory as it needs. Each insertion allocates one link and each removal frees one, and the list can keep growing until the computer runs out of memory. You never have to guess its size in advance.

An array's size is fixed when you create it, which leads to one of two problems. If the array is too small, it overflows when more data arrives than you planned for. If it's too large, the unused cells waste memory. A vector (Hour 2) eases the problem because it can grow, but growing is expensive. The vector has to grab a new, larger block of memory, usually about twice as big, and copy every item into it. Right after it grows, much of the new block sits unused.

The list pays for its flexibility in two ways. First, there is no random access. You can't jump to the 500th link; you have to walk there. That also rules out algorithms that leap into the middle of the data, such as the binary search of Hour 3. Second, every link carries a pointer as well as its data. When the data is a single small number, the pointer can double the memory each item needs.

So linked lists shine when the amount of data is hard to predict and insertions and deletions are frequent. Arrays win when you know roughly how many items you'll have and you need to reach them by position.

Today's C++ Standard Library has ready-made linked lists. std::forward_list is singly linked like this hour's LinkList, and std::list is doubly linked like the lists of Hour 10. They call new and delete for you. Writing your own, as in this hour, is still the best way to understand what they do and what they cost.

Summary

  • A linked list is a chain of link objects. Each link holds a data item and a pointer, pNext, to the next link.
  • The LinkList object holds only pFirst, the address of the first link. The last link's pNext is NULL, and in an empty list pFirst itself is NULL.
  • Class Link is self-referential, because it contains a pointer to an object of its own type.
  • Items in a list have relationships instead of positions. The only way to reach an item is to follow the chain from the start.
  • insertFirst() points the new link at the old first link, then points pFirst at the new link. The order matters, and the whole job is O(1).
  • removeFirst() reroutes pFirst to the second link and must delete the old link, because C++ has no garbage collector.
  • To traverse a list, start a pointer at pFirst and repeat pCurrent = pCurrent->pNext until it becomes NULL.
  • Finding or removing a link with a given key takes about N/2 comparisons, O(N). Removal needs pPrevious so it can fix the link before the target.
  • Compared with arrays, lists insert and delete without moving anything and never run out of room early. They give up fast access by index and spend extra memory on a pointer per link.

Q&A

When should I choose a linked list over an array?
Choose a list when you can't predict how much data you'll have, and when insertions and deletions are common, especially at the front or in the middle. Choose an array when you know roughly how many items there will be and you need to reach them by index, for example to run a binary search.
Why do I have to delete links myself?
Every link was created with new, and in C++ that memory stays allocated until someone calls delete. If you lose the last pointer to a link without deleting it, the memory leaks. For the same reason, a complete list class would normally have a destructor that walks the list and deletes every remaining link when the list itself goes away.
Can a link hold more than a couple of numbers?
Yes. A link can hold a string, a whole object such as a Person record, or a pointer to an object stored elsewhere. With large objects the pointer approach is common, because the link stays small and the object never has to be copied.
Is following pointers slow?
Each step is fast, just one memory read. The trouble is the number of steps. Reaching the 500th link takes 500 of them, while an array index gets there in one. That is the price of storing relationships instead of positions.

Quiz

  1. What does pFirst contain when a list is empty?

    Answer

    NULL. The constructor puts it there, and isEmpty() tests for it.

  2. insertFirst() performs pNewLink->pNext = pFirst; and then pFirst = pNewLink;. What goes wrong if you swap them?

    Answer

    The address of the old first link is overwritten before it has been copied into the new link. The new link ends up pointing to itself, and the rest of the list is lost (and its memory leaks).

  3. Why does remove() need a pPrevious pointer as well as pCurrent?

    Answer

    Deleting a link means changing the pNext of the link before it. A singly linked list can't move backward, so the code keeps pPrevious one step behind pCurrent to remember that earlier link.

  4. What are the Big O times of insertFirst() and of find()?

    Answer

    insertFirst() is O(1), a fixed two assignments. find() is O(N), about N/2 comparisons on average.

  5. Name one advantage and one disadvantage of a linked list compared with an array.

    Answer

    Advantages: insertion and deletion move no items, and the list grows and shrinks as needed. Disadvantages: there's no fast access by index (so no binary search), and each link needs extra memory for its pointer.

  6. Starting with an empty list, you call insertFirst() with the keys 10, 20 and 30, in that order, and then call removeFirst() once. Which keys does displayList() show?

    Answer

    20 then 10. The list was 30, 20, 10, and removeFirst() took away 30.

Part II · Abstract Data Types

Hour 9 Abstract Data Types

The same stack or queue can be built on an array or on a linked list, and the program that uses it can't tell which. This hour does exactly that, and then uses the result to explain abstract data types, which describe a data structure by what it does and keep the details of how it does it out of sight.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How to build a stack on a linked list
  • How a double-ended list keeps a pointer to its last link, and what that buys you
  • How to build a queue on a double-ended list
  • What data types, abstraction and abstract data types are
  • How ADTs help you design programs, and why "abstract" is a relative term

An abstract data type, or ADT, is a way of looking at a data structure that concentrates on what it does and ignores how it does it. You have already used two of them. The stack of Hour 6 offered push, pop and peek, and the queue of Hour 7 offered insert, remove and peek. Behind those operations, both classes kept their items in arrays. Nothing about the operations themselves requires an array, though.

The first half of this hour rebuilds the stack and the queue on top of the linked lists from Hour 8. The programs that use them hardly change, and they can't tell the difference. Once you've watched that happen, the idea of an ADT stops being vague, and the second half of the hour looks at what ADTs are and how they help you design software.

A Stack Implemented By a Linked List

Look back at insertFirst() and removeFirst() from Hour 8. One puts an item at the front of the list, and the other takes the front item off. If you call the front of the list the top of a stack, those two functions are push and pop. The linkStack.cpp program makes that connection official.

It uses a slimmed-down version of the Hour 8 list. Each link carries a single double called dData. And removeFirst() now returns the value it removes, because a stack's pop() has to hand the item back to the caller.

The one new detail is in removeFirst(). It copies the link's data into key before it deletes the link, since after delete the data is gone. The traversal in displayList() is the same walk as in Hour 8, squeezed into a for loop: start at pFirst, stop at NULL, and follow pNext at each step.

Now the stack itself. Class LinkStack contains a LinkList object as its only data member, and every one of its member functions is a one-liner that passes the job to the list.

Stack (top-->bottom): 40 20
Stack (top-->bottom): 80 60 40 20
Stack (top-->bottom): 40 20

Each push puts a new link at the front of the list, so the most recent item is always first, which is to say on top. The two pops remove 80 and then 60, the last two items pushed, leaving 40 and 20. LinkStack doesn't even need a constructor of its own. When a LinkStack is created, C++ automatically runs the constructor of its theList member, which sets pFirst to NULL.

Now compare this main() with the one in Hour 6. The push and pop calls are exactly the same. The only change is the line that creates the stack. StackX needed a size, as in StackX theStack(10);, while LinkStack theStack; needs none, because a linked stack never fills up until the computer runs out of memory. For the same reason, LinkStack has no isFull(). Everything else about the storage is invisible to the user of the class. That invisibility is the whole point of this hour.

Both versions push and pop in O(1) time. In the array version, each operation moves top and reads or writes one cell. In the list version, each one changes a pointer or two and calls new or delete.

Double-Ended Lists

A double-ended list is an ordinary linked list with one addition. Besides pFirst, the list object keeps a second pointer, pLast, that points to the last link.

Double-ended list. A linked list that keeps pointers to both its first and its last link, so either end can be reached in one step.

With pLast available, you can attach a new link at the end of the list directly. In an ordinary list you'd first have to walk all N links to find the end, an O(N) job. With pLast it takes a couple of assignments, O(1). Inserting at the end is exactly what a queue needs, as you'll see in the next section.

The firstLastList.cpp program implements a double-ended list. Its Link class is the one-number link from linkStack.cpp.

Each function has to take care of a special case, the moment when pFirst and pLast must change together.

  • insertFirst() works as before, except that when the list is empty, the new link is also the last link, so pLast must point to it too. The emptiness test has to come first, while pFirst still tells the truth about the old list.
  • insertLast() makes the old last link's pNext point to the new link and then moves pLast to the new link. When the list is empty there's no old last link to attach to, so the new link becomes the first link instead. The new link's own pNext is already NULL, set by the Link constructor, which correctly marks it as the end.
  • removeFirst() works as before, except when it removes the only link. Then the list becomes empty, and pLast must become NULL as well. Otherwise it would go on pointing at a link that has just been deleted.

The main() in firstLastList.cpp inserts 22, 44 and 66 at the front, inserts 11, 33 and 55 at the end, and displays the list. Then it removes the first two items and displays the list again.

List (first-->last): 66 44 22 11 33 55
List (first-->last): 22 11 33 55

The items inserted at the front pile up in reverse order (66 44 22), while the items inserted at the end line up in the order they arrived (11 33 55). The two calls to removeFirst() take away 66 and 44.

A double-ended list does nothing for removing the last link, though. To remove it you would have to make the next-to-last link's pNext NULL and move pLast back to that link. The only way to find the next-to-last link is to walk from pFirst, which is O(N), because the pointers lead only forward. The doubly linked list of Hour 10 solves this by giving every link a backward pointer as well.

Implementing a Queue Using a Linked List

A queue inserts items at the rear and removes them from the front. A double-ended list does both of those in O(1) time: insertLast() adds a link at the end, and removeFirst() takes one off the front. So linkQueue.cpp wraps a FirstLastList inside a LinkQueue class, in the same way LinkStack wrapped a LinkList. Each program in this hour is a self-contained file with its own copy of the list class. In this program's copy, displayList() prints only the items, and displayQueue() puts a label in front of them.

The main() for this program inserts 20 and 40 and displays the queue, inserts 60 and 80 and displays it again, and then removes two items and displays what's left.

Queue (front-->rear): 20 40
Queue (front-->rear): 20 40 60 80
Queue (front-->rear): 60 80

Items leave in the order they arrived. The first two in, 20 and 40, are the first two out. Compare this with the array-based Queue class of Hour 7. That class needed a fixed size, a count of items, and wraparound code to move front and rear back to the start of the array. None of that is needed here. The front of the queue is simply pFirst, the rear is pLast, and the list grows and shrinks as items come and go.

The applet below makes the "same interface, different insides" idea visible. One set of buttons drives two implementations at once: an array version like StackX and Queue on one side, and a linked-list version like LinkStack and LinkQueue on the other. Every push or insert goes to both, so you can compare what each one does with the same request.

Try it. Give both implementations the same work.

  1. With the toggle set to Stack, type a few values and press Push after each one. The array version fills cells upward from the bottom, while the list version adds each new link at the front.
  2. Press Pop a few times. Both versions hand back the same items in the same order, last in, first out.
  3. Switch the toggle to Queue. Use Ins and Rem. The array version moves its front and rear markers through its cells, while the list version adds links at pLast and removes them at pFirst.
  4. Keep inserting. The array version has a fixed number of cells, and the list version has no such limit.

Data Types and Abstraction

With two stacks and two queues in hand, it's time to look at the idea behind them. The phrase "abstract data type" has two halves, and each is worth taking apart.

Data Types

The phrase data type is used first for built-in types such as int and double. When you declare an int, you get more than a place to keep a number. You get a set of values, the whole numbers within a certain range (on a typical 32-bit system, from about −2.1 billion to about +2.1 billion). You also get a set of operations that are allowed on those values, such as +, −, *, / and comparisons. The operations are part of the type. You can use % to find the remainder when one int is divided by another, but C++ won't let you apply % to a double.

Data type. A set of values, together with the operations that can be performed on those values.

Classes let you create data types of your own. A class says what data its objects hold and which member functions may operate on that data, just as the language defines the values and operators of an int. A stack class is a new data type whose operations are push, pop and peek. A queue class is a data type with insert, remove and peek. Once such a class is written, you can declare a stack as easily as you declare an int.

A data type is values plus operations
TypeValuesOperations
intWhole numbers in a fixed range+ − * / %, comparisons
doubleNumbers with fractional parts+ − * /, comparisons (no %)
StackA collection of items, only the top one reachablepush, pop, peek, isEmpty
QueueA collection of items in arrival orderinsert, remove, peek, isEmpty
ListA collection of items in linear orderinsert, delete, read an item

Abstraction

To abstract something is to consider it apart from its detailed specification or implementation. An abstraction keeps the essential idea and leaves out the machinery. When you drive a car, you think of it as something that speeds up when you press the pedal. You don't think about fuel pressure or valve timing, even though they are what make the car move.

In object-oriented programming, then, an abstract data type is a class considered without regard to its implementation. It is a description of the data the class holds, plus a list of the operations that can be carried out on that data and instructions on how to use them. Users of the class know what each operation does. They don't know how it does it, and they don't need to.

Abstract data type (ADT). A data type described only by its data and the operations allowed on it, without saying how it is implemented.

The stack is a good example. For the main() in Hour 6 and the main() earlier in this hour, a stack was simply "something you push items onto and pop them off, where the last item pushed is the first one popped". That description is the ADT. StackX, with its vector, and LinkStack, with its linked list, are two different implementations of the same ADT.

The Interface

The set of operations an ADT offers to the outside world is called its interface. In a C++ class, the interface is the list of public member functions, along with any rules for using them, such as "check isEmpty() before you call pop()". Everything private belongs to the implementation: the data members, plus any helper functions the class uses internally. A user who sticks to the interface never depends on the private parts, which is why those parts can be replaced.

ADT Lists

The word "list" is used for an ADT too. A list, sometimes called a linear list, is a group of items arranged in a linear order, one after another. Typical operations are insert an item, delete an item, and read an item (for example, the item at a given place in the order). Don't confuse this list ADT with the linked list. A list ADT can be implemented with an array or with a linked list, in the same way that a stack can.

Using ADTs as a Design Tool

The ADT idea is a practical help when you design a program. Before you decide how to store your data, decide what you need to do with it. Perhaps the program needs the most recently added item, or items in the order they arrived, or fast search by key. Those needs define the operations, and the operations define the ADT: a stack, a queue, or something else.

Only after the operations are settled do you choose an implementation, and you choose the one that makes the most frequent operations fast. Then you write the rest of the program against the interface alone. Two good things follow. The design stays clean, because the code that uses the data structure contains no storage details. And you can change the implementation later without touching that code. If an array-based stack turns out to overflow in real use, you can drop in the linked-list version, and the calling code keeps working, as you saw with LinkStack.

For stacks and queues, Big O doesn't settle the choice, because both versions do their main operations in O(1) time. The deciding question is usually how much data to expect.

  • Use an array when you know in advance roughly the largest number of items you'll need to hold, and you want speed. The array version is quicker in practice, because it doesn't call new and delete for every item, and it spends no memory on pointers.
  • Use a linked list when you can't predict how many items there will be. It never fills up, and it uses memory only for the items it actually holds.
Two ways to implement a stack or a queue
Array (StackX, Queue)Linked list (LinkStack, LinkQueue)
Main operationsO(1)O(1)
SizeFixed when created, so check isFull()Grows as needed
Memory per itemJust the itemThe item plus a pointer
Extra work per operationNoneA new or a delete

Abstract Is a Relative Term

Abstraction comes in degrees. Take the priority queue of Hour 7. As an ADT, it is defined by its operations: insert an item, and remove the item with the smallest key. In Hour 7 you implemented it with an ordered array. It could also be implemented with a heap, a structure this book doesn't cover. From the priority queue's point of view, the ordered array is just the implementation. But the ordered array is itself an abstraction, built on something lower down, the computer's memory, which is a long row of numbered storage locations.

So stacks, queues and priority queues are more abstract than arrays and linked lists, which in turn are more abstract than raw memory. Which of these you call "the ADT" and which "the implementation" depends on where you're standing. To someone writing a program that schedules jobs, the priority queue is the ADT and the array is a hidden detail. To the person writing the PriorityQ class, the array is a tool with its own interface of cells and indices. Even the linked list can be seen as an ADT, with an interface of insertFirst(), find() and remove() that hides how its pointers are arranged.

Summary

  • A stack can be built on a linked list. LinkStack's push() calls insertFirst() and its pop() calls removeFirst(), so the front of the list is the top of the stack.
  • Code that uses LinkStack looks the same as code that uses the array-based StackX, except that a linked stack needs no size and never fills up.
  • A double-ended list keeps a pLast pointer as well as pFirst, so inserting at the end is O(1). Removing the last link is still slow, because the next-to-last link can't be reached without a walk.
  • A queue can be built on a double-ended list, inserting with insertLast() and removing with removeFirst(). No wraparound or item count is needed.
  • A data type is a set of values plus the operations allowed on them. Classes let programmers create new data types.
  • An abstract data type is a class considered without regard to its implementation: its data and its operations. The operations form its interface.
  • A list (linear list) is an ADT too, and it can be implemented with an array or a linked list.
  • When designing, settle the operations first, then pick the implementation that makes the frequent ones fast. Use arrays when the maximum size is known and speed matters, and linked lists when the amount of data is unpredictable.
  • Abstraction is relative. A priority queue is built on an array, which is built on memory, and what counts as the ADT depends on your point of view.

Q&A

If the array versions are faster, why build stacks and queues on lists at all?
Because you often can't know how many items a stack or queue will have to hold. An array sized too small overflows, and one sized too large wastes memory. The list version always has room for one more item and uses memory only for what it holds. When the size is known, the array is the better choice.
Is a linked list a data structure or an ADT?
It depends on your point of view. Seen from LinkStack, the linked list is the implementation, a data structure. Seen from its own users, it is described by operations such as insertFirst() and find(), which makes it an ADT with its own interface.
Could I build a queue on an ordinary, single-ended list?
Yes, but one of the two operations would be slow. Either you insert at the end, which means walking to the end first, or you remove from the end, which means walking to the next-to-last link. Both walks are O(N). The pLast pointer of a double-ended list is what makes both queue operations O(1).
Why doesn't LinkStack have a constructor?
It doesn't need one. When a LinkStack is created, C++ automatically constructs its theList member, and the LinkList constructor sets pFirst to NULL. That empty list is exactly the state an empty stack should start in.

Quiz

  1. What is an abstract data type?

    Answer

    A data type considered without regard to how it is implemented. It is described by the data it holds and the operations (the interface) that can be performed on that data.

  2. Which LinkList member function does LinkStack's push() call?

    Answer

    insertFirst(). The front of the list serves as the top of the stack, and pop() calls removeFirst().

  3. Why is a double-ended list a good base for a queue?

    Answer

    Its pLast pointer lets insertLast() add items at the rear in O(1) time, and removeFirst() takes them from the front in O(1) time. Those are exactly the two operations a queue needs.

  4. What is a data type?

    Answer

    A set of values plus the operations that can be performed on them. For int, the values are whole numbers in a range and the operations include +, −, *, / and %.

  5. When would you choose an array-based stack over a linked-list stack?

    Answer

    When you know in advance about how many items the stack must hold and you want speed. The array avoids a new or delete for every operation and needs no pointers.

  6. In FirstLastList's removeFirst(), why must pLast be set to NULL when the only link is removed?

    Answer

    Otherwise pLast would keep pointing at the link that was just deleted. The list would be empty at the front yet claim to have a last link, and any code that followed pLast (to peek at the rear of a queue, say) would be using a dangling pointer. Setting both pointers to NULL keeps the empty list consistent.

Part II · Abstract Data Types

Hour 10 Specialized Lists

Two variations on the linked list solve two different problems. A sorted list keeps its items in key order as they arrive, which makes it a handy priority queue and even a way to sort. A doubly linked list gives every link a backward pointer as well as a forward one, so you can travel in both directions and remove the last link as easily as the first.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How a sorted linked list keeps its items in order, and how it compares with a sorted array
  • How to insert a new item into a sorted list in C++
  • How a sorted list can sort an array (the list insertion sort), and what that costs
  • How a doubly linked list works: traversal in both directions, and insertion and deletion anywhere
  • When the extra pointers of a doubly linked list are worth their price

The lists of Hour 8 and Hour 9 kept their links in whatever order you happened to insert them, and they could only be walked from front to back. This hour lifts both limits. First you'll keep a list in order by key, and then you'll give each link a second pointer so the list can be walked backward too.

Sorted Lists

In the lists you've seen so far, the order of the links had nothing to do with their keys. In a sorted list, the links are kept in order by key, usually ascending, with the smallest key first.

Sorted list. A linked list whose links are always kept in key order. Each new link is inserted at its proper place instead of at one end.

Most operations work just as before. Finding a link, or deleting a specific one, still means walking from the front and comparing keys along the way. The change is in insertion. A new link can't simply go at the front. It must go in its proper place, just after the last link with a smaller key and just before the first link with a larger one. So every insertion now includes a search.

Sorted Lists and Sorted Arrays

A sorted list does much the same job as the ordered array of Hour 3, and each one has an edge over the other.

  • Insertion is faster in the list. Both structures have to find the right spot. After that, the array must shift every larger item up one cell to open a gap, while the list just changes two pointers. The list also never fills up.
  • Searching is faster in the array. Binary search works by jumping straight to the middle of the remaining range, and that needs random access by index. A list can only be searched link by link, so its searches stay at O(N).

So a sorted list is a good substitute for a sorted array when insertions are frequent or the amount of data is hard to predict. It also makes a simple priority queue, because the smallest item is always at the front, where it can be removed in one step. And, as the next section shows, it can be used to sort an array.

The LinkList Workshop Applet in Sorted Mode

The LinkList Workshop applet from Hour 8 can build a sorted list. When you press New, it asks whether the new list should be sorted or unsorted. Choose sorted, and from then on Ins puts each new link in order. It walks from the start of the list until it reaches the first link with a larger key, then links the new one in just before it. The applet below is set to sorted mode.

Try it. Insert keys that land in different places.

  1. Press New for a fresh sorted list.
  2. Type a key that falls in the middle of the list's range and press Ins. Watch pCurrent walk until it meets a larger key, with pPrevious one step behind. The new link goes between the two.
  3. Insert a key smaller than all the others. It becomes the new first link.
  4. Insert a key larger than all the others. pCurrent runs off the end, and the new link becomes the last one.
  5. Use Find and Del as before. They still walk the list one link at a time.

C++ Code to Insert an Item

The sortedList.cpp program uses one-number links like those of Hour 9, and its SortedList class keeps the usual pFirst. The interesting member function is insert().

Like remove() in Hour 8, insert() needs two pointers. pCurrent looks at each link in turn, and pPrevious trails one link behind, because the link before the insertion point is the one whose pNext will have to change. The loop moves both pointers forward as long as the current key is smaller than the new one. It can stop in three situations.

  • At the very start. The list is empty, or the new key is no larger than the first key. The loop body never runs, pPrevious is still NULL, and the new link becomes the first link: pFirst = pNewLink.
  • In the middle. pCurrent stops at the first link whose key is at least as big as the new key. The new link goes between pPrevious and pCurrent.
  • Past the end. Every key was smaller, so pCurrent ran off the end and is NULL. The new link goes after pPrevious, the old last link. Its pNext gets the NULL in pCurrent, which correctly marks it as the new end.

The last two situations need exactly the same assignments, which is why the code has only one if. In every case the new link points forward to pCurrent, and whichever pointer used to lead to pCurrent (either pFirst or pPrevious->pNext) now leads to the new link. Unlike in insertFirst(), the order of these two assignments doesn't matter here, because pCurrent keeps its own copy of the address of the next link.

The sortedList.cpp Program

Besides insert(), the SortedList class has isEmpty(), displayList(), and a remove() that takes off the first link and returns its key. It is the removeFirst() of Hour 9 under a new name. Because the list is sorted, the first link always holds the smallest key, so remove() always hands back the minimum.

The main() function inserts 20 and 40 and displays the list. Then it inserts 10, 30 and 50, displays the list again, removes one item, and displays it a third time.

List (first-->last): 20 40
List (first-->last): 10 20 30 40 50
List (first-->last): 20 30 40 50

The three new keys exercise all three cases of insert(). The 10 went to the front (the loop never ran), the 30 went into the middle, and the 50 went at the end (pCurrent ran off the list). The single remove() took away 10, the smallest item.

Efficiency of Sorted Linked Lists

Inserting or deleting an arbitrary item in a sorted list takes about N/2 comparisons on average, because the item could belong anywhere along the list. That's O(N). A search for a key that isn't there can stop as soon as it reaches a larger key, but on average it still covers about half the list. Finding or removing the smallest item, on the other hand, is O(1), since it is always at the front.

That combination makes a sorted list a reasonable priority queue when insertion speed isn't critical. Compare it with the ordered-array priority queue of Hour 7. Both take O(N) time to insert and O(1) time to remove the minimum, but the list's insertion moves no items, and the list never fills up.

Sorted array and sorted list compared
OperationSorted arraySorted linked list
Search for a keyO(log N), binary searchO(N), about N/2 comparisons
Insert a new itemO(N), find the place, then about N/2 movesO(N), about N/2 comparisons and no moves
Find the smallest itemO(1)O(1), it's the first link
SizeFixed when createdGrows and shrinks as needed

List Insertion Sort

A sorted list can serve as a fairly efficient sorting mechanism. Suppose you have an array of unsorted items. Take them out of the array one at a time and insert each one into a sorted list. They fall into order automatically as they go in. Then remove them from the list one at a time, always from the front, and put them back into the array. They come out smallest first, so the array ends up sorted. Lafore calls this the list insertion sort.

The listInsertionSort.cpp program works this way. Here the idea is written as a function that sorts a vector in place, using the SortedList class from the previous section.

The program's main() fills an array with 10 random numbers, displays it, sorts it through the list, and displays it again. Because the numbers are random, your output will differ from this run.

Unsorted array: 59 69 41 56 84 15 86 81 37 35
Sorted array:   15 35 37 41 56 59 69 81 84 86

Efficiency of the List Insertion Sort

Start with the comparisons. The first item goes into an empty list without any. Each later item is compared, on average, with about half of the items already in the list before its place is found. Adding that up over all N items gives roughly N²/4 comparisons: about 25 for 10 items and about 250,000 for 1,000 items. That grows as N², so the list insertion sort is still an O(N²) algorithm, in the same class as the bubble sort and insertion sort of Hours 4 and 5.

The copies are where it shines. Each item is copied only twice, once from the array into a link and once from the link back into the array. That makes 2N copies in all: 20 for 10 items, 2,000 for 1,000. The ordinary insertion sort of Hour 5 copies an item every time it shifts one, and the number of shifts grows as N² (about N²/4 on random data, or roughly 250,000 copies for 1,000 items). When copying an item takes much longer than comparing keys, as it does with large records, the list version wins by a wide margin.

Insertion sort and list insertion sort on N random items
Insertion sort (Hour 5)List insertion sort
ComparisonsAbout N²/4About N²/4
CopiesAbout N²/4, growing as N²2N
Copies for 1,000 itemsabout 250,0002,000
Extra memoryOne temporary variableA whole list of N links

The drawback is memory. While the sort runs, the data exists twice, once in the array and once in the list, and every link adds a pointer on top. So the list insertion sort needs about twice as much memory as the array alone. It's a good choice when copies are expensive and memory is plentiful. For large amounts of data, the advanced sorts of Hours 12 to 14 do far better than any O(N²) method.

Doubly Linked Lists

The Trouble with Going Backward

Every list so far has had a built-in limitation. You can only travel forward. The statement pCurrent = pCurrent->pNext takes you to the next link in one step, but there is no matching step to the previous link. To go back, you have to start at pFirst again and walk until you reach the link before the current one.

The book illustrates the problem with a text editor. Suppose the editor stores a document as a linked list, one link per line of text. Moving the cursor down a line is quick, because you just follow pNext. Moving the cursor up a line means finding the previous line, and in a singly linked list that means a walk from the top of the document every time the user presses the up arrow.

A doubly linked list fixes this by giving each link two pointers, pNext to the following link and pPrevious to the one before it.

Doubly linked list. A linked list in which each link points both to the next link and to the previous one, so the list can be traversed in either direction.

The list object, of class DoublyLinkedList, keeps pointers to both ends, pFirst and pLast, so it is double-ended as well. The first link's pPrevious and the last link's pNext are both NULL.

Traversal

Two display functions walk the list in opposite directions. displayForward() starts at pFirst and follows pNext, exactly like displayList() in earlier hours. displayBackward() is its mirror image. It starts at pLast and follows pPrevious.

Insertion

The DoublyLinkedList class has three insertion functions. insertFirst() puts a link at the front, insertLast() puts one at the end, and insertAfter() puts one just after the link holding a given key. Here is the class, with the first two written out.

Compare insertFirst() with the Hour 9 version. There is one new job. The old first link used to have a NULL pPrevious, and now it must point back at the new link. If the list was empty, there's no old first link, and the new link becomes the last link as well. insertLast() is the mirror image. The old last link points forward to the new link, the new link points back to it, and pLast moves to the new link.

insertAfter() is the most involved of the three. It first finds the link with the given key, then fits the new link in right after it.

Once the search has found the link, pCurrent points to it, and four pointers must change to fit the new link in after it.

  1. The new link's pNext points to the link that used to follow pCurrent.
  2. The new link's pPrevious points back to pCurrent.
  3. The link that used to follow pCurrent must point back to the new link. If pCurrent was the last link, there is no such link, and pLast moves to the new link instead.
  4. pCurrent's pNext points to the new link.

The order matters again. Change 3 reaches the old successor through pCurrent->pNext, so it must happen before change 4 overwrites that pointer. If change 4 came first, change 3 would reach the new link instead. The new link would end up pointing back at itself, and the old successor would still point back at pCurrent.

Deletion

There are three deletion functions: removeFirst(), removeLast() and removeKey(). removeFirst() works as in a double-ended list, with one extra step. After pFirst moves to the second link, that link becomes the new first link, so its pPrevious is set to NULL. If the removed link was the only one, pLast becomes NULL too.

removeLast() is where the backward pointers pay off. In a singly linked list, removing the last link required a walk to find the next-to-last link. Here the next-to-last link is simply pLast->pPrevious, one step away.

Like removeFirst(), removeLast() expects a list that isn't empty, so the caller should check isEmpty() first. When it removes the only link, the list becomes empty, so pFirst is set to NULL, and pLast picks up the NULL from the removed link's pPrevious.

removeKey() searches for the key and then cuts pCurrent out of the list in both directions. In the general case, when the link has neighbors on both sides, it takes two statements.

  • pCurrent->pPrevious->pNext = pCurrent->pNext; makes the link before pCurrent point forward past it.
  • pCurrent->pNext->pPrevious = pCurrent->pPrevious; makes the link after pCurrent point back past it.

The special cases replace one of those statements. If pCurrent is the first link, there's no link before it, so pFirst moves instead. If it's the last link, pLast moves instead. If it's the only link, both happen, and the list is left empty. Notice also that removeKey() doesn't need a pPrevious pointer trailing behind pCurrent, as remove() did in Hour 8. The link being deleted already knows its predecessor.

The doublyLinked.cpp Program

The main() in doublyLinked.cpp exercises every function. It inserts 22, 44 and 66 at the front and 11, 33 and 55 at the end, then displays the list forward and backward. Next it calls removeFirst(), removeLast() and removeKey(11) and displays the list again. Finally it calls insertAfter(22, 77) and insertAfter(33, 88) and displays the result.

List (first-->last): 66 44 22 11 33 55
List (last-->first): 55 33 11 22 44 66
List (first-->last): 44 22 33
List (first-->last): 44 22 77 33 88

The backward display is the forward one reversed, which shows that the pPrevious pointers are consistent with the pNext pointers. removeFirst() took 66, removeLast() took 55, and removeKey(11) took 11 from the middle. Then 77 went in after 22, and 88 went in after 33. Because 33 was the last link, that final insertion also moved pLast to the 88 link.

When you write doubly linked list code, test it by displaying the list in both directions. A forgotten pPrevious update often leaves the forward walk looking fine while the backward walk goes wrong.

Deques, and the Cost of Two Pointers

A doubly linked list is a natural base for the deque of Hour 7, the double-ended queue that can insert and delete at either end. The deque's insertLeft() and insertRight() become insertFirst() and insertLast(), and removeLeft() and removeRight() become removeFirst() and removeLast(). All four are O(1). A double-ended singly linked list can't make that promise, because its removeLast() would need an O(N) walk.

The extra pointer has a price, though. Every insertion and deletion must now change four pointers instead of two, so the code is longer and has more places for a mistake to hide. Each link is bigger too, since it carries two pointers along with its data. When a program never needs to move backward or remove from the end, a singly linked list is the leaner choice.

Summary

  • A sorted list keeps its links in key order. Each insertion walks the list with pCurrent and pPrevious to find the spot just after the last smaller key.
  • Compared with a sorted array, a sorted list inserts faster (nothing moves) and can grow, but it searches more slowly, because binary search needs random access.
  • Inserting or deleting an arbitrary item in a sorted list is O(N), about N/2 comparisons. Finding or removing the smallest item is O(1), which makes the sorted list a simple priority queue.
  • The list insertion sort inserts every array item into a sorted list and then removes them from the front back into the array.
  • It makes about N²/4 comparisons, so it is still O(N²), but only 2N copies, far fewer than the ordinary insertion sort. The price is about twice the memory.
  • A doubly linked list gives each link a pPrevious pointer as well as pNext, so it can be traversed backward, and the last link can be removed in O(1) time.
  • insertAfter() changes four pointers, and removeKey() fixes one forward and one backward pointer, with special cases at the first and last links.
  • A doubly linked list is a natural base for a deque. Its costs are four pointer changes per insertion or deletion instead of two, and a bigger link.

Q&A

Is a sorted list better than a sorted array?
It depends on the mix of operations. If the program mostly searches, the sorted array wins, because binary search is O(log N). If it mostly inserts and deletes, or the amount of data is unpredictable, the sorted list wins, because it never shifts items and never fills up.
If the list insertion sort makes so few copies, why not use it all the time?
Its comparisons still grow as N², and it needs about twice the memory. It beats the ordinary insertion sort when copies are expensive, but for large amounts of data the advanced sorts of Hours 12 to 14 are much faster.
Does a doubly linked list have to keep a pLast pointer?
No. Backward pointers and a pointer to the last link are separate ideas, and a list can have either without the other. The book's doubly linked list has both, which is what lets it insert and remove at the end in O(1) time and display itself backward.
What is the most common mistake in doubly linked list code?
Updating the forward pointers and forgetting one of the backward ones, or doing the updates in the wrong order. The list then looks right when displayed forward and wrong when displayed backward, which is why testing both directions is a good habit.

Quiz

  1. Compared with a sorted array, what is a sorted linked list better at, and what is it worse at?

    Answer

    It is better at insertion (no items move, and it can grow without limit). It is worse at searching, because it can't use binary search, so a search takes O(N) time instead of O(log N).

  2. About how many comparisons and how many copies does the list insertion sort make for N items?

    Answer

    About N²/4 comparisons, but only 2N copies: one into the list and one back into the array for each item.

  3. In the sorted list's insert(), what does it mean if pPrevious is still NULL when the loop ends?

    Answer

    The loop never advanced. Either the list was empty or the new key was no larger than the first key, so the new link must become the first link, and pFirst is set to point to it.

  4. What does the pPrevious pointer in each link of a doubly linked list make possible?

    Answer

    Moving backward through the list. That allows displayBackward(), an O(1) removeLast(), and deletion by key without a trailing pointer. It also lets a text editor move the cursor up a line cheaply.

  5. How many pointers does insertAfter() change when it inserts in the middle of a doubly linked list?

    Answer

    Four: the new link's pNext and pPrevious, the following link's pPrevious, and the current link's pNext.

  6. Why is removing the last link easy in a doubly linked list but slow in a double-ended singly linked list?

    Answer

    Removing the last link means changing the next-to-last link. In a doubly linked list that link is pLast->pPrevious, one step away. In a singly linked list the only way to find it is to walk from pFirst, which is O(N).

Part III · Recursion and Quicksort

Hour 11 Recursion

Recursion is a programming technique in which a function calls itself. It sounds like a trick that could never end, yet it is one of the most useful tools in programming, and it is the key to mergesort, quicksort and the tree algorithms later in the book.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How to compute triangular numbers with a loop and with recursion
  • The three characteristics every recursive function shares, and what recursion costs
  • How recursion can produce every arrangement of the letters in a word
  • How binary search can be written recursively, and what "divide and conquer" means
  • How the computer carries out recursion with a stack, and how you can do the same

Recursion is a programming technique in which a function calls itself. The first time you see it, it can look like a dog chasing its own tail. It works because each call tackles a smaller version of the problem than the call before it, until the problem becomes so small that the answer is obvious.

This hour works through several examples: triangular numbers, anagrams, and a recursive version of binary search. Along the way you'll see what makes a recursive function work, what it costs, and how the computer actually carries it out. Recursion is the foundation for the rest of Part III. The Towers of Hanoi and mergesort in Hour 12, the quicksort of Hours 13 and 14, and the tree algorithms of Hours 15 to 20 all depend on it.

Demonstrating Recursion with Triangular Numbers

The Pythagoreans, the circle of ancient Greek mathematicians around Pythagoras, are said to have seen something mystical in the series 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, and so on. Each term is the previous term plus n, where n is the term's position in the series. The second term is 1 + 2 = 3, the third is 3 + 3 = 6, the fourth is 6 + 4 = 10, and the fifth is 10 + 5 = 15.

These are called triangular numbers, because each one can be drawn as a triangle of objects: a row of 1, a row of 2 beneath it, then a row of 3, and so on. The fourth triangular number, 10, is a triangle with rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4 objects. For the code that follows, it helps to tip the triangle over and think of it as columns, a column of 4, then 3, then 2, then 1.

Triangular number. A member of the series 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, …, in which the nth term is the sum of the whole numbers from 1 to n.

Finding the nth Term with a Loop

To find the nth triangular number, add up the column heights: n for the tallest column, n − 1 for the next one, and so on down to 1. A loop does that directly.

For n = 4, the loop adds 4, 3, 2 and 1 and returns 10. Nothing about this is surprising. The interesting part is that the same answer can be reached by a completely different route.

Finding the nth Term with Recursion

Look at the columns again. The nth triangular number is the tallest column, which is n high, plus the sum of all the remaining columns. And the remaining columns form a smaller triangle, the (n − 1)th triangular number. So if you already had a function that could compute triangular numbers, you could get the nth one as n plus that function's answer for n − 1.

That is the recursive idea, and the function you "already have" is the very function you're writing.

Each call hands a slightly smaller job to another call of the same function. triangle(4) needs the total of the three columns to its right, so it asks triangle(3), which asks triangle(2), and so on. You can picture a line of assistants. Each one takes care of a single column and passes the rest of the job down the line, then adds its own column to whatever answer comes back.

The Base Case

Something has to stop the chain. If triangle() always called itself, the calls would go on forever, or in practice until the program ran out of memory and crashed. The recursive version stops when n is 1. The first triangular number is simply 1, so the function returns 1 without calling itself again. A condition like this, where the function answers directly, is called the base case. Every recursive function needs at least one, and every chain of calls must eventually reach it.

Base case. The version of a problem that a recursive function can solve directly, without calling itself. It is what stops the recursion.

This triangle() assumes n is at least 1. Called with 0 or a negative number, it would sail past the base case and keep calling itself with smaller and smaller arguments until the program crashed.

What's Really Happening

To watch the recursion at work, you can add output statements that report each time the function is entered and each time it returns.

Here is what it prints when main() calls triangle(5).

Entering: n=5
Entering: n=4
Entering: n=3
Entering: n=2
Entering: n=1
Returning 1
Returning 3
Returning 6
Returning 10
Returning 15

Each time triangle() is called, it gets its own fresh copy of n. The calls with n = 5, 4, 3 and 2 each stop partway through, waiting for the call below them to return. Only the call with n = 1 can answer at once, and it returns 1. Then the waiting calls finish in reverse order. The n = 2 call adds its 2 to the 1 it got back and returns 3. The n = 3 call returns 3 + 3 = 6, the n = 4 call returns 4 + 6 = 10, and finally the n = 5 call returns 5 + 10 = 15 to main().

The Triangle applet below replays this process one step at a time. It shows the stack of unfinished calls growing as the function calls itself and shrinking as each call returns, with an "Entering" or "Returning" line for every step.

Try it. Watch the calls pile up and unwind.

  1. Choose n = 5 and press Step repeatedly. Each step either enters a new call, which adds a level to the stack, or returns from one, which removes a level.
  2. Notice that no call returns until the call with n = 1 has been entered. Then the returns come back 1, 3, 6, 10, 15.
  3. Press Reset, choose n = 8, and press Run. At its deepest point the stack holds eight unfinished calls, and the final answer is 36.

Characteristics of Recursive Functions

Simple as it is, triangle() has the three characteristics that every recursive function shares.

  1. It calls itself.
  2. When it calls itself, it does so to solve a smaller problem.
  3. There is some version of the problem that is simple enough for the function to solve and return without calling itself. This is the base case.

In triangle(), the smaller problem is the triangle with one column fewer, and the base case is the one-column triangle. Every call moves one step closer to the base case, which guarantees that the chain of calls comes to an end.

The Cost of Recursion

Recursion is not especially efficient. Every function call has overhead. Control has to jump to the start of the function, and the arguments and the address to return to have to be saved, which the computer does by pushing them onto an internal stack. When the function returns, they are popped off again. A recursive triangle(1000) makes 1,000 calls and pays that overhead every time, while the loop version just goes around its loop 1,000 times. The loop is usually faster.

There is a memory cost as well. All the unfinished calls wait on the stack at the same time, so a recursion that goes very deep, many thousands of calls, can use up the space set aside for that stack. This is called a stack overflow, and it usually crashes the program.

Recursion earns its place for a different reason. It can make a problem conceptually simpler. For some problems the recursive solution is short and clear, while a loop version would be long and hard to get right. The anagram example later in this hour is one such problem, and the Towers of Hanoi and the fast sorts of the coming hours are others.

Mathematical Induction

Recursion has a counterpart in mathematics. Mathematical induction is a way of defining something in terms of itself. Using it, the triangular numbers can be defined like this.

  • tri(n) = 1, if n = 1
  • tri(n) = n + tri(n − 1), if n > 1

The first line is the base case, and the second is the recursive step. Put side by side with the recursive C++ function, the definition reads almost line for line like the code. The definition only looks circular. Each use of it refers to a smaller n, and the smallest case is defined outright.

Factorials

Factorials are another classic example of the same pattern. The factorial of n, written n!, is the product of the whole numbers from 1 to n. It can be defined recursively: the factorial of n is n times the factorial of n − 1, and by definition the factorial of 0 is 1.

The first ten factorials
nn!
01
11
22
36
424
5120
6720
75,040
840,320
9362,880

The function is triangle() with two small changes: the base case is n = 0 instead of n = 1, and the operation is multiplication instead of addition. Factorials grow far faster than triangular numbers, though.

A 32-bit int can hold 12! = 479,001,600, but 13! is 6,227,020,800, which is too big to fit. With int arithmetic, this function gives wrong answers for any n above 12.

Demonstrating Recursion with Anagrams

Here is a problem where recursion gives a neat solution that would be hard to find any other way. Suppose you want to list all the anagrams of a word. In this hour, an anagram means any arrangement of the word's letters, whether or not the result is a real word. The three-letter word cat has six: cat, cta, atc, act, tca and tac.

Try listing the anagrams of a five-letter word by hand and you'll soon find how easy it is to miss some or write others twice. You need a system.

The Algorithm

The system Lafore uses works on the rightmost letters of the word. To anagram a word of n letters:

  1. Anagram the rightmost n − 1 letters.
  2. Rotate all n letters.
  3. Repeat these steps n times.

To rotate a group of letters means to shift every letter one position to the left, except the leftmost letter, which moves around to the right end. Rotating cat gives atc, rotating again gives tca, and a third rotation brings back cat.

Each rotation gives a different letter the first position of the group. While that letter sits in front, step 1 produces every arrangement of the letters behind it. After n rotations, each of the n letters has had its turn in front, and the group is back the way it started.

That leaves the question of how to anagram the rightmost n − 1 letters in step 1. The answer is to do it the same way, by anagramming the rightmost n − 2 of them, rotating those n − 1, and repeating. That is the recursion. The group shrinks by one letter at each level, until it is a single letter, which has only one arrangement and needs no work. That is the base case.

Here is how the algorithm handles cat. The outer level rotates all three letters, three times. Before each rotation, the inner level anagrams the last two letters, which means showing the word, swapping the last two letters by rotating them, and showing the word again.

Anagramming cat
TurnLetter in frontInner level showsThen all three rotate
1ccat, ctacat becomes atc
2aatc, actatc becomes tca
3ttca, tactca becomes cat

The C++ Code

The anagram program keeps the word in a string data member called workStr, with its length in size and a running total of words displayed in count. The recursive member function doAnagram() takes one argument, newSize, the number of letters at the right end of the word that it should anagram. The first call passes the length of the whole word.

The loop runs newSize times, once for each letter that will take a turn at the front of the group. Inside it, the function calls itself to anagram the smaller group, then rotates its own group. The display happens only at the level where newSize is 2. At that moment the call to doAnagram(1) has just returned without doing anything, so the word holds a fresh arrangement that no other level has displayed. If every level displayed the word, the same arrangement would be printed several times.

rotate() works out where its group begins. If the word has 4 letters and the group has 3, the group starts at position 4 − 3 = 1. It saves the group's first letter, slides the other letters one cell to the left, and drops the saved letter into the last cell. displayWord() numbers each arrangement and starts a new line after every sixth one. It uses setw(), so the program includes the iomanip header.

The Output

Given the word cats, the program prints all 24 arrangements.

 1 cats    2 cast    3 ctsa    4 ctas    5 csat    6 csta
 7 atsc    8 atcs    9 asct   10 astc   11 acts   12 acst
13 tsca   14 tsac   15 tcas   16 tcsa   17 tasc   18 tacs
19 scat   20 scta   21 satc   22 sact   23 stca   24 stac

The pattern is easy to see. The first six arrangements all begin with c, the next six with a, then six with t and six with s. Each block of six is every arrangement of the other three letters, produced by the level below while one letter held the front position.

A word of n letters has n! arrangements: n choices for the first letter, n − 1 for the second, and so on. So cats, with 4 letters, has 4! = 24, and a five-letter word has 5! = 120. A 10-letter word has 10! = 3,628,800, which would take a while to print. If the word contains a repeated letter, some arrangements come out more than once. The algorithm treats the two t's in tot as different letters, so it prints tot, tto and ott twice each.

Try it. Watch the arrangements appear in the order the rotations produce them.

  1. Leave the word as cats and press Anagram. Check that the 24 results match the output above.
  2. Try a three-letter word and match the six results against the table for cat.
  3. Try a five-letter word and confirm that it produces 120 arrangements.
  4. Try a word with a repeated letter, such as tot, and spot the duplicates.

Demonstrating Recursion in a Binary Search

Remember the binary search of Hour 3. It finds a key in an ordered array by repeatedly halving the range: look at the middle cell, decide which half must hold the key, and repeat on that half. In Hour 3 the find() function did this with a loop that adjusted lowerBound and upperBound each time around. The same algorithm can be written recursively, and it's a natural fit, because each step is a smaller copy of the same problem, a search of half the range.

The binarySearch.cpp program adds these member functions to the OrdArray class of Hour 3, which keeps its items in a vector<double> called v and their count in nElems.

The user of the class calls find() just as in Hour 3, and never needs to know that recursion is involved. find() simply starts the search with the full range, 0 to nElems − 1. The real work happens in recFind(), which only find() needs to call.

Where the Hour 3 loop changed lowerBound or upperBound and went around again, recFind() passes the new bounds to a fresh call of itself. It has two base cases, one for each way a search can end. Either the middle cell holds the key (found), or the range has become empty because lowerBound has passed upperBound (not found, reported by returning nElems). Our version checks for the empty range first, so it never looks at a cell outside the range. The book's version tests for a match first. Both give the same answers.

Suppose the array holds 0, 11, 22, 33, 44, 55, 66, 77, 88 and 99, and you search for 55. The first call looks at index 4 (44), the second at index 7 (77), and the third finds 55 at index 5.

Each call works on half the range of the call before it, so the recursion never goes deep. A 10-item array needs at most 4 cells examined, and a million-item array at most about 20, the same counts as in Hour 3. The recursive version is still O(log N). It does pay the small overhead of a function call at each step, which the loop version avoids.

Divide and Conquer

The recursive binary search is an example of the divide-and-conquer approach. You divide a big problem into smaller problems and solve each one separately. Each smaller problem is divided the same way, until you reach problems simple enough to solve directly. Binary search is an unusually easy case, because after dividing it only has to solve one of the halves, since the key can't be in both. Mergesort (Hour 12) and quicksort (Hours 13 and 14) also divide their data in two, but they have to deal with both halves, so their recursive functions call themselves twice.

Divide and conquer. An approach that splits a problem into smaller subproblems, solves each one (often recursively), and combines the results.

Recursion Versus Stacks

You've seen that each call of triangle() has its own copy of n, and that unfinished calls wait while deeper calls do their work. The computer keeps track of all this with a stack. When a function is called, the code the compiler generates pushes the arguments and the return address, the place in the caller where execution should continue afterward, onto an internal stack. The function reads its arguments from the top of that stack. When it returns, the return address and the arguments are popped off, which uncovers the values belonging to the call that is still waiting underneath.

So recursion is a stack in disguise. The last call made is the first one to finish, which is exactly the last-in, first-out rule of Hour 6. It follows that any recursive algorithm can be rewritten to use a stack of your own in place of the recursive calls.

Simulating What the Compiler Does

The book first shows a literal simulation of what the compiler does for triangle(). It defines a small class that bundles an argument together with a return address, keeps a stack of objects of that class, and runs the whole computation as a loop around a switch statement. Each case of the switch handles one numbered step of calling or returning, and a variable that says which step comes next plays the part of the return address. The result is a mechanical imitation of calls and returns, and it produces the same answers as the recursive function.

That simulation is not easy reading, which is rather the point. It shows how much bookkeeping recursion quietly does for you. Lafore then boils the idea down to a much simpler function.

A Simpler Stack Version

The function works in two phases that mirror the two halves of the recursive trace. The first loop pushes n, n − 1, and so on down to 1, just as the recursive calls went down from triangle(5) to triangle(1), each one leaving its own n behind on the stack. The second loop pops the values and adds them up, just as the returns came back up, each adding its own n. The function uses the StackX class of Hour 6, changed to hold int values instead of doubles. The size, 10,000, only needs to be larger than any n the function will be given.

Why Use a Stack

Replacing recursion with your own stack is worthwhile for a few reasons. Sometimes the stack version is more efficient, because it avoids the overhead of real function calls and stores only what it needs, here a single number per level instead of arguments plus a return address. It can also avoid stack overflow, since your own stack can be made as big as memory allows, while the system's call stack is usually much more limited. And writing the stack version is a good way to see what recursion really does behind the scenes.

For triangular numbers, the plain loop at the start of this hour beats both versions. The stack technique matters most for algorithms that have no such simple loop, such as some of the sorting and tree algorithms in the hours ahead.

Summary

  • A recursive function calls itself. Each call works on a smaller version of the problem, until it reaches a base case that it can solve without calling itself.
  • The nth triangular number is n plus the (n − 1)th, and the first is 1. The recursive triangle() follows that definition directly.
  • Every call gets its own copy of its arguments. The calls go down to the base case, and then the returns come back up, each adding its own part of the answer.
  • Every recursive function calls itself, does so to solve a smaller problem, and has a base case. Without a base case, the recursion runs until the program crashes.
  • Recursion is usually slower than a loop because of the overhead of each call, and very deep recursion can overflow the stack. It is used because it makes some problems conceptually simpler.
  • Mathematical induction defines things in terms of themselves, just as recursion does. Factorials fit the same pattern: n! = n × (n − 1)!, with 0! = 1.
  • To anagram a word of n letters, anagram the rightmost n − 1 letters, rotate all n, and repeat n times. A word of n letters has n! arrangements.
  • Binary search can be written recursively. It is still O(log N), and it is an example of divide and conquer, in which only one of the two halves has to be solved.
  • The compiler implements function calls with a stack of arguments and return addresses, so any recursive algorithm can be rewritten with an explicit stack.

Q&A

Is a recursive solution ever faster than a loop?
Seldom. Each recursive call pushes arguments and a return address and then pops them again, and a loop avoids that work. Recursion's value lies in clarity. For some problems, such as the anagrams in this hour or the sorts to come, the recursive version is much easier to write and to trust.
If every call runs the same function, how can each one have its own n?
Each call gets its own set of arguments and local variables, stored in its own section of the stack. The n that belongs to triangle(5) sits lower in the stack, untouched, while triangle(4) works with its own n on top.
Can every recursive function be rewritten without recursion?
Yes. At worst you imitate what the compiler does, with a stack of your own, as stackTriangle() does. Sometimes a plain loop is enough, as with triangular numbers and factorials.
What exactly happens if I forget the base case?
The function keeps calling itself, and every unfinished call occupies space on the stack. Soon the stack runs out of room and the program crashes with a stack overflow.

Quiz

  1. What are the three characteristics of a recursive function?

    Answer

    It calls itself. When it does, it is to solve a smaller problem. And there is a base case, a version of the problem simple enough to solve without calling itself.

  2. What happens if a recursive function has no base case?

    Answer

    It calls itself endlessly. In practice the unfinished calls fill up the stack and the program crashes.

  3. What does triangle(4) return, and how many calls of triangle() does it take?

    Answer

    It returns 10 (4 + 3 + 2 + 1), using four calls: with n = 4, 3, 2 and 1.

  4. How many anagrams does a five-letter word with no repeated letters have?

    Answer

    5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

  5. Why is a recursive function usually slower than an equivalent loop?

    Answer

    Each call has overhead. Control must be transferred to the function, and its arguments and return address must be pushed onto the stack and later popped off. A loop does none of that.

  6. What does "divide and conquer" mean, and how does binary search use it?

    Answer

    It means splitting a problem into smaller problems and solving each one, often recursively. Binary search splits the range in half and then only has to search the one half that could contain the key.

Part III · Recursion and Quicksort

Hour 12 Applied Recursion

This hour applies recursion to two classic problems. The Towers of Hanoi puzzle turns out to need only a few lines of code, and mergesort sorts data far faster than the O(N²) methods you have used so far.

In this hour you'll learn

  • What the Towers of Hanoi puzzle is, and the legend that goes with it
  • How to see a pile of disks as smaller piles, and solve it in three recursive steps
  • Why n disks need 2ⁿ − 1 moves
  • How to merge two sorted arrays into one
  • How mergesort sorts by splitting and merging, and how its C++ code works
  • Why mergesort runs in O(N log N) time, and what it costs in memory

The Towers of Hanoi

The Towers of Hanoi is an ancient puzzle made of three columns and a set of disks. Every disk has a different diameter, and each has a hole through its center so it can slide down over a column. The columns are called towers A, B and C.

At the start, every disk is stacked on tower A, widest at the bottom and narrowest at the top. Your job is to move the whole stack to tower C.

Two rules make this harder than it sounds. You may move only one disk at a time, always the top disk of some tower. And you may never set a disk down on a disk smaller than itself. Tower B is there to help, and you can use it as often as you like.

Lafore passes on the legend that usually travels with the puzzle. Somewhere in India, the story goes, a remote temple holds three towers encrusted with diamonds and a pile of 64 golden disks. Monks work in shifts around the clock, shifting the pile from one tower to another under the same two rules. When the final disk comes to rest, the world will end.

You can relax. As you'll see shortly, 64 disks need 2⁶⁴ − 1 moves. Working at one move per second without a single break, the monks would need about 585 billion years.

The Towers Workshop Applet

The book's Towers Workshop applet lets you choose how many disks to play with. You can then solve the puzzle yourself by dragging disks from tower to tower. You can also press Step to see the solution one move at a time, or Run to watch the applet solve it from start to finish.

Lafore suggests working a few puzzles by hand before you let the applet show you how. Three disks take 7 moves and four take 15. On the first tries it is easy to trap yourself, with a small disk sitting on exactly the tower you need next. After a little practice a rhythm appears, and that rhythm is what the recursive solution captures.

The re-creation below behaves like the original, except that you click instead of drag. Click the tower whose top disk you want to move, then click the tower where it should go. A counter shows your moves next to the minimum, 2ⁿ − 1 for n disks.

Try it. Solve two small puzzles by hand, then watch the machine.

  1. Set the disk count to 3 and press New.
  2. Move the disks yourself by clicking a tower and then its destination. Aim to rebuild the pile on C in 7 moves.
  3. Set the count to 4, press New, and try again. The minimum is 15.
  4. Press New, then press Step over and over. Notice that the largest disk moves only once, exactly halfway through.
  5. Choose 8 disks and press Run. All 255 moves follow the same pattern.

Moving Subtrees

To describe the solution, it helps to give the piles names. Lafore calls the starting pile of disks a tree, and any smaller pile sitting on top of it a subtree. (The binary trees that begin in Hour 15 are a separate idea; here the words simply describe piles of disks.) With four disks, the top three form a subtree, the top two form a smaller subtree, and the top disk by itself is a subtree of one.

Now think about the largest disk, number 4. It can't move while anything sits on top of it. It also needs an empty tower to land on, because every other disk is smaller than it is. So at the moment disk 4 travels from A to C, tower C must be empty and the other three disks must all be stacked on tower B.

That one observation splits the puzzle into three jobs. First, move the three-disk subtree from A to B. Second, move disk 4 from A to C. Third, move the three-disk subtree from B to C, where it lands on top of disk 4.

The middle job is a single move. The first and third jobs are the original puzzle again, only with three disks and with the towers playing different parts. Each of those can be split the same way, into a two-disk job, one move, and another two-disk job. A problem that contains smaller copies of itself is exactly the kind of problem recursion handles well.

The Recursive Algorithm

To state the solution in general terms, name the towers by the part they play instead of by letter. S is the source, where the pile starts, D is the destination, where it must end up, and I is the intermediate tower, the spare. To move a pile of n disks from S to D, you follow three steps.

  1. Move the subtree made of the top n − 1 disks from S to I.
  2. Move the remaining disk, the largest one, from S to D.
  3. Move the subtree from I to D.

The base case is a subtree of just one disk. Nothing sits on top of it, so nothing has to be cleared away, and you move it straight from S to D. Every recursive call works on a pile one disk smaller than its caller's pile, so the calls always get down to this case.

The part that takes getting used to is that the towers trade roles from one call to the next. In step 1 the subtree has to end up on I, so for that call I is the destination and D serves as the spare. In step 3 the subtree starts on I, so I is the source and S becomes the spare. Here is the complete plan for three disks, written as jobs inside jobs.
