  • Move 3 disks from A to C, with B as the spare:
    • Move 2 disks from A to B, with C as the spare:
      • Disk 1 from A to C
      • Disk 2 from A to B
      • Disk 1 from C to B
    • Disk 3 from A to C
    • Move 2 disks from B to C, with A as the spare:
      • Disk 1 from B to A
      • Disk 2 from B to C
      • Disk 1 from A to C

Read the innermost lines from top to bottom and you have the seven moves that solve the three-disk puzzle.

The towers.cpp Program

The C++ version follows the three steps almost word for word. The function doTowers() takes the number of disks in the pile, then the names of the three towers in the order source, intermediate, destination. Disks are numbered by size, 1 for the smallest, so a pile of topN disks always has disk topN at its bottom.

When topN is 1, the function prints a single move and returns. Otherwise it makes two recursive calls with one print statement between them.

Watch the order of the tower arguments. The first call passes src, dest, inter, so the spare and the destination swap places and the smaller disks go to the spare. The second call passes inter, src, dest, so the pile starts from the spare and the original source becomes the new spare.

main() calls doTowers(nDisks, 'A', 'B', 'C') with nDisks set to 3. The program prints one line per move.

Disk 1 from A to C
Disk 2 from A to B
Disk 1 from C to B
Disk 3 from A to C
Disk 1 from B to A
Disk 2 from B to C
Disk 1 from A to C

These are the same seven moves as the nested plan. Each call to doTowers() prints exactly one line, so the number of calls equals the number of moves. The calls never nest deeply, though. At any moment the chain of unfinished calls holds at most one call per pile size, so even 64 disks would need only 64 levels of recursion.

Now count the moves. Write moves(n) for the number of moves needed with n disks. One disk takes one move. A larger pile needs the moves for n − 1 disks, then one move, then the moves for n − 1 disks again, so moves(n) = 2 × moves(n − 1) + 1.

Starting from moves(1) = 1, that rule gives 3, 7, 15, 31 and so on. Each result is one less than a power of 2, which means moves(n) = 2ⁿ − 1.

Moves needed to solve the Towers of Hanoi
DisksMoves (2ⁿ − 1)

201,048,575
6418,446,744,073,709,551,615

Every extra disk doubles the work and adds one move. Growth of this kind is called exponential, and it leaves even N² behind almost at once. Twenty disks already need more than a million moves. Sixty-four disks need so many that the monks, at one move per second, will be busy for those 585 billion years.

No cleverer method can beat 2ⁿ − 1 moves. Whenever the largest disk moves, the other n − 1 disks must all be piled on the third tower, out of its way. Getting them there before its first move is an (n − 1)-disk puzzle, and so is carrying them onto it after its last move. So every solution needs at least 2 × moves(n − 1) + 1 moves.

Mergesort

The second application of recursion is a sort, and a much faster one than those you've met so far. The bubble sort of Hour 4 and the insertion sort of Hour 5 take O(N²) time. Mergesort takes O(N log N).

For large arrays the gap is enormous. With N = 10,000, N² is 100,000,000, while N × log₂N is only about 133,000, roughly 750 times smaller. If each step took one microsecond, the simple sort would run for about 100 seconds and mergesort would be done in about 0.13 seconds.

Mergesort is also easy to understand and fairly easy to code, easier than the quicksort of Hour 13. Its one real drawback is memory, because it needs a second array, called the workspace, as large as the array being sorted. If your data only just fits in memory, mergesort is ruled out. If memory is plentiful, it is an excellent choice.

Merging Two Sorted Arrays

The heart of mergesort is a simpler job, merging two arrays that are already sorted. The result is a third array that holds all the items of both, also in sorted order.

Think of two piles of exam papers, each already sorted by student name. To combine them, you look at the top paper of each pile, move the one whose name comes first in the alphabet onto a new pile, and repeat. When one pile runs out, you move the rest of the other pile across as it is, since it is already in order. Merging arrays works exactly the same way.

The book's example merges array A, which holds 4 items, with array B, which holds 6, into array C, which has room for 10. The program keeps an index into each array. At every step it compares the front items of A and B, copies the smaller one into the next free cell of C, and advances the index of the array it copied from.

Merging A = {23, 47, 81, 95} with B = {7, 14, 39, 55, 62, 74}
StepComparisonCopy into C
123 with 77 from B
223 with 1414 from B
323 with 3923 from A
439 with 4739 from B
555 with 4747 from A
655 with 8155 from B
762 with 8162 from B
874 with 8174 from B, which is now empty
9none81 from A
10none95 from A

After step 8, B has nothing left, so there is nothing to compare. The last two steps simply copy the remaining items of A, which are already in order. C ends up holding 7 14 23 39 47 55 62 74 81 95. Ten items found their places with only eight comparisons.

Here is the merge as a C++ function, with a small main() that runs the example. The arrays are ordinary C++ arrays of int, and each array's size is passed in beside it.

The first while loop runs as long as both arrays still have items to offer. Each pass compares the two front items, copies the smaller one into C, and moves two indexes forward, cDex and the index of the array that supplied the item. A statement such as arrayC[cDex++] = arrayA[aDex++] does the copy and both increments at once.

When the first loop ends, one of the arrays has run dry. The next two loops copy whatever is left of the other one. Only one of them does any work, because the array that emptied first fails its loop test straight away. The program's output is the merged array.

7 14 23 39 47 55 62 74 81 95

This listing compares with <=, so when two keys are equal the one from A is copied first. Items with equal keys then keep their original order, a property called stability. The book's listing uses <, which takes the item from B on a tie. Both versions produce a correctly sorted result.

Sorting by Merging

Merging only works on arrays that are already sorted, which at first seems to leave you where you started. Mergesort gets around this with a simple plan. Divide the array in half, sort each half, and then merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array.

Each half is sorted the same way, by mergesort itself. The half is divided into two quarters, each quarter is sorted, and the two sorted quarters are merged. The quarters in turn are split into eighths, and so on down. This is the divide-and-conquer approach you met with recursive binary search in Hour 11.

The splitting stops when a piece holds a single item. An array of one item is already sorted, so that is the base case. From there the work runs back up. Pairs of single items merge into sorted runs of 2, pairs of those runs merge into runs of 4, then 8, until one run fills the whole array.

The picture shows the work level by level, but the program does it in a different order. Each call finishes sorting its lower half before it even starts on the upper half, so the left side of the array is completely sorted before the right side is touched. For the eight items above, the seven merges happen in this order.

The order of merges when sorting 64 21 33 70 12 85 44 3
MergeCellsResult
10–121 64
22–333 70
30–321 33 64 70
44–512 85
56–73 44
64–73 12 44 85
70–73 12 21 33 44 64 70 85

The array's size doesn't have to be a power of 2. When a range holds an odd number of items, its two halves differ in size by one. Twelve items split into 6 and 6, each 6 splits into 3 and 3, and each 3 splits into 2 and 1. Merging works just as well on runs of unequal length.

The mergeSort Workshop Applet

The mergeSort Workshop applet runs the algorithm on a row of bars of different heights. As it works, short sorted runs appear at the left end and grow, merging with their neighbors into longer and longer runs that spread to the right. The applet marks the range it is currently merging, and it counts comparisons and copies as it goes.

The re-creation below does the same. It marks the two runs being merged, reports each comparison and copy in a message line, and keeps both counts on screen.

Try it. Watch the sorted runs grow.

  1. Press New for ten random bars, then press Step repeatedly. Small sorted runs form at the left end and merge into longer ones, and the right half of the row isn't touched until the left half is sorted.
  2. Watch the comparison and copy counts as the runs get longer.
  3. Switch Size to 100 bars and press Run. Sorted runs form on the left and spread to the right.
  4. Press Reverse and run it again. The copy count doesn't change, and the comparison count drops. Mergesort hardly cares how the data starts out.

C++ Code for Mergesort

The mergeSort.cpp program wraps the data in a class called DArray. The class keeps the items in a vector<double> named theVect and counts them in nElems. Besides the usual insert() and display(), it offers a public mergeSort() function, backed by two private helpers that do the real work.

mergeSort() is the only sorting function a user of the class calls. It creates the workspace, a vector exactly as long as the data, and hands it to recMergeSort() together with the bounds of the whole array.

recMergeSort() is the whole algorithm in a few lines. If the range holds a single item, it returns at once, since there is nothing to sort. (The test uses >= so that an empty array is handled safely too.) Otherwise it finds the middle of the range, calls itself on the lower half, calls itself on the upper half, and finally merges the two halves, which by then are both sorted.

Pass the workspace by reference, as vector<double>&. Without the &, every call receives its own copy of the entire vector. The sort still gives the right answer, but it wastes most of its time allocating and copying vectors.

The merging is done by a member function also named merge(), but it differs from the merge.cpp version in two ways.

First, its two input runs are not separate arrays. They lie next to each other inside theVect. The lower run occupies cells lowPtr through mid, and the upper run occupies highPtr (which is always mid + 1) through upperBound. The pointers lowPtr and highPtr play the parts that aDex and bDex played before.

Second, the merged items go into the workspace, starting at cell 0 each time, and the final for loop copies them back over the cells the two runs came from. That round trip is the reason the workspace exists. If the merge wrote straight into theVect, it would overwrite items of the lower run before they had been merged.

main() creates a DArray, inserts twelve numbers (64, 21, 33, 70, 12, 85, 44, 3, 99, 0, 108 and 36), displays them, calls mergeSort(), and displays them again. display() is a plain loop that prints every item.

64 21 33 70 12 85 44 3 99 0 108 36
0 3 12 21 33 36 44 64 70 85 99 108

Efficiency of the Mergesort

Mergesort runs in O(N log N) time. The simplest way to see why is to count copies, and the simplest arrays to count are those whose size is a power of 2.

Look back at the eight-item picture. Below the single items there are log₂8 = 3 levels of merging, producing runs of 2, runs of 4 and the final run of 8. At each level every item takes part in exactly one merge, so each level copies all 8 items into the workspace and all 8 back again. In general there are log₂N levels, so the items are copied into the workspace N × log₂N times in all, and the same number of times back.

Comparisons take a little more thought, because their number depends on the data. Merging two runs that hold n items between them takes at most n − 1 comparisons. That worst case happens when the items of the two runs interleave, so that neither run empties until the very end.

For two runs of equal length, the best case is n/2 comparisons. It happens when every item of one run is smaller than every item of the other; that run is used up after n/2 comparisons, and the rest is copied without any.

Copies and comparisons in mergesort, for N a power of 2
Nlog₂NCopies into workspace (N × log₂N)Total copiesComparisons, max (min)
21241 (1)
428165 (4)
83244817 (12)
1646412849 (32)
325160320129 (80)
646384768321 (192)
12878961,792769 (448)

Two patterns run through the comparison column. The minimum is exactly half of N × log₂N, since in the best case each level needs only N/2 comparisons. The maximum is N × log₂N − N + 1. There are N − 1 merges in all, and each one needs at most one comparison fewer than the number of items it handles.

The eight-item example sits right on the worst case. Its seven merges used 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 7 = 17 comparisons and made 48 copies, just as the table predicts, because every one of its merges interleaved its runs completely.

Now compare the simple sorts. Bubble sort on 128 items makes 128 × 127 / 2 = 8,128 comparisons, more than ten times mergesort's worst case of 769. The gap keeps widening as N grows, because N² grows far faster than N × log₂N.

Summary

  • The Towers of Hanoi puzzle asks you to move a pile of disks from tower A to tower C, one disk at a time, without ever putting a disk on a smaller one.
  • Every pile (a tree) contains smaller piles (subtrees). To move n disks, move the top n − 1 disks to the spare tower, move the largest disk to the destination, then move the n − 1 disks on top of it.
  • The base case is a pile of one disk, which moves directly. The towers trade the roles of source, intermediate and destination from one call to the next.
  • The solution takes 2ⁿ − 1 moves, because moves(n) = 2 × moves(n − 1) + 1. Each extra disk doubles the work.
  • Merging combines two sorted arrays into one sorted array by repeatedly copying the smaller front item. Both inputs must already be sorted.
  • Mergesort splits an array in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges the halves. A subarray of one item is the base case.
  • Mergesort runs in O(N log N) time. There are log₂N levels of merging, and each level copies all N items into the workspace and back.
  • Its main drawback is that it needs a workspace array as large as the array being sorted.

Q&A

Is the Towers of Hanoi good for anything besides teaching?
Not much in everyday programming. Its value is as a demonstration. A puzzle that seems to need a clever strategy turns out to have a three-step solution once you look at it recursively. It is also a vivid reminder that some problems take exponential time however you solve them.
Could I solve the puzzle without recursion?
Yes. As Hour 11 explained, any recursive algorithm can be rewritten to keep its own stack in place of the chain of function calls. The recursive version is the clearest way to express the idea.
Why not always use mergesort, since it beats the simple sorts so badly?
It needs extra memory as large as the array itself, which can be a problem with very large data. Quicksort, the subject of the next two hours, is usually faster in practice and sorts in place. And for very small arrays a simple insertion sort can win, because it has almost no overhead.
Does mergesort care whether the data starts out sorted?
Hardly at all. For a given N it always makes the same number of copies, and its comparisons can only vary between the minimum and maximum figures in the table. Insertion sort is quite different. It is very fast on almost-sorted data and very slow on inversely sorted data.

Quiz

  1. How many moves does the Towers of Hanoi take with 5 disks?

    Answer

    31. The formula 2ⁿ − 1 gives 2⁵ − 1 = 31, and so does doubling the four-disk answer and adding one (2 × 15 + 1).

  2. What are the three steps for moving a pile of n disks from tower S to tower D?

    Answer

    Move the top n − 1 disks from S to the intermediate tower I. Move the largest disk from S to D. Move the n − 1 disks from I to D.

  3. What is the base case in doTowers(), and what does the function do there?

    Answer

    The base case is a pile of one disk (topN == 1). The function prints the move of disk 1 from the source tower to the destination tower and returns.

  4. What must be true of two arrays before you can merge them?

    Answer

    Each must already be sorted, in the same order. Merging relies on the smallest remaining item of each array always being at its front.

  5. How much extra memory does mergesort need?

    Answer

    A workspace array the same size as the array being sorted, so memory use roughly doubles.

  6. What is the Big O efficiency of mergesort, and how many copies does it make when N is 64?

    Answer

    O(N log N). With N = 64 there are log₂64 = 6 levels, so it makes 64 × 6 = 384 copies into the workspace and 768 copies in total.

Part III · Recursion and Quicksort

Hour 13 Quicksort

Quicksort is the sort most programmers reach for, because in most situations it is the fastest. It is built on a simpler operation called partitioning, so this hour masters partitioning first and then turns it into a complete recursive sort.

In this hour you'll learn

  • What partitioning is, and how the Partition Workshop applet shows it
  • How the two-pointer partition algorithm works, in concept and in C++
  • Why partitioning takes O(N) time
  • How quicksort combines partitioning with recursion
  • Why the rightmost item makes a handy pivot, and how the pivot lands in its final place
  • How the basic quicksort's C++ code and the quickSort1 applet work

Quicksort is the most popular sorting algorithm, and with good reason. In most situations it is the fastest way to sort data held in memory, running in O(N log N) time. It was invented by C.A.R. (Tony) Hoare in 1962.

The whole algorithm rests on one simpler operation, partitioning. Once partitioning makes sense, quicksort itself takes only a few more lines, so that is where this hour begins.

Partitioning

To partition data is to divide it into two groups. Every item with a key larger than some chosen value goes into one group, and every item with a smaller key goes into the other.

People partition things all the time without using the word. A company might split its personnel records into employees who live within 15 miles of the office and those who live farther away, perhaps to organize car pools. A school might divide its students into those with grade point averages above 3.5 and those below, to see who qualifies for an honors program.

Pivot value. The value that decides which group each item joins during a partition. Items with smaller keys go to one side, and items with larger keys go to the other.

The Partition Workshop Applet

The Partition Workshop applet starts with 12 bars of random heights, and it can also show 100. A horizontal line across the bars marks the pivot value. Two arrows labeled leftPtr and rightPtr start at the two ends of the row and work toward each other as you press Step or Run.

When the applet finishes, the row falls into two groups. Every bar to the left of the dividing point is shorter than the pivot line, and every bar to the right is taller.

Look closely at the result and you'll see that partitioning is a long way from sorting. Inside each group the bars are still in no particular order. For example, 96 comes before 17 on the left, and 188 comes before 111 on the right.

Partitioning isn't stable either. Swaps can carry an item a long way across the array, so two items with equal keys may end up in the opposite order from the one they started in.

Notice also where the dividing point falls. The applet picks its pivot value fairly arbitrarily, so the dividing point is rarely in the middle of the array. In this example it happens to land exactly halfway, six bars and six bars, but that is luck. A pivot value near the top of the range would put most of the bars in the left group.

The re-creation below partitions the bars the same way. It draws the pivot line and the two pointers, explains each step in a message line, and counts comparisons and swaps.

Try it. Watch the two pointers divide the bars.

  1. Press New for a fresh set of random bars and find the dashed pivot line.
  2. Press Step repeatedly. leftPtr skips short bars and stops at a tall one, rightPtr skips tall bars and stops at a short one, and then the two bars are swapped.
  3. When the pointers cross, check that every bar left of the division is below the line and every bar to its right is above it.
  4. Notice that neither group is sorted. Then set Size to 100 and press Run to watch a bigger partition.

The Partition Algorithm

The algorithm uses two pointers that start at opposite ends of the array and move toward each other. They are array indexes, not C++ pointers. leftPtr moves to the right, and rightPtr moves to the left.

leftPtr keeps moving as long as it finds items smaller than the pivot, since those are already in the correct group. It stops at the first item that is larger, because that item belongs in the right-hand group. rightPtr does the mirror-image job. It moves left past items larger than the pivot and stops at the first smaller one.

When both pointers have stopped, each one is resting on an item that sits on the wrong side, so the algorithm swaps the two items. That one swap fixes both of them. The pointers then set off again, and the stop-and-swap cycle repeats until the pointers meet or cross. At that moment the partition is complete, and leftPtr marks the first item of the right-hand group.

Picture tidying a bookshelf so that the paperbacks end up on the left and the hardcovers on the right. Your left hand walks in from the left end until it touches a hardcover, and your right hand walks in from the right end until it touches a paperback. You swap those two books and keep going. When your hands meet, the shelf is divided.

Here is the complete partition of the twelve bars from the figures, one round per row.

Partitioning the twelve bars around the pivot value 99
RoundleftPtr stops atrightPtr stops atAction
1cell 0 (149)cell 10 (34)swap 149 and 34
2cell 2 (188)cell 8 (58)swap 188 and 58
3cell 4 (130)cell 6 (96)swap 130 and 96
4cell 6 (130)cell 5 (17)pointers have crossed, so stop

In round 4, leftPtr moves past 17 and stops at 130 in cell 6. rightPtr moves one cell, onto 17 in cell 5, and stops there. The pointers have crossed, so the work is done. The partition is at cell 6, the first cell of the right-hand group.

One situation needs special care. If every item happens to be smaller than the pivot, leftPtr never finds a reason to stop, and it would run right off the end of the array into memory that doesn't belong to it. The mirror case, with every item larger than the pivot, sends rightPtr off the other end. So each scan also checks that its pointer is still inside the range.

C++ Code for Partitioning

The partition.cpp program keeps its data in a class called ArrayPar, built much like DArray from Hour 12. It stores the items in a vector<double> and adds two members that matter here, a swap() helper and the partitionIt() function.

partitionIt() takes the bounds of the range to partition and the pivot value, and it returns the index where the right-hand group begins. The outer while(true) loop repeats the stop-and-swap cycle. Inside it, the first do loop moves leftPtr and the second moves rightPtr. Once both have stopped, the if checks whether they have met or crossed; if they have, break ends the loop, and if not, the two items are swapped and the cycle starts again.

This code is more delicate than it looks. Each pointer steps first and looks second, so the pointers start one cell outside the range, at left - 1 and right + 1, and their first steps land on the two end cells. Stepping first also guarantees progress. After a swap, the two items under the pointers are on their correct sides, and the next round moves past them instead of examining them again.

The loop conditions also settle what happens to items equal to the pivot. Neither scan moves past one, so an equal item stops both pointers and gets swapped. That looks like wasted effort, yet it pays off when many keys are the same.

With an array of ten identical keys, the pointers meet in the middle after five swaps and split the array into two equal halves. If the scans skipped equal keys instead, leftPtr would run all the way to the end and the split would be as lopsided as possible.

The book writes the range tests as leftPtr < right and rightPtr > left, which park a pointer on the last cell of the range instead of letting it step one cell past. The two forms give the same result except when every item is smaller than the pivot. In that case this version returns right + 1, which correctly reports an empty right-hand group.

main() fills an ArrayPar with 16 random numbers between 0 and 199 and displays them. It then partitions the whole array around the pivot value 99, reports where the partition fell, and displays the array again. Because the data is random, the partition index changes from run to run. Here is one run.

41 67 134 100 169 124 78 158 162 64 105 145 81 27 161 91
Pivot is 99, Partition is at index 7
41 67 91 27 81 64 78 158 162 124 105 145 169 100 161 134

Seven of the sixteen numbers were below 99, so they fill cells 0 through 6, and the larger group starts at index 7. Within each group the numbers are still jumbled.

Efficiency of the Partition Algorithm

Partitioning runs in O(N) time. The two pointers start at opposite ends and move toward each other one cell at a time, and they stop when they meet. Between them they cover the array once, so the work grows in step with N.

Comparisons are easy to count. Every item is compared with the pivot, and where the pointers cross, a cell or two gets compared twice. That makes about N + 2 comparisons. In the twelve-bar example, leftPtr made 7 comparisons and rightPtr made 7, for 14 in all.

Swaps depend on how the data is arranged, and there are always fewer swaps than comparisons. The worst arrangement is inverse order, where every item in the left half belongs on the right and every item in the right half belongs on the left. Then every pair is swapped, which comes to N/2 swaps.

Random data needs fewer. With a pivot near the middle value, only about half the items in each half are on the wrong side, so there are roughly N/4 swaps. The twelve-bar example needed just 3.

Basic Quicksort

A partition leaves an array divided into two groups, each still unsorted. Quicksort finishes the job with recursion.

The Quicksort Algorithm

The basic quicksort has three steps.

  1. Partition the array or subarray into a left group with smaller keys and a right group with larger keys.
  2. Call itself to sort the left group.
  3. Call itself to sort the right group.

The base case is a subarray with one item, or none. Such a subarray is already sorted, so the function returns without doing anything.

Those three steps are enough because, after a partition, every key in the left group is smaller than every key in the right group. No item will ever need to cross from one group to the other, so each group can be sorted on its own. When both groups are sorted, the whole array is sorted, with no merging needed at the end.

Compare this with mergesort. Mergesort splits the array without looking at the data and does its real work afterward, when it merges. Quicksort does its real work first, when it partitions, and has nothing left to do once its recursive calls return.

Choosing a Pivot Value

Quicksort still needs a rule for choosing the pivot value. Lafore's answer is to use the key of an actual item in the subarray as the pivot value. That item is called the pivot. It can be chosen more or less at random, and the simplest choice is the rightmost item of the subarray.

While the partition runs, the pivot stays put at the right end. partitionIt() divides the other items, the ones from left to right - 1, into the usual two groups.

When the partition finishes, the pivot is still at the far right, beyond the larger group, though it belongs between the two groups. One way to get it there would be to shift the whole right-hand group one cell to the right, opening a gap, but that could mean moving nearly N items.

A single swap does the job instead. Exchange the pivot with the item at leftPtr, the leftmost item of the right-hand group. That item moves to the far right end, which is still part of the right-hand group. The right-hand group was in no particular order anyway, so nothing is lost.

After that swap, the pivot has every smaller key to its left and every larger key to its right. It is therefore in its final sorted position, and it will never move again. The recursive calls leave it out and sort only the ranges on either side of it.

The rightmost pivot has one more benefit. It sits at the end of the range that leftPtr scans toward, and leftPtr stops at any item that isn't smaller than the pivot, including the pivot itself. So leftPtr can never run past the pivot, and the range test on that scan can be dropped. A value placed at the end of a range to stop a scan like this is called a sentinel.

C++ Code for Quicksort

The quickSort1.cpp program uses a class named ArrayIns, which stores its data the same way as ArrayPar. Its public quickSort() function calls recQuickSort(0, nElems - 1) to sort the whole array. These are the two functions that do the work.

recQuickSort() first checks the size of its range. If right - left is zero or less, the range holds one item or none, and the function returns. Otherwise it takes the rightmost item as the pivot, partitions the range, and calls itself twice, once for each side of the pivot's new home.

This partitionIt() is the one from partition.cpp with three changes. rightPtr starts at right instead of right + 1, so its first step lands on right - 1 and the pivot is never examined. The leftPtr scan has no range test, because the pivot is its sentinel. And after the loop, one more swap() moves the pivot from cell right to cell leftPtr, whose index the function returns.

The rightPtr scan still needs its range test, because nothing guarantees a small item at the left end of the range to stop it. The book's listing tests rightPtr > 0. Testing against left, as here, stops the scan a little sooner and gives the same result.

Here is how the program sorts the twelve bars from the figure. The first call partitions cells 0 to 11 around 55, which lands in cell 6. The call for the left side partitions cells 0 to 5 around 27, which lands in cell 3, and then cells 0 to 2 are partitioned around 12. Only when everything left of cell 6 is sorted does the program turn to cells 7 to 11.

Seven partitions sort the twelve items. The other calls all get a range of one item or none, and they return at once. main() fills the array with 16 random numbers from 0 to 99, displays them, sorts them, and displays them again. One run produced this output.

41 67 34 0 69 24 78 58 62 64 5 45 81 27 61 91
0 5 24 27 34 41 45 58 61 62 64 67 69 78 81 91

With 12 bars, pressing Step shows every detail of each partition. The applet marks the range being worked on, highlights the pivot (the rightmost bar of the range), and draws the pivot line across the bars. You watch leftPtr and rightPtr stop and swap, and at the end you see the pivot swapped into its final place between the two groups. The re-creation below shows the same things, with a message for every step.

Try it. Follow one partition in detail, then watch the whole sort.

  1. Press New for twelve random bars, then press Step. Find the pivot, the rightmost bar of the range, and the dashed line at its height.
  2. Keep stepping. Watch the pointers stop and swap, then watch the final swap that moves the pivot into place. That bar is now sorted for good.
  3. Notice that the next range the applet works on is the left group. The right group waits until the left side is finished.

A First Look at Efficiency

Quicksort runs in O(N log N) time on average, and the call tree above shows why. The ranges on each level of the tree are separate, and together they cover nearly the whole array. A partition is O(N), so each level costs about N steps. The number of levels depends on the pivots.

If the pivots split their ranges roughly in half, the ranges shrink from N items to N/2, then N/4, N/8 and so on, and they reach single items after about log₂N levels. About N steps on each of about log₂N levels gives N × log₂N in all. The twelve items above needed three levels of partitioning, close to log₂12, which is about 3.6.

That reasoning assumes the pivots behave. The rightmost item works well for random data, but some arrangements of data make it a terrible choice, and quicksort then slows to a crawl. Hour 14 shows what goes wrong and how to fix it.

Summary

  • Partitioning divides data into two groups around a pivot value, with smaller keys in one group and larger keys in the other.
  • The partition algorithm moves leftPtr and rightPtr toward each other from the two ends. Each stops at an item on the wrong side, the two items are swapped, and the process repeats until the pointers cross.
  • Partitioning leaves each group unsorted, and it isn't stable.
  • Partitioning takes O(N) time, with about N + 2 comparisons and at most about N/2 swaps.
  • Quicksort, invented by C.A.R. Hoare in 1962, partitions a range and then calls itself to sort the left group and the right group. A range of one item or none is the base case.
  • quickSort1 uses the rightmost item as the pivot. After partitioning the other items, it swaps the pivot to the boundary between the groups, which is its final sorted position.
  • A pivot at the right end is a sentinel for leftPtr, so that scan needs no range test.
  • Quicksort averages O(N log N). Each level of recursion partitions about N items, and pivots that split ranges near the middle give about log₂N levels.

Q&A

Why is it called quicksort if it can be slow?
In most situations it is the fastest sort available. The slow case needs particular arrangements of data, such as data that is already sorted, and Hour 14 shows how to make that case extremely unlikely.
Does the pivot have to be the rightmost item?
No. Any item in the range would work. The rightmost one is convenient because it can stay out of the way during the partition, and it doubles as a sentinel. Hour 14 replaces it with a smarter choice.
Why does partitionIt() stop at items equal to the pivot instead of skipping them?
Skipping them would make partitions badly unbalanced when the data holds many equal keys. By stopping and swapping, the pointers meet near the middle of a run of equal keys and split it evenly.
Why doesn't quicksort need a workspace array like mergesort's?
It rearranges items by swapping them within the array itself, and it has no merge step at the end. The only extra memory it uses is the stack space for its recursive calls.

Quiz

  1. What does partitioning do to an array?

    Answer

    It rearranges the items into two groups around a pivot value, with the smaller keys on the left and the larger keys on the right. The items within each group stay in no particular order.

  2. Why does partitioning take O(N) time?

    Answer

    The two pointers start at opposite ends and move toward each other until they meet, so each item is compared with the pivot about once. That is about N + 2 comparisons and at most about N/2 swaps.

  3. In quickSort1, why is the pivot in its final sorted position once partitionIt() returns?

    Answer

    The final swap puts it at the boundary between the groups. Every item to its left is smaller and every item to its right is larger, and later calls sort only the two sides, so nothing will ever move it.

  4. What is the base case of recQuickSort()?

    Answer

    A range that holds one item or none, which the code detects with right - left <= 0. Such a range is already sorted, so the function returns at once.

  5. Who invented quicksort, and when?

    Answer

    C.A.R. (Tony) Hoare, in 1962.

  6. Is partitioning stable?

    Answer

    No. Swaps can move items long distances, so two items with equal keys may end up in the opposite order from the one they started in.

Part III · Recursion and Quicksort

Hour 14 Improving Quicksort

The basic quicksort of Hour 13 slows to a crawl on data that is already in order. This hour fixes that with a smarter pivot, speeds up the smallest subarrays, and sums up how fast quicksort really is.

In this hour you'll learn

  • Why sorted and inversely sorted data drag the basic quicksort down to O(N²)
  • How median-of-three partitioning picks a better pivot, and how its C++ code works
  • How the quickSort2 applet compares with quickSort1 on inversely sorted data
  • Two ways to hand small partitions to an insertion sort
  • Why quicksort runs in O(N log N) time on average, and how it compares with the other sorts

Problems with Inversely Sorted Data

If you tried the last step of the quickSort1 exercise in Hour 13, you have already seen the problem. Given inversely sorted bars, the applet grinds through the sort far more slowly than it does with random ones. Data that is already sorted the normal way is just as bad.

The trouble lies in the pivot. A partition works best when the pivot value is the median of the items, the value with half the items above it and half below, because then the range splits into two equal halves. The further the pivot is from the median, the more lopsided the split. With inversely sorted data, the rightmost item is as far from the median as it can possibly be, since it is the smallest item in the range.

A pivot like that divides almost nothing. The left group is empty, the pivot takes one cell, and the other N − 1 items all end up in the right group. Picture splitting a class into students shorter and taller than a chosen classmate, and always choosing the shortest one. Everybody else lands in the taller group, and you have made almost no progress.

The next partition runs into the same trouble. With inversely sorted data, the swap that puts each pivot in place moves the largest item to the right end, so the pivots alternate between the smallest and the largest item left in the range. Either way, one group comes out empty every time. With data that is already sorted, the rightmost item is always the largest, and the result is the same.

Instead of about log₂N levels of recursion there are now N levels, and each level partitions just one item fewer than the level above it. The comparisons add up to about N + (N − 1) + (N − 2) + … + 1, which is roughly N²/2. The twelve inversely sorted bars in the first figure cost 76 comparisons, a little more than 12²/2 = 72. Quicksort has turned into an O(N²) sort, no better than the bubble sort of Hour 4.

There is a second danger. Every recursive call occupies space on the machine's call stack until it returns. With N levels of recursion, a large array can use up all of that space, and the program then crashes with a stack overflow instead of merely running slowly.

Median-of-Three Partitioning

People have proposed many ways to choose a better pivot. The ideal would be the true median of the subarray, since it always splits the range in half. Finding the true median, though, means examining every item, which takes longer than the sort can afford at every step.

The usual compromise is to look at just three items, the first, the middle and the last, and use the median of those three as the pivot. This is called median-of-three partitioning. Putting three items in order takes at most three comparisons, so choosing the pivot stays quick.

For sorted and inversely sorted data, the middle item is the true median of the range, so median-of-three picks an ideal pivot and the partitions stay well balanced. For random data, the median of three items is unlikely to be the smallest or largest item in the range. The worst case is still possible in principle, but it takes an unusual arrangement of data to trigger it.

Take the sorted numbers 10, 20, 30 and so on up to 90. The first, middle and last items are 10, 50 and 90, and their median, 50, is also the median of all nine numbers. The range splits into four items on each side of the pivot, as evenly as it possibly can.

Sorting the three sample items brings two bonuses. The first is speed in the inner loops. After the sort, the left item is no larger than the pivot, and the pivot itself sits just inside the right end.

The left item therefore stops rightPtr, and the pivot stops leftPtr. Both act as sentinels, so neither scan needs a range test. The inner loops run for every item on every level of recursion, so removing a test from them pays off.

The second bonus is less work. The left and right items are already on their correct sides, so the partition can skip them. The median is parked in cell right - 1, out of the way, and the partition deals only with cells left + 1 through right - 2. When the pointers cross, the pivot is swapped from right - 1 into its final place, just as before.

In the example, the partition covers cells 1 through 6 with the pivot 53. In the first round, leftPtr stops at 66 in cell 2 and rightPtr stops at 49 in cell 6, and the two are swapped. In the second round, leftPtr stops at 81 in cell 5 and rightPtr at 28 in cell 4, so the pointers have crossed. Swapping the pivot into cell 5 gives 17 35 49 12 28 53 66 81 92, with 53 in its sorted position.

C++ Code for Median-of-Three

The quickSort2.cpp program keeps the ArrayIns class of quickSort1.cpp and rewrites its private functions. recQuickSort() now gets its pivot from medianOf3(), and it passes small ranges to a new function, manualSort().

recQuickSort() starts by measuring its range, because the median-of-three method needs at least four items. With three, ordering the left, center and right items already sorts the whole range and leaves nothing to partition, and with two, the three sample positions overlap and the sentinels are lost. So a range of three or fewer items goes to manualSort(), which sorts it directly. Larger ranges get a median-of-three pivot, a partition and two recursive calls, as before.

medianOf3() finds the middle of the range and then makes three compare-and-swap steps. The first two leave the smallest of the three items in the left cell, and the third puts the center and right cells in order. The function then swaps the median into cell right - 1 and returns its value, which becomes the pivot.

Traced on the example from the figures, the left, center and right items start as 92, 17 and 53. The first step swaps 92 and 17, the second finds 17 and 53 already in order, and the third swaps 92 and 53, leaving 17, 53 and 92. The last swap moves 53 from cell 4 into cell 7 and sends the 28 that was there back to cell 4.

This partitionIt() is shorter than the one in quickSort1.cpp. leftPtr starts at left, so its first step lands on left + 1. rightPtr starts at right - 1, the pivot's cell, so its first step lands on right - 2. Neither scan tests the range, because the sentinels guarantee that both will stop, and the final swap uses right - 1, where the pivot was parked.

manualSort() treats the three small sizes separately. One item needs no work. Two items need one comparison and perhaps a swap. Three items need the same three compare-and-swap steps that medianOf3() uses, which is enough to put any three items in order.

main() is the same as in quickSort1.cpp. It fills the array with 16 random numbers, displays them, sorts them and displays them again. Here is one run.

48 96 94 91 31 77 2 3 17 68 9 33 23 52 78 99
2 3 9 17 23 31 33 48 52 68 77 78 91 94 96 99
