The quickSort2 Workshop applet uses median-of-three partitioning, and like manualSort() it sorts ranges of three or fewer items directly. Its display looks like the quickSort1 applet's. The lesson comes from running the two applets on the same kind of data.

Give quickSort2 inversely sorted bars and it stays fast. Each median-of-three pivot splits its range near the middle, the ranges shrink quickly, and the sort finishes in a small fraction of the steps quickSort1 needs. With random data, the two applets perform much more alike.

The re-creation below puts both algorithms in one applet, so you can compare them side by side. It starts with inversely sorted bars.

Try it. Race the two quicksorts on inversely sorted data.

  1. Choose quick1 in the algorithm menu, set Size to 100, and press Run. When it finishes, note the comparison and swap counts.
  2. Press Reverse to restore the inverse order, choose quick2, and press Run. Compare the counts with quick1's.
  3. Press New and run quick1 on random bars, then press New again and run quick2. The gap between them is much smaller now.
  4. Set Size to 12, choose quick2, and use Step. Watch the left, center and right bars being put in order before each partition, and the smallest ranges being sorted directly.

Counting comparisons in the C++ code of Hours 13 and 14 tells the same story as the applet. For 1,000 items in random order, quickSort1 makes about 11,800 comparisons and quickSort2 about 10,400. For the same items in inverse order, quickSort1 makes 500,498 comparisons with its recursion 1,000 calls deep, while quickSort2 makes 12,915.

Handling Small Partitions

Median-of-three already forced one special case, manualSort() for ranges of three items or fewer. The same idea can be pushed further. Quicksort is built for big arrays, and on a tiny subarray its machinery costs more than it saves. Every little range still pays for a function call, a median-of-three and a partition, while a simple sort could put a handful of items in order with far less fuss.

The waste adds up because the recursion is widest at the bottom. Each level holds about twice as many ranges as the level above it, so most of quicksort's calls are made on ranges of just a few items.

The insertion sort of Hour 5 is the natural helper. It is O(N²), but for a few items that hardly matters, and its overhead is tiny. There are two ways to combine it with quicksort.

Using an Insertion Sort for Small Partitions

The first way sets a cutoff. Any subarray smaller than the cutoff is sorted with an insertion sort instead of being partitioned any further. Lafore's quickSort3.cpp uses a cutoff of 10, and Donald Knuth recommends a cutoff of about 9. The best value depends on your computer, your compiler and your data, so it pays to experiment.

The new recQuickSort() looks like the quickSort2 version, except that it compares the size with the cutoff. Every range that reaches medianOf3() now holds at least ten items, so manualSort() is no longer needed.

insertionSort() is the insertion sort from Hour 5, adapted to work on the cells from left to right instead of the whole array. The outer loop takes each item in turn and holds it in temp. The inner loop shifts larger items one cell to the right until it finds the gap where temp belongs, stopping at left at the latest.

Insertion Sort Following Quicksort

The second way turns the idea around. Quicksort ignores every subarray smaller than the cutoff and leaves it unsorted. When the recursion is finished, the array is made of small blocks. Each block holds exactly the items that belong in it, in the right place relative to the other blocks, only jumbled among themselves.

A single insertion sort over the whole array then finishes the job. As Hour 5 showed, insertion sort is very fast on almost-sorted data, because no item has far to travel. Here no item sits more than a block's length from its final cell, so this last pass takes roughly linear time.

Both approaches give a modest speedup, and neither one changes quicksort's Big O. The size of the gain depends on the system, anywhere from a few percent to a few tens of percent.

Time it before you tune it. How much a cutoff helps depends on the machine, the compiler and the data, and on some systems the difference is small. Run both versions on data like yours and keep whichever is faster.

Efficiency of Quicksort

Quicksort runs in O(N log N) time on average. Its worst case is O(N²), but with median-of-three pivots that case becomes rare.

The reason for N log N is the one sketched in Hour 13. The ranges on each level of recursion are separate and together hold about N items, and partitioning is linear, so each level costs about N steps. When the pivots split ranges near the middle, the ranges halve from one level to the next. There is one range of N items, then two of N/2, then four of N/4, and so on, down to ranges of a single item after about log₂N levels.

About N steps on each of about log₂N levels gives N × log₂N steps. For a million items log₂N is about 20, so quicksort needs something like 20 million steps, where an O(N²) sort would need about a trillion.

The splits don't have to be perfect. Suppose every pivot split its range one quarter to three quarters. The largest range would still shrink by a fixed fraction at every level, so the number of levels would still grow like log N, at about 2.4 × log₂N. That is why a pivot that is merely reasonable, such as the median of three, is good enough.

Quicksort and the Other Sorts

Mergesort is also O(N log N), yet quicksort usually beats it in practice, for two reasons. First, quicksort sorts in place. It needs no workspace array and none of the copying into and out of one. Second, its inner loops are extremely tight, since each step of a scan is little more than one comparison and one increment.

Mergesort keeps one advantage of its own. Its running time is guaranteed, because it never degrades to O(N²) whatever the data, while quicksort's speed depends on getting reasonable pivots.

The sorts of Hours 4 to 14 compared
SortAverageWorst caseExtra memoryNotes
Bubble sortO(N²)O(N²)NoneSimplest, and usually the slowest
Insertion sortO(N²)O(N²)NoneVery fast on almost-sorted data
MergesortO(N log N)O(N log N)A workspace of N itemsSpeed hardly depends on the data
QuicksortO(N log N)O(N²), rare with median-of-threeNone beyond the recursion stackUsually the fastest in practice

Hour 24 returns to these trade-offs when it sums up which structures and algorithms to use when.

Summary

  • With the rightmost item as the pivot, sorted and inversely sorted data make every partition lopsided, with one group of N − 1 items and one empty group.
  • Lopsided partitions mean N levels of recursion instead of about log₂N, roughly N²/2 comparisons, O(N²) time, and a risk of overflowing the stack.
  • The ideal pivot is the median, but finding it takes too long. Median-of-three uses the median of the first, middle and last items instead.
  • Median-of-three keeps sorted and inversely sorted data balanced and makes the worst case rare for any data.
  • Ordering the three sample items puts sentinels at both ends, so the inner loops need no range tests, and the partition only has to cover cells left + 1 to right − 2.
  • Median-of-three needs at least four items, so quickSort2 sorts ranges of three or fewer with manualSort().
  • Small subarrays can be finished by an insertion sort, either one at a time below a cutoff (10 in the book, about 9 according to Knuth) or in one pass over the almost-sorted array at the end. Both give a modest speedup.
  • Quicksort averages O(N log N) and has a rare O(N²) worst case. It sorts in place and is usually faster than mergesort.

Q&A

Could I just pick the pivot at random?
Yes. A randomly chosen item is very unlikely to be the smallest or largest over and over, so it also escapes the sorted-data trap. Median-of-three has the extra benefit of setting up sentinels for the inner loops, and it doesn't depend on a random number generator.
Why does manualSort() handle exactly three items or fewer?
Median-of-three needs at least four items. With three, sorting the three sample items already sorts the whole range, and with two or one, the sample positions overlap and the sentinels disappear. Sorting such tiny ranges directly is simple and fast.
Does a cutoff change quicksort's Big O?
No. The insertion sorts work on blocks of fewer than ten items, so each item costs at most a few extra steps. The total stays proportional to N log N, and only the constant in front of it changes.
Is quicksort ever the wrong choice?
Sometimes. If a slow run can never be tolerated, mergesort's guaranteed O(N log N) is safer. If the data is known to be almost sorted already, an insertion sort alone may be quickest. And for a handful of items, any simple sort will do.

Quiz

  1. Why does inversely sorted data slow quickSort1 down to O(N²)?

    Answer

    The rightmost pivot is always the smallest or largest item in its range, so every partition leaves one group empty and the other with all the remaining items. That gives N levels of recursion instead of about log₂N, and roughly N²/2 comparisons.

  2. Which items does median-of-three examine, and which one becomes the pivot?

    Answer

    It examines the first, middle and last items of the subarray, puts them in order, and uses the middle value of the three as the pivot.

  3. Why does quickSort2 need manualSort() for subarrays of three items or fewer?

    Answer

    Median-of-three partitioning needs at least four items. With fewer, there is nothing left to partition, or the sample positions overlap and the sentinels that stop the scans are lost.

  4. What cutoff does Knuth suggest for switching to an insertion sort?

    Answer

    About 9 items. The book's quickSort3.cpp uses 10.

  5. What are the two ways to combine insertion sort with quicksort?

    Answer

    Either sort each subarray below the cutoff with an insertion sort as soon as the recursion reaches it, or leave all the small subarrays unsorted and run one insertion sort over the whole, almost-sorted array at the end.

  6. What are quicksort's average and worst-case Big O efficiencies, and how does its memory use compare with mergesort's?

    Answer

    O(N log N) on average and O(N²) in the worst case, which median-of-three makes rare. Quicksort sorts in place, apart from its recursion stack, while mergesort needs a workspace array as large as the data.

Part IV · Trees

Hour 15 Binary Trees

An ordered array finds items quickly but inserts them slowly, and a linked list does the reverse. A binary search tree is quick at both. This hour explains what a tree is, gives you the words for its parts, and shows how to find, insert and delete nodes in C++.

In this hour you'll learn

  • Why a tree can beat both an ordered array and a linked list
  • The vocabulary of trees: root, parent, child, leaf, subtree, level and key
  • How the Tree Workshop applet works, and how a tree is built from two C++ classes
  • How to find a node and how to insert a new one
  • How to delete a node in each of the three possible cases

Why Use Binary Trees?

Every structure so far has forced a trade. The ordered array of Hour 3 searches fast, because binary search needs only about log₂N comparisons. Inserting is slow, since every larger item must shift one cell to the right to make room, and deleting shifts them back. On average half the array moves, so both operations are O(N).

The linked list of Hours 8 to 10 has the opposite strengths. Once you are at the right spot, inserting or deleting a link means changing a pointer or two. Getting to the spot is the problem, because you can't jump into the middle of a list the way binary search jumps into an array. You walk from pFirst one link at a time, visiting half the list on average, so finding is O(N) even in a sorted list.

A tree combines the good halves of both. In a binary search tree that stays reasonably balanced, finding, inserting and deleting all take O(log N) time. For a million items that is about 20 steps per operation, where the array or the list needed hundreds of thousands. This hour and the next cover ordinary binary search trees, and Hours 17 to 20 show how to keep a tree balanced.

What Is a Tree?

A tree is a set of nodes connected by edges. The nodes usually stand for entities such as employees, car parts or airline reservations, and the edges show how those entities are related. In a C++ program an edge is a pointer. The program travels from node to node by following pointers, normally only downward, since a node keeps no pointer back up to its parent.

Computer trees are drawn upside down, with the root at the top and the leaves at the bottom, more like an organization chart than an oak. In a general tree, called a multiway tree, a node may have many children; you'll build one in Hours 19 and 20. In a binary tree each node has at most two. This hour is about one important kind of binary tree, the binary search tree.

Tree Terminology

Trees have a vocabulary of their own, and you'll meet these words for the rest of the book. The figure marks several of them.

  • Path. The sequence of nodes you pass through when you walk along edges from one node to another. The path from 50 to 30 runs through 25 and 37.
  • Root. The node at the top. A tree has exactly one, and exactly one path leads from it to any other node. If two routes led to the same node, the structure wouldn't be a tree.
  • Parent. Every node except the root has one edge running up to another node, its parent. 37 is the parent of 30 and 43.
  • Child. The nodes joined to a node from below. 30 and 43 are the children of 37.
  • Leaf. A node with no children, such as 12, 30, 43, 62 and 93.
  • Subtree. Any node can be seen as the root of a smaller tree made of its children, their children, and so on down. The subtree rooted at 75 holds 75, 62, 87 and 93.
  • Visiting. Arriving at a node in order to do something with it, such as checking or displaying its key. Passing through a node on the way somewhere else doesn't count.
  • Traversing. Visiting every node in some fixed order, such as ascending order of keys. Hour 16 covers it.
  • Levels. How many generations a node is from the root. The root is on level 0, its children on level 1, their children on level 2, and so on.
  • Keys. The data field used for searching. The number drawn inside each circle is that node's key.
  • Binary tree. A tree in which every node has at most two children, called the left child and the right child. A node may have two children, one, or none.

A binary search tree adds one rule. A node's left child has a smaller key than the node, and its right child has a key greater than or equal to it. The rule holds for whole subtrees, so every key to the left of 50 is below 50 and every key to its right is 50 or more. That arrangement is what makes fast searching possible.

Binary search tree. A binary tree in which, for every node, the left subtree holds only smaller keys and the right subtree holds only keys greater than or equal to the node's key.

A Tree Analogy in Your Computer

You already use a tree every day. The directories on a disk form a hierarchy, with the root directory (such as C:\) at the top, subdirectories below it, and files at the ends of the branches. A full file name such as C:\SALES\EAST\NOVEMBER\SMITH.DAT is literally a path from the root down to one leaf. File systems borrowed the words root and path from tree theory.

Two differences stand out. A directory can hold any number of entries, so the file system is a multiway tree rather than a binary one. And directories only organize things, while the data itself lives in the files at the leaves. In a binary search tree every node, the root included, holds data.

Unbalanced Trees

A tree's shape depends on the order in which its keys arrive. Keys in random order tend to build a bushy tree, with about as many nodes on each side of every node. Keys in sorted or nearly sorted order go to the same side one after another, and the tree grows lopsided.

In the figure, nearly every key after 20 is larger than the ones before it. Finding 70 takes five steps, although seven nodes fit into a tree of three levels. Keys in exactly sorted order make a straight line, no faster to search than a linked list. Hour 17 starts from that worst case, and until then the speeds claimed for trees assume a reasonably balanced shape.

Basic Binary Tree Operations

The everyday jobs are finding the node with a given key, inserting a node, and deleting one. Traversing, which visits every node in order, is the topic of Hour 16. It helps to watch the operations before reading the code.

The Tree Workshop Applet

The book's Tree Workshop applet draws a binary search tree of up to five levels, which hold at most 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 nodes. Fill builds a tree with however many random nodes you ask for. Find sends a red arrow from the root down the path toward the key you typed. Ins makes the same trip and adds a node where the path runs out, Trav steps through an inorder traversal, and Del deletes a node.

Watch the arrow during a find. It visits at most one node per level, so no search in the applet takes more than five steps. With Ins, notice that the new node always appears at the bottom of a branch. Random fills also tend to leave a few branches deeper than the rest, a mild case of imbalance.

Try it. The re-created applet below works like the book's.

  1. Press Fill to grow a random tree.
  2. Type a key that is in the tree and press Find. Count the nodes on its path.
  3. Type a key that is not in the tree and press Ins. It follows the same path and settles into an empty spot at the bottom.
  4. Type the key of a leaf and press Del. Repeat with a node that has one child, then with a node that has two children, and read the message for each case.

Representing the Tree in C++ Code

In C++ a tree is built from two classes. A Node holds one node's data plus a pointer to each child, and a Tree holds a pointer to the root and provides the operations.

iData is the key, and dData stands in for the rest of the record, which in a real program might be a name, an address and a salary. A NULL child pointer means that child doesn't exist. The constructor sets both pointers to NULL, so every new node starts out as a leaf. The book's Node has a constructor with no arguments and fills in the data afterward; passing the data in, as here, shortens the insertion code.

The Tree class stores only pRoot. Every node can be reached by following child pointers down from the root, and an empty tree simply has a NULL root. This hour covers find(), insert() and the ideas behind remove(); Hour 16 adds traversal and display.

Some programs store a tree in an array instead of using pointers. The root goes in cell 0, and the children of the node in cell i go in cells 2i+1 and 2i+2. A tree with gaps wastes cells, though, and a deletion can mean moving many items. This book uses pointers throughout.

Finding a Node

To find a key, start at the root and compare. If the key you want is smaller than the current node's key, move to the left child. If it is larger, move to the right child, and if the two are equal, you've found it. If the child you need is missing, the key isn't in the tree, since that empty spot is the only place it could have been.

A search for 50 in the same tree would take the same route as far as 57. There it would need 57's left child, find it missing, and report that 50 isn't in the tree. Here is the function.

pCurrent moves down one level per pass. The loop ends when it reaches a matching node or becomes NULL, and either way the function returns it. The book's version assumes the tree isn't empty and tests for NULL after each move; testing at the top of the loop, as here, also handles an empty tree. The caller gets a pointer, so it can display or change the node, as in if(pFound != NULL) pFound->displayNode();.

The search visits at most one node per level, and a balanced tree of N nodes has about log₂N levels, so finding is O(log N). The applet's 31-node tree never needs more than 5 comparisons, and a balanced million-node tree needs about 20. That is the same growth rate as binary search in an ordered array.

Inserting a Node

To insert a node, first find where it belongs by searching for the new key as if it were already there. The search ends by trying to move to a missing child, and that empty spot is where the new node goes, as a child of the last node visited.

A new node always becomes a leaf, and no existing node moves, so insertion never disturbs the rest of the tree. Since it follows the same path as find(), insertion is also O(log N) in a balanced tree, plus a fixed amount of work to attach the node.

There is one programming wrinkle. When the search reaches the empty spot, pCurrent is NULL and no longer tells you where you came from. So the code keeps a second pointer, pParent, one step behind. When pCurrent falls off the tree, pParent is the node that receives the new child.

An empty tree gets the new node as its root. Otherwise the loop walks down like find(), never stopping early, and the final comparison chooses pParent's left or right pointer. The book attaches the node inside the loop the moment it sees the NULL child, with the same effect. A key equal to the current node's key goes right, down the else branch; Hour 16 explains what that means for duplicate keys.

Deleting a Node

Deletion is the most complicated of the common operations. It starts with a search that records two extra facts: pParent, the parent of the node to delete, and isLeftChild, which says whether the node is its parent's left or right child. Deleting always changes one of the parent's child pointers, so you need both. When the root itself is deleted, the code changes pRoot instead.

What happens next depends on how many children the node has, which gives three cases.

Case 1: The Node Has No Children

To delete a leaf, set the parent's pointer to it, left or right according to isLeftChild, to NULL. The node is now cut off from the tree. The program also calls delete to free its memory, since C++ won't do that automatically.

Case 2: The Node Has One Child

A node with one child has only that child, and the child's subtree, beneath it. Connect the node's parent straight to the child, skipping the node being deleted, and the whole subtree moves up a level. The order is preserved, because everything below the deleted node was already on the correct side of the parent.

The code has more variations than the idea. The only child may be on the left or the right, and the deleted node may be a left child, a right child or the root. Each time, the pointer that used to lead to the deleted node is changed to lead to its child.

Case 3: The Node Has Two Children

A node with two children can't simply be replaced by one of them. If the right child moved up, it would also have to adopt the deleted node's left child, and it may already have a left child of its own.

Instead, the node is replaced by its inorder successor, the node with the next-highest key. The successor is larger than everything in the deleted node's left subtree and no larger than anything else in its right subtree, so it can take the deleted node's place without breaking the order.

Inorder successor. The node whose key comes right after a given node's key in ascending order. For a node with a right child, it is the node with the smallest key in the right subtree.

Finding the Successor

Go to the node's right child, then follow left-child pointers until you reach a node with no left child. That node is the successor. Every step to the left leads to a smaller key, so the node where you stop holds the smallest key on the right.

The successor can't have a left child, or the trip would have gone further. It may have a right child, though, and that child must be looked after when the successor moves. getSuccessor() finds the successor and, if it lies deeper than the right child, also makes two of the new connections.

pSuccessor slides left from the right child while pSuccessorParent trails one step behind. If the successor is the right child itself, the function just returns it. Otherwise it first carries out steps 1 and 2 of the list below. The book's version walks down with a third pointer, pCurrent, until that pointer becomes NULL, which comes to the same thing.

When the Successor Is the Right Child

If the deleted node's right child has no left child, that right child is the successor, and the job is easy. The successor moves up into the deleted node's place, keeps its own right subtree, and adopts the deleted node's left child into its empty left slot. In the figure above, deleting 40 would work this way. 40's right child, 45, has no left child, so 45 moves up under 25 and takes 30 (with 35 still attached) as its left subtree.

When the Successor Is Further Down

When the successor lies deeper, somewhere down the left side of the right subtree, four pointers change. In the figure, 25 is being deleted and its successor is 30, which has a right child, 35.

  1. Plug the successor's right child into the slot the successor is leaving, the left pointer of the successor's parent. 40's left child becomes 35.
  2. Plug the deleted node's right child into the successor's right pointer. 30's right child becomes 40.
  3. Point the deleted node's parent at the successor, or set pRoot to it if the root is being deleted. 50's left child becomes 30.
  4. Give the successor the deleted node's left child. 30's left child becomes 12.

Steps 1 and 2 happen in getSuccessor(), and steps 3 and 4 in remove(). Step 1 must come before step 2, or overwriting the successor's right pointer would lose 35 and everything below it. Here is the end of remove(), including the two-children case; the search has already set pCurrent, pParent and isLeftChild.

Each case in this version only chooses a pReplacement for pCurrent. For a leaf it is NULL, for one child it is that child, and for two children it is the successor, after the successor has adopted pCurrent's left subtree. One block then points the parent, or pRoot, at the replacement, and delete frees the old node. The book writes the parent connection out inside each case, with the same logic. The complete remove() is part of the full program in Hour 16.

Is Deletion Necessary?

Because deletion is so involved, some programs skip it. Each node gets a bool field such as isDeleted, and deleting a node just sets the flag to true. The other operations treat marked nodes as if they weren't there.

The tree never shrinks this way, and dead nodes still sit on the search paths. That is acceptable when deletions are rare, or when old records must be kept anyway, as with a company's files on its former employees.

Summary

  • An ordered array searches in O(log N) but inserts and deletes in O(N). A linked list inserts and deletes quickly but searches in O(N). A balanced binary search tree does all three in O(log N).
  • A tree is a set of nodes joined by edges. It has one root, every other node has exactly one parent, and nodes without children are leaves. The root is on level 0.
  • In a binary search tree each node has at most two children. Keys in its left subtree are smaller than its key, and keys in its right subtree are greater than or equal to it.
  • A disk's directory structure is a familiar multiway tree, and a full file name is a path from the root to a leaf.
  • Keys that arrive in sorted or nearly sorted order build a lopsided tree that searches slowly.
  • In C++, a Node holds the data plus pLeftChild and pRightChild, and the Tree holds only pRoot.
  • To find a key, go left for smaller keys and right for larger ones. A missing child means the key isn't there.
  • A new node goes where the search for it runs out of tree, so it always becomes a leaf. A trailing pParent pointer lets the code attach it.
  • Deleting a leaf sets the parent's pointer to NULL, and deleting a node with one child links its parent to that child. A node with two children is replaced by its inorder successor, the leftmost node of its right subtree.

Q&A

If my data rarely changes, do I still need a tree?
Maybe not. An ordered array is simpler, and binary search on it is as fast as a tree search. The tree pays off when insertions and deletions are frequent. With a million items, an array insertion moves about half a million items on average, while a tree insertion needs about 20 comparisons and one pointer change.
Could deletion use the next-lower key instead of the next-higher one?
Yes. The node with the next-lower key is the largest key in the left subtree, found by going left once and then right as far as possible. It works just as well, with every left and right swapped. The book uses the successor, and so does the code here.
Why does the Tree class hold only a pointer to the root?
Because every other node can be reached from the root by following child pointers. It also makes an empty tree easy to recognize, since pRoot is simply NULL.
Is every binary tree a binary search tree?
No. A binary tree only limits each node to two children. The ordering rule is what makes it a search tree. The expression trees in Hour 16 are binary trees whose shape follows an arithmetic formula instead of key order.

Quiz

  1. In a binary search tree, which child of a node has a key smaller than the node's key?

    Answer

    The left child. In fact every node in the left subtree has a smaller key, and every node in the right subtree has a key greater than or equal to the node's.

  2. What is the largest number of nodes a binary tree with five levels can hold?

    Answer

    31, because 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31. That is the limit of the Tree Workshop applet.

  3. Where does a newly inserted node always end up?

    Answer

    At a leaf position. It becomes the left or right child of the last node the search visited, in the spot where the search found a missing child.

  4. What are the three cases you must handle when deleting a node?

    Answer

    No children (set the parent's pointer to NULL), one child (connect the parent directly to that child), and two children (replace the node with its inorder successor).

  5. How do you find the inorder successor of a node that has two children?

    Answer

    Go to its right child, then keep going to left children until you reach a node with no left child. That node holds the smallest key in the right subtree.

  6. What is the Big O time for finding a node in a balanced binary search tree of N nodes?

    Answer

    O(log N). The search visits one node per level, and a balanced tree of N nodes has about log₂N levels.

Part IV · Trees

Hour 16 Traversing Binary Trees

Traversing a tree means visiting every node once, in a fixed order. This hour shows the three standard orders and the short recursive functions behind them, finds the smallest and largest keys, measures how fast trees really are, and assembles everything into a complete C++ program.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How inorder, preorder and postorder traversals work, and how recursion carries them out
  • How an expression tree turns into prefix and postfix notation
  • How to find the minimum and maximum keys
  • Why tree operations take O(log N) time, and what happens to duplicate keys
  • How the complete tree.cpp program fits together

Traversing the Tree

To traverse a tree is to visit every node exactly once, in some set order. Programs traverse trees less often than they find, insert or delete nodes, but traversal is how you print a tree's contents in sorted order or process every record in it. It is also one of the neatest uses of recursion (Hours 11 and 12) you'll ever see.

There are three simple orders, named for when a node is visited compared with its two subtrees. Preorder visits the node before its subtrees, inorder between them, and postorder after them. For binary search trees, inorder is the one you'll use most.

Inorder Traversal

An inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits the nodes in ascending order of their keys. The tree is never sorted into a list, yet a few lines of code read it out in order. When you need a sorted listing of the data, this is how you get it.

The recursive function inOrder() receives a pointer, pLocalRoot, to the node at the top of the subtree it should traverse. It does three things:

  1. Call itself to traverse the node's left subtree.
  2. Visit the node.
  3. Call itself to traverse the node's right subtree.

The base case is an empty subtree. When pLocalRoot is NULL, the function returns at once without doing anything.

The keys come out in ascending order because every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node's key, so step 1 prints all of them first, and every key in the right subtree is larger, so step 3 prints them afterward. The same reasoning holds inside each subtree, all the way down. A traversal of the whole tree starts with the call inOrder(pRoot).

Here, visiting a node means printing its key. It could just as well mean adding up salaries, writing records to a file or counting nodes.

Traversing a Three-Node Tree

To watch the recursion at work, trace inOrder() on a tiny tree with root A, left child B and right child C. The letters are only names, so you can follow the order of the visits.

The calls made by inOrder(A)
StepCall runningWhat it does
1inOrder(A)Calls inOrder(B) for A's left subtree
2inOrder(B)Calls inOrder(NULL) for B's left child
3inOrder(NULL)Finds nothing and returns at once
4inOrder(B)Visits B
5inOrder(B)Calls inOrder(NULL) for B's right child, which returns at once
6inOrder(B)Is finished and returns to inOrder(A)
7inOrder(A)Visits A
8inOrder(A)Calls inOrder(C) for its right subtree
9inOrder(C)Calls inOrder(NULL) for C's left child, which returns
10inOrder(C)Visits C
11inOrder(C)Calls inOrder(NULL) for C's right child, then returns to inOrder(A)
12inOrder(A)Is finished and returns to its caller; the traversal is over

The output is B A C. The function was called seven times, three times for real nodes and four times for NULL children, and every call returned to the one that made it.

Any binary tree has exactly one more NULL child pointer than it has nodes, so traversing N nodes takes 2N + 1 calls. That is still O(N).

Traversing with the Workshop Applet

In the Tree Workshop applet, each press of Trav moves the inorder traversal one step. The red arrow shows the node the algorithm has reached, and each time a node is visited its key joins a list at the bottom of the display. For a tree with 50 at the root, 30 and 60 as its children, and 20 and 40 below 30, the list grows 20, then 20 30, then 20 30 40, then 20 30 40 50, and finally 20 30 40 50 60.

Notice how the traversal moves. It first runs down the left edge to the smallest key without visiting anything on the way. After that, as the recursive calls return, it climbs back to parents to visit them and dives into right subtrees, passing through some nodes more than once while visiting each only once.

Try it. The re-created applet can traverse in all three orders.

  1. Press Fill, choose In from the order menu, and press Trav. Check that the keys come out in ascending order.
  2. Switch the menu to Pre and traverse again. The root comes out first, and every node appears before the nodes below it.
  3. Switch to Post. Now the root comes out last, and every node appears after its descendants.

Preorder and Postorder Traversals

Move the visit and you get the other two orders. A preorder traversal visits the node first, then traverses its left subtree, then its right subtree. A postorder traversal traverses the left subtree, then the right subtree, and visits the node last. The code has the same shape as inOrder(); only the line that visits the node moves.

The three orders applied to the seven-node tree above
OrderRuleOutput
Preordernode, left, right50 30 20 40 70 60 80
Inorderleft, node, right20 30 40 50 60 70 80
Postorderleft, right, node20 40 30 60 80 70 50

Preorder and postorder don't list a binary search tree in sorted order, so they are less useful there. They come into their own with other kinds of binary trees. One example is an expression tree, also called a parse tree, which represents an arithmetic expression. Each operator is a node, and its two children are its operands, which may be single variables or whole subexpressions.

Traversing this tree in each order writes the expression in a different notation.

  • Inorder gives A*B+C, the familiar infix form with each operator between its operands. The parentheses are lost, though, and without them the expression means (A*B)+C. To print a correct infix expression, you'd output an opening parenthesis before each operator's left operand and a closing one after its right operand.
  • Preorder gives *A+BC. This is prefix notation, in which each operator comes before its two operands. It never needs parentheses. The * applies to A and to +BC, and +BC means B+C.
  • Postorder gives ABC+*. This is postfix notation, also called Reverse Polish Notation, in which each operator follows its operands. Some calculators work this way, and a postfix expression is easy to evaluate with a stack (Hour 6).

To evaluate ABC+* with A = 2, B = 3 and C = 4, read left to right. Push 2, 3 and 4. The + pops 4 and 3 and pushes 7, and the * pops 7 and 2 and pushes 14, which is 2×(3+4).

Postorder has one more job in C++. To free every node in a tree, you must delete a node's children before the node itself, because once a node is gone you can't safely follow its pointers. A postorder traversal handles children first, so it is exactly what the tree's destructor needs, as the full program shows.

Finding Maximum and Minimum Values

The ordering rule makes the extremes easy to find. For the minimum, start at the root and go to its left child, then to that node's left child, and so on until you reach a node with no left child. That node holds the smallest key in the tree. For the maximum, keep going right instead.

Each function follows a single path down and returns a pointer to the node it finds, or NULL for an empty tree. The book's minimum() walks on until pCurrent becomes NULL and returns the last real node, which it keeps in pLast. Stopping one step earlier, as here, gives the same answer.

The minimum node has no left child, but it may have a right child, so it isn't necessarily a leaf. The successor search of Hour 15 is really a minimum search that starts at a node's right child. Both functions visit one node per level, so they are O(log N) in a balanced tree.

The Efficiency of Binary Trees

Finding, inserting and deleting all walk down the tree one level at a time, doing a fixed amount of work at each level. Their running time is therefore proportional to the number of levels, and the question is how many levels a tree of N nodes has.

Look at full trees, in which every level is completely filled. Each level holds twice as many nodes as the one above it, so the totals grow quickly.

Nodes and levels in a full binary tree
Number of nodesNumber of levels
11
32
73
154
315
1,02310
32,76715
1,048,57520
33,554,43125
1,073,741,82330

A full tree with L levels holds 2L − 1 nodes, so L = log₂(N+1). Real trees are seldom full, but a balanced one has about log₂N levels, which makes the common operations O(log N). A balanced tree of a million nodes needs about 20 comparisons per search, and one of a billion nodes about 30.

You may see the last two rows given as 33,554,432 and 1,073,741,824. Those are the powers of two 2²⁵ and 2³⁰, one more than a full tree of 25 or 30 levels actually holds.

Now compare the other structures. An ordered array also searches in O(log N), but inserting into a million-item array moves 500,000 items on average, while a tree insertion takes about 20 comparisons and one pointer change. Deletion from the array is just as slow. A linked list can insert at its front instantly, but finding or deleting a particular item means walking through half the list.

Speed of the basic operations
StructureSearchInsertionDeletion
Unordered arrayO(N)O(1)O(N)
Ordered arrayO(log N)O(N)O(N)
Linked listO(N)O(1)O(N)
Binary search tree, balancedO(log N)O(log N)O(log N)
Binary search tree, degenerated into a lineO(N)O(N)O(N)

Only the tree is fast at all three, as long as it stays balanced. Traversal is the one slower operation. It has to visit every node, so it is O(N) whatever the tree's shape, but that is rarely a problem because traversal is seldom part of the time-critical work of a program.

Duplicate Keys

Look again at insert() from Hour 15. When the new key equals the current node's key, the code takes the else branch and goes right. So a duplicate always lands in the right subtree of its twin, where it becomes the node that comes right after its twin in key order.

The trouble is that find() stops at the first match, the copy nearest the root, and never sees the others. You have two choices. You can forbid duplicates by having insert(), or the code that calls it, check with find() first and refuse a key that is already there. Or you can modify find() and the other functions to keep searching the right subtree for further copies. Many applications, such as a database keyed on unique ID numbers, never allow duplicates anyway.

Implementing a Binary Search Tree in C++

The pieces from this hour and the last come together in the program tree.cpp. The Node class is the one from Hour 15. The Tree class gains the traversal functions, minimum() and maximum(), a display function and a destructor. Here is its declaration.

The recursive helpers take a Node* so they can call themselves on subtrees. Code outside the class has no access to nodes, so the helpers are private, and the public traverse() starts the chosen one at pRoot. find(), insert() and getSuccessor() are exactly as shown in Hour 15.

The remove() Function

Here is the complete remove(), with the search and all three deletion cases.

The loop is the search, recording pParent and isLeftChild on the way down. The chain of if tests then picks pReplacement, which is NULL for a leaf, the only child when there is just one, or the inorder successor when there are two. A single block links the replacement into the parent (or pRoot), and delete frees the node.

The book's remove() repeats that linking block inside each case, and it assumes the tree isn't empty, because it reads the root's key before testing anything. This version's loop tests pCurrent first, so for an empty tree it simply returns false.

Traversing and Cleaning Up

traverse() uses a switch to start preOrder(), inOrder() or postOrder() at the root. The destructor calls destroy(pRoot), which is a postorder traversal whose visit is delete. Children are freed before their parent, so no pointer is followed after its node is gone. Without a destructor, every node would stay allocated after the Tree object disappeared. The helper's name is ours; what matters is the postorder.

Displaying the Tree

displayTree() draws the tree in text, one level per line, so you can check its shape. It prints 32 blanks before the root and halves the spacing on each new line, which keeps every node roughly centered above its two children. A missing node prints as --, and the display stops after a row in which no node has a child.

The book's version keeps the nodes of the current row on a stack. As it prints each node, it pushes that node's two children onto a second stack for the next row, or two placeholders if the node itself is missing, so every position lines up. The columns align only when all keys are two digits wide.

The main() Function

main() creates a Tree and inserts 11 nodes with the keys 50, 25, 75, 12, 37, 43, 30, 33, 87, 93 and 97, which produce the tree in the figure. It then loops, asking you to type the first letter of show, insert, find, delete or traverse. The i, f and d choices go on to ask for a key, and t asks for 1, 2 or 3 to choose preorder, inorder or postorder.

Here is a short session. Showing the tree prints it level by level, and an inorder traversal lists the keys in ascending order. Deleting 25, a node with two children, brings its successor 30 up into its place, and 33 moves into 30's old slot under 37.
