Summary

  • Traversing a tree visits every node once. The three standard orders are preorder (node, left, right), inorder (left, node, right) and postorder (left, right, node).
  • Each traversal is a short recursive function whose base case is a NULL subtree. Only the position of the visit differs.
  • An inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in ascending order.
  • In an expression tree, inorder gives infix notation (without its parentheses), preorder gives prefix notation, and postorder gives postfix notation.
  • Postorder deletes children before their parent, which is what a C++ destructor needs.
  • The minimum is at the end of the path of left children from the root, and the maximum at the end of the path of right children.
  • A full tree of L levels holds 2L − 1 nodes, so a balanced tree of N nodes has about log₂N levels. Find, insert and delete are O(log N); traversal is O(N).
  • The insertion code sends a duplicate key to the right, but find() sees only the first copy, so many programs forbid duplicates.
  • The tree.cpp program combines find, insert, remove, three traversals, a text display and a destructor behind a simple menu.

Q&A

Can a tree be traversed without recursion?
Yes. The recursive version quietly uses the computer's own stack to remember where to return. You can do the same work with an explicit stack of node pointers (Hour 6), pushing nodes as you go left and popping them to visit. The recursive version is much shorter, which is why the book uses it.
Does a traversal care whether the tree is balanced?
The number of visits is N either way. The depth of the recursion does depend on the shape. In a balanced tree the calls nest about log₂N deep, but in a tree that has degenerated into a line they nest N deep, which for a very large tree could use up the stack.
What is a preorder listing good for in a binary search tree?
It records the tree's shape. Every node comes before its descendants, so if you insert the keys into an empty tree in preorder, you get back exactly the same tree.
How do I keep duplicates out of the tree?
Call find() before insert() and skip the insertion if the key is already there, or build the same check into insert() itself.

Quiz

  1. A binary search tree has 40 at the root, 20 and 60 as its children, 10 and 30 as the children of 20, and 50 as the left child of 60. What does an inorder traversal print?

    Answer

    10 20 30 40 50 60. An inorder traversal of a binary search tree always produces the keys in ascending order.

  2. What does a preorder traversal of the expression tree for A*(B+C) produce, and what is that notation called?

    Answer

    *A+BC, which is prefix notation. Each operator comes before its two operands.

  3. How do you find the node with the largest key?

    Answer

    Start at the root and keep going to the right child until you reach a node with no right child. That node holds the maximum.

  4. About how many levels does a balanced tree of 1,000,000 nodes have?

    Answer

    About 20, since a full tree of 20 levels holds 1,048,575 nodes. A search therefore needs about 20 comparisons.

  5. Where does insert() put a key that duplicates one already in the tree?

    Answer

    In the right subtree of the existing node, because an equal key takes the "go right" branch. It becomes the node that follows its twin in key order.

  6. Why does the Tree destructor delete the nodes in postorder?

    Answer

    Postorder handles both children before their parent. If a parent were deleted first, its child pointers could no longer be followed safely, and the nodes below it would be lost without being freed.

Part IV · Trees

Hour 17 Red-Black Trees

An ordinary binary search tree turns slow when its data arrives in order. A red-black tree prevents that by coloring every node and obeying four rules that keep the tree balanced. This hour builds your feel for those rules through hands-on experiments with color flips and rotations.

In this hour you'll learn

  • Why sorted input cripples an ordinary binary search tree
  • The four red-black rules, black height and null children
  • How to drive the RBTree Workshop applet
  • What color flips and rotations do, through four experiments
  • How a rotation moves nodes and whole subtrees while keeping the tree in order

Our Approach to the Discussion

Red-black trees are among the most complicated structures in this book. The insertion algorithm has several special cases, and the code is long and hard to follow. So the book doesn't start with code. It takes a conceptual approach, and you learn by experimenting with the RBTree Workshop applet.

The applet lets you insert nodes and then repair the tree yourself with color changes and rotations, while it tells you whenever a rule is broken. After some trial and error you'll have a feel for what each repair does. Hour 18 turns that feel into precise rules for inserting a node.

Top-Down Insertion

There are two ways to organize a red-black insertion. In top-down insertion, the algorithm may change the tree's structure on its way down from the root to the insertion point, clearing away trouble before it gets there. In bottom-up insertion, it first finds the insertion point and inserts the node, then works back up the path repairing any damage. The book uses the top-down approach.

Balanced and Unbalanced Trees

Try inserting the keys 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, in that order, into an ordinary binary search tree. 10 becomes the root. 20 is larger, so it becomes 10's right child, and 30 is larger than both, so it becomes 20's right child. Every new node ends up as the right child of the one before.

Degenerates to O(N)

The result is really a linked list with an unused left pointer in every node. To find 50 you must pass through every node, so searching is O(N) instead of O(log N). With 10,000 items a search could take 10,000 comparisons, where a balanced tree would need about 14. Insertion suffers just as much, since it has to find its place first.

This happens whenever the data arrives already sorted. Ascending keys send every node to the right, descending keys send every node to the left, and partly sorted data builds a partly lopsided tree. Data often does arrive in order, for example when it is read from a file that was sorted earlier, so the problem is a practical one.

Balance to the Rescue

A balanced tree has roughly the same number of descendants on the left of each node as on its right, so its number of levels stays close to log₂N. The hard part is staying balanced as nodes come and go. A red-black tree does it by checking a few rules during every insertion and deletion and rearranging the tree when a rule is broken. The checks are local and cheap, so the balance costs little.

Red-Black Tree Characteristics

A red-black tree is a binary search tree with two extra features. First, every node has a color, red or black. The applet draws red and black circles, and in code the color is just one more field in the node. Second, whenever a node is inserted or deleted, certain rules about the arrangement of colors are enforced, and those rules are what keep the tree balanced.

The Red-Black Rules

Here are the four rules.

  1. Every node is either red or black.
  2. The root is always black.
  3. If a node is red, its children must be black. The reverse isn't required, so a black node may have black children.
  4. Every path from the root to a leaf, or to a null child, must contain the same number of black nodes.

The number of black nodes on a path from the root to a leaf is the path's black height, so rule 4 says that every such path has the same black height. In the valid tree below, every path from 50 down to a missing child passes through exactly two black nodes.

Black height. The number of black nodes on a path from the root to a leaf or null child. In a red-black tree it is the same for every such path.

A null child is a child that could exist but doesn't. A leaf has two null children, and a node with only a right child has a null left child. Rule 4 counts the paths that end at null children as well as the paths that end at leaves. That matters, because a lopsided shape can hide behind a missing child. A black root with a single black child has only one leaf, so counting leaves alone would find nothing wrong, while the path to the root's null child shows the imbalance at once.

Duplicate Keys

Duplicate keys are awkward in red-black trees. A rotation can carry a node from the right side of its twin to the left side, so the convention that equal keys go right no longer holds, and a search can miss some copies. The discussion in these hours assumes that every key is unique.

The Actions

When an insertion breaks a rule, two kinds of action can repair it. You can change the colors of nodes, and one particular three-node recoloring, the color flip, is especially useful. Or you can perform rotations, which rearrange nodes so that some move up and others move down. Insertion and deletion use combinations of these to keep all four rules true.

Color flip. Changing a black node that has two red children to red, and both children to black. If the node is the root, it stays black.

Using the RBTree Workshop Applet

The RBTree Workshop applet draws a red-black tree with red and black nodes. Unlike the Tree applet, it doesn't fix anything for you. It inserts a node wherever an ordinary binary search tree would put it, and then it's up to you to repair the tree. After every action it checks the four rules and reports what it finds.

Clicking on a Node

Several buttons act on one particular node, so you first select a node by clicking it. A red arrow then points to it. That is the node that will be flipped, rotated around, or recolored.

The Buttons

The RBTree applet's buttons
ButtonWhat it does
StartMakes a new tree containing only a black root with the key 50.
InsInserts a node with the key typed in the Number box. New nodes are always red, and nothing is fixed afterward.
DelDeletes the node with the typed key. (Our re-creation leaves this button out.)
FlipColor flip on the selected node. A black node with two red children turns red and its children turn black, except that the root stays black.
RoLRotates left, with the selected node at the top of the rotation.
RoRRotates right, with the selected node at the top of the rotation.
R/BToggles the selected node between red and black, for experimenting.

New nodes are red for a good reason. Adding a red node doesn't change the number of black nodes on any path, so it can never break rule 4. At worst it breaks rule 3, when its parent is also red, and that is the easier rule to repair.

Text Messages

A message area reports on the tree after each action. It tells you when a red node has a red child, when black heights differ, or when the root isn't black, and it confirms when the tree is red-black correct. The re-created applet shows the same information in a status line that checks all four rules.

Where's the Find Button?

There isn't one. Searching a red-black tree works exactly like searching any binary search tree, because colors play no part in a search. And Ins already performs that search to locate the insertion point, so a separate Find button would show nothing new.

Below is the re-created applet in manual mode. The steps walk you through the first experiment in the next section.

Try it. Experiment 1, by hand.

  1. Press Start. A black root, 50, appears.
  2. Type 25 and press Ins, then type 75 and press Ins. The status line reports a correct tree.
  3. Type 12 and press Ins. The status line reports a red node with a red child.
  4. Click 50 to select it and press Flip. 25 and 75 turn black, 50 stays black, and the tree is correct again.

Experimenting

Each of the following experiments teaches one idea. Try them in the applet above as you read.

Experiment 1: Inserting Two Red Nodes

Press Start to get a lone black 50, then insert 25. The new red node becomes 50's left child. A red child under a black parent breaks no rule, and every path still holds one black node. Insert 75 and it becomes a red right child, which is also legal. You now have a black node with two red children, a perfectly balanced little tree.

Now insert 12. It goes to the left of 25, and since 12 and 25 are both red, rule 3 is broken. The fix is a color flip at 50. Select 50 and press Flip. 25 and 75 turn black, and 50 would turn red, but it is the root, so it stays black. 12 is now a red child of a black node, and all four rules hold.

Look at what the flip did to the black heights. Before it, every path held one black node; afterward every path holds two, 50 plus either 25 or 75. All paths gained the same amount, so rule 4 still holds. A flip at the root is how a red-black tree adds one to its black height.

Experiment 2: Rotations

Press Start again and insert 25, then 12. Now 50, 25 and 12 form a line down the left side. Both 25 and 12 are red, which breaks rule 3, and the tree is plainly lopsided. A flip can't help, because 50 doesn't have two red children.

The cure is a rotation. Select 50 and press RoR. 25 rises to become the root, with 12 as its left child and 50 as its right child. The shape is now balanced, but the colors moved with their nodes, so the new tree breaks three rules at once.

Finish with R/B. Select 25 and make it black, then select 50 and make it red. The result is a black root with two red children, balanced and correct. The rotation fixed the shape, and the color changes fixed the rules.

Experiment 3: Color Flips and a Rotation Together

Start again and insert 25, 75 and 12, flipping at 50 when 12 arrives, as in Experiment 1. Then insert 37. It becomes 25's right child, a red node under a black one, so nothing needs fixing.

Insert 6. It lands under 12 as a red child of a red node, breaking rule 3. This time 25 is a black node with two red children, 12 and 37, so select 25 and flip it. 25 turns red and 12 and 37 turn black, and since 25's parent, 50, is black, no new conflict appears. Next insert 18, which becomes the red right child of the black 12 and needs no fixing.

Now insert 3. It lands under 6, which is red, so rule 3 is broken again. 12 is black with two red children, so flip at 12. That clears the conflict at the bottom but creates a new one higher up, because 12 is now red and so is its parent, 25. A flip can push a problem up the tree.

25's sibling, 75, is black, so another flip at 50 isn't possible. Rotate instead. Select 50 and press RoR, so 25 rises to the root and 50 moves down to its right, while 25's old right child, 37, crosses over to become 50's left child. Then use R/B to make 25 black and 50 red. Every rule now holds, and the nine nodes fit in four levels, as few as nine nodes allow.

Flips and rotations work as a team. A flip moves redness up the tree, and when that leaves two reds in a row, a rotation removes them. Hour 18 turns these moves into exact rules, doing the flips on the way down so that such conflicts are always easy to fix.

Experiment 4: An Unbalanced Tree

Now try to build a lopsided tree on purpose. Press Start and insert 60, 70 and 80 without fixing anything. Each new node becomes the right child of the one before, making a line down the right side. As soon as 70 goes in, the status line reports a red node with a red child.

Try recoloring your way out. If you make 70 black to separate the reds, the paths through 70 contain two black nodes while the path from 50 to its null left child contains one, so rule 4 breaks instead. No choice of colors makes a line of three or more nodes legal, which is why these error messages are a reliable sign of imbalance.

Rotations are the cure. Press Start again and insert 60 and 70. With 50, 60 and 70 in a line, select 50, press RoL, and recolor 60 black and 50 red. Then insert 80 and flip at 60; insert 90, rotate left at 70 and make 80 black and 70 red; insert 100 and flip at 80. The keys arrived in ascending order, yet the tree stays bushy.

More Experiments

Invent your own sequences, such as keys in descending order or alternating high and low values, and notice when a flip is enough and when you need a rotation. However the keys arrive, you can always repair the tree without letting it grow lopsided.

The reason is that rules 3 and 4 together forbid a lopsided shape. Rule 4 gives every path from the root to a null child the same number of black nodes, say B. Rule 3 forbids two reds in a row, so a path holds at most one red node for each black one and is at most 2B nodes long, while no path can be shorter than B. So no path is ever more than twice as long as any other. The balance is only approximate, but it is enough to keep searches O(log N).

Rotations

To balance a tree you have to move nodes physically, because recoloring never changes the shape. A rotation must do two things at once. It must raise some nodes and lower others to improve the balance, and it must keep the tree a valid binary search tree, with smaller keys to the left and larger ones to the right. A rotation that scrambled the order would break every later search.

Simple Rotations

Every rotation has a top node, which need not be the root of the whole tree. In a right rotation with node T at the top, T moves down and to the right, into the position of its own right child, and T's left child moves up to take T's place. T must have a left child, since that child is what rises. A left rotation is the mirror image. T's right child rises, T moves down to the left, and T must have a right child.

In the figure, 12 rises one level along with its parent, while 75 sinks one level along with its parent. The inorder listing, 12 25 50 75, is the same before and after, which confirms that the order was kept.

The Weird Crossover Node

That example hid a complication. Suppose 25 also has a right child, 37, and you rotate right around 50 again. 25 rises and 50 comes down as 25's new right child, but that slot already holds 37. So 37 moves across to become 50's left child, a slot that fell vacant when 25 moved up.

The order is still correct. 37 was in 25's right subtree, so it is larger than 25, and in 50's left subtree, so it is smaller than 50. As 50's left child it sits exactly where such a key belongs. 37 is called an inside grandchild of 50, because it lies on the side of 25 that faces the middle of the tree, while 12 is an outside grandchild. You'll meet these terms again in Hour 18.

Subtrees on the Move

In a real tree, each node in a rotation may carry a whole subtree, and the subtrees move with their roots. The figure shows the same right rotation with triangles standing for subtrees.

Subtree A moves up one level along with 25. Subtree B crosses over to become 50's left subtree and stays at the same depth. Subtree C moves down one level with 50. Every key in A is less than 25, every key in B lies between 25 and 50, and every key in C is greater than 50, both before and after the rotation.

However large the subtrees are, the rotation changes only three pointers: 50's left pointer, 25's right pointer, and the pointer that used to lead down to 50 (in its parent, or pRoot). The nodes inside A, B and C are not touched at all.

Human Beings Versus Computers

Rotations are hard to picture at first, and it's normal to stare at a tree wondering where each node will land. The applet makes them concrete. Rotate, look at the result, and undo it with a rotation in the other direction at the new top node. After a few tries the pattern becomes familiar.

For a computer, a rotation is easy. It is a handful of pointer assignments and takes the same time no matter how big the subtrees are. Here is a sketch of a right rotation using the Node class of Hour 15. It is our own illustration rather than the book's; Hour 18 describes what a complete insertion routine needs.

pUp is the left child that rises. The crossover subtree moves from pUp's right side to pTop's left side, and then pTop becomes pUp's right child. The caller stores the returned pointer wherever pTop used to hang, as in pRoot = rotateRight(pRoot);, which is the third pointer change. A left rotation swaps every left and right, and either one runs in O(1) time.

Summary

  • Keys inserted in sorted order turn an ordinary binary search tree into a line, and searching degrades from O(log N) to O(N).
  • A red-black tree is a binary search tree whose nodes are colored red or black and which obeys four rules during insertion and deletion.
  • The rules: every node is red or black, the root is black, a red node's children are black, and every path from the root to a leaf or null child has the same number of black nodes, the black height.
  • A null child is a missing child where a node could have one. Rule 4 counts the paths that end at null children.
  • New nodes are always red. Broken rules are repaired by color changes, including color flips, and by rotations.
  • A color flip turns a black node with two red children red and its children black. At the root the root stays black, and the black height grows by one.
  • A rotation raises one node and lowers another while keeping the keys in order. In a right rotation the top node's left child rises, and the inside grandchild crosses over to become the old top node's left child.
  • Whole subtrees move with their roots, yet a rotation changes only three pointers.
  • Rules 3 and 4 together guarantee that no path is more than twice as long as any other, so the tree stays roughly balanced.

Q&A

Why not just rebuild the whole tree whenever it gets lopsided?
You could read the keys out in order and build a perfectly balanced tree from them, but that takes O(N) time, and the tree would be slow between rebuilds. A red-black tree does a little O(log N) work on every insertion, so it is never badly out of balance.
Do the colors slow down searching?
No. A search ignores colors completely and runs exactly as in an ordinary binary search tree. The colors cost one extra field per node and some extra work during insertion and deletion.
Is a red-black tree perfectly balanced?
No. Its paths can differ in length by up to a factor of two. That is balanced enough to guarantee O(log N) searches, and allowing that much slack is what keeps the repairs cheap.
What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up insertion?
They schedule the same kinds of repairs differently. Bottom-up insertion adds the node first and then walks back up the path fixing problems, which requires some way to get from a node to its parent. Top-down insertion fixes things during the single trip down, and that is the approach this book follows.

Quiz

  1. What are the four red-black rules?

    Answer

    1. Every node is red or black. 2. The root is always black. 3. If a node is red, its children must be black. 4. Every path from the root to a leaf or null child contains the same number of black nodes.

  2. What is the black height of a path?

    Answer

    The number of black nodes on the path from the root to a leaf or null child. Rule 4 requires it to be the same for every such path.

  3. What is a null child?

    Answer

    A child that could exist but doesn't, such as the missing left child of a node that has only a right child. Rule 4 counts the paths that end at null children, so an imbalance can't hide behind a missing child.

  4. What does a color flip do?

    Answer

    It changes a black node with two red children to red and both children to black. If the node is the root, it stays black, which raises the black height of every path by one.

  5. In a right rotation with node T at the top, which node moves up, where does T go, and what happens to the crossover node?

    Answer

    T's left child moves up into T's place, and T moves down to become that child's right child. The rising child's old right child, the inside grandchild, crosses over to become T's new left child.

  6. Why does data that arrives in sorted order hurt an ordinary binary search tree?

    Answer

    Every new key goes to the same side as the last one, so the tree becomes a line like a linked list. Searching then takes O(N) time instead of O(log N).

Part IV · Trees

Hour 18 Red-Black Tree Insertions

In Hour 17 you kept a red-black tree legal by hand, picking each color flip and rotation yourself. This hour turns that trial and error into a recipe a program can follow, so that every insertion leaves the tree balanced.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How top-down insertion flips colors on its way down the tree
  • What X, P, and G are, and how to tell an outside grandchild from an inside one
  • The three situations that can follow an insertion, and the rotations that repair each one
  • How to repair a conflict that a color flip creates halfway down
  • Why deletion is harder, and how efficient red-black trees are
  • What insertion code needs, and where AVL trees and multiway trees fit in

Inserting a New Node

With the RBTree applet in Hour 17, you were the brains of the operation. You inserted a node, read the complaint in the message area, and chose a flip or a rotation that looked promising. A program can't guess like that. It needs a rule for every situation, decided in advance.

This hour supplies those rules for insertion. They follow the top-down approach, in which all the repairs happen on the way down to the insertion point, plus one small fix at the bottom. Every step is judged against the four red-black rules, so keep them in view.

  1. Every node is either red or black.
  2. The root is always black.
  3. If a node is red, its children must be black.
  4. Every path from the root to a leaf or to a null child contains the same number of black nodes (the black height).

Preview of the Insertion Process

Insertion starts as in an ordinary binary search tree (Hour 15). From the root you go left for a smaller key and right for a larger one, until the next step would lead to a null child. The new node is attached there. The red-black version adds three kinds of repair work to that trip.

  1. Color flips on the way down. Whenever the search passes a black node with two red children, it flips the colors of all three nodes.
  2. Rotations after the node is inserted. The new node is always red. If its parent is red too, rule 3 is broken, and one or two rotations plus a few color changes repair it.
  3. Rotations on the way down. A flip can itself leave a red node under a red parent. The same kind of rotation fixes that at once, and then the search carries on.

Step 3 actually happens during the descent, before step 2. We'll still take them in the order listed, because the repairs after insertion are easier to picture, and the repairs on the way down reuse the same moves.

X, P, and G

The rules need names for three related nodes. X is the node that caused a rule to break. Sometimes it is the node just inserted, and sometimes it is a node whose color a flip just changed. P is X's parent, and G is X's grandparent (the parent of P).

X is an outside grandchild of G when it is on the same side of P as P is of G, so both are left children or both are right children. X is an inside grandchild when the sides differ, for example when X is a right child and P is a left child. Trace G, P, and X with a finger. A straight slant means outside, and a zigzag means inside. An outside grandchild takes one rotation to repair, and an inside grandchild takes two.

Each picture has a mirror image with P on G's right side. If P were 75, a right child 87 would be an outside grandchild and a left child 62 an inside one. The rules work the same way there, with every rotation reversed.

Color Flips on the Way Down

As the search descends, it examines each node before moving on. If the node is black and both its children are red, the search performs a color flip, turning the node red and its two children black. This is the applet's Flip button from Hour 17, now applied automatically.

A flip never disturbs rule 4. Every path through the flipped node used to count a black node at the parent's level and none at the child's level. Afterward it is the other way around. The black simply slides down one level, so every black height stays the same. If the flipped node is the root, it stays black (rule 2) while its children still turn black, so every path gains one black node. All paths gain equally, rule 4 still holds, and the tree's black height grows by one, just as in Hour 17's first experiment.

Rule 3 is the one a flip can break. If the flipped node's parent is red, two reds now sit in a row, and a rotation on the way down is needed (covered at the end of this section). If the parent is black, the flip is complete.

Flipping before anything is broken clears away one troublesome arrangement, a red parent whose sibling is also red. Every black node with two red children along the path gets flipped, so by the time the search reaches the bottom, the new node's parent never has a red sibling. The repair after insertion is then always one of a few simple cases. (In Hour 20 you'll see that a flip does the same job as splitting a full node in a 2-3-4 tree.)

Here is a flip in context. Suppose you have inserted 50, 25, 75, 12, and 37. The root flip happened when 12 arrived, and 37 became a red child of black 25. Now insert 30. At 50 there is nothing to do, because its children are black. At 25 the search finds a black node with two red children and flips it. The parent of 25 is the black root, so rule 3 is safe. The search continues to 37, and 30 becomes its red left child.

Rotations After the Node Is Inserted

The new node is always red because a red node adds nothing to any black height, so rule 4 can't break. A new black node would lengthen only the paths running through it, which would put rule 4 out of step all over the tree. With a red node, only rule 3 is at risk.

Call the new node X. If its parent P is red, then G must exist and must be black, since the root is always black and rule 3 held before X arrived. What happens next depends on P's color and on X's position, which gives three possibilities.

Possibility 1: P Is Black

There is nothing to do. A red node under a black one breaks no rule and changes no black height. You have already seen this case twice: 37 under black 25, and 30 under black 37.

Possibility 2: P Is Red and X Is an Outside Grandchild

X and P are both red, and they sit in a straight line below G. Three steps repair the damage.

  1. Switch the color of G.
  2. Switch the color of P.
  3. Rotate with G at the top, in the direction that raises X. If X and P are left children, that is a right rotation.

Start with the root 50 and insert 25 and 75, which become red children. Insert 12. On the way down 50 gets flipped; being the root, it stays black, while 25 and 75 turn black. Then 12 goes in as a red child of black 25 (Possibility 1). Now insert 6. It becomes the red left child of red 12. X is 6, P is 12, and G is 25, so X is an outside grandchild. Switch 25 to red and 12 to black, then rotate right at 25. Node 12 rises into 25's place under 50, with 6 on its left and 25 on its right.

The rotation turns the lopsided chain 25, 12, 6 into a small balanced triangle with the middle key on top. The color switches give that triangle a black top and two red children, so it still adds exactly one black node to every path through it, as black 25 did before.

Possibility 3: P Is Red and X Is an Inside Grandchild

When the path from G to X bends, a single rotation at G only moves the bend to the other side. The repair takes four steps.

  1. Switch the color of G.
  2. Switch the color of X (not P this time).
  3. Rotate with P at the top, in the direction that raises X. X takes P's place, and the three nodes now form a straight line.
  4. Rotate with G at the top, in the direction that raises X again.

Use the same starting tree, but insert 18 instead of 6. It becomes the red right child of red 12, so X is 18, P is 12, and G is 25, and X is an inside grandchild. Switch 25 to red and 18 to black. Rotate left at 12, so that 18 takes 12's place and 12 becomes its left child. Now 25, 18, and 12 form a straight line, as in the outside case. Rotate right at 25, and 18 rises again while 25 becomes its right child. The result is black 18 with red children 12 and 25.

One pattern links the two repairs. Whichever of X, P, and G finishes on top turns black, and the other two finish red. In Possibility 2 that node is P, and in Possibility 3 it is X, which is why X's color gets switched instead of P's.

What About Other Possibilities?

One more arrangement is imaginable, a red P whose sibling (X's uncle) is also red. The rotation recipe would fail there, because G would end up red above a red node. Fortunately it can't happen. If P and its sibling were both red, G would be a black node with two red children, and the search flipped every such node on its way down.

So at the bottom, P is either black, or red with a black or missing sibling. The three possibilities cover everything, and that is the real payoff of the flips.

Rotations on the Way Down

A flip turns the flipped node red. If its parent is red too, rule 3 breaks in the middle of the descent, and the algorithm repairs it right away, before taking another step down. The moves are the ones you just learned, with a new cast. X is now the node that was flipped. For an outside grandchild, switch the colors of G and P and rotate once at G. For an inside grandchild, switch the colors of G and X, rotate at P, and then rotate at G. Each example below builds a tree and then inserts one key that triggers the problem.

Outside Grandchild on the Way Down

Insert 50, 25, 75, 12, 37, 6, and 18. Along the way 12 triggers the root flip, and 6 triggers a flip at 25 (harmless, because 25's parent is black). By the end, 6 and 18 are red children of black 12.

Now insert 3. The search passes red 25 and reaches 12, which is black with two red children, so it flips. But 12's parent, 25, is red. With X = 12, P = 25, and G = 50, X is an outside grandchild. Switch 50 to red and 25 to black, then rotate right at 50. Since 50 was the root, 25 becomes the new root, and 37 crosses over from 25 to become 50's left child (the crossover node of Hour 17). The search resumes from 12, and 3 settles in as a red child of black 6.

Inside Grandchild on the Way Down

For the bent version, insert 50, 25, 75, 12, 37, 31, and 43. This time 31 triggers the flip at 25, and by the end 31 and 43 are red children of black 37.

Now insert 28. The search reaches 37, black with two red children, and flips it, which leaves red 37 under red 25. With X = 37, P = 25, and G = 50, X is an inside grandchild. Switch 50 to red and 37 to black. Rotate left at 25: 37 takes 25's place, and 31 crosses over to become 25's right child. Rotate right at 50: 37 becomes the root, and 43 crosses over to become 50's left child. Each rotation moves one crossover node. The search continues from 37, and 28 becomes a red child of black 31.

The book's RBTree applet leaves every repair to you, so you can replay these examples there by hand. For Possibility 2, for instance, you would select 25 and press R/B, select 12 and press R/B, then select 25 and press RoR. Our re-creation below starts in an automatic mode instead, where each press of Ins carries out the whole top-down algorithm and writes every flip and rotation to a log. Its Manual setting works like the book's applet, if you want to make the repairs yourself.

Try it. Predict each move, then check it against the log.

  1. Press Start for a tree holding only the black root 50. Insert 25, 75, 12, and 6, one at a time. The log should show a flip at 50, then an outside-grandchild repair.
  2. Press Start again and insert 25, 75, 12, and 18 to see the inside case, with two rotations.
  3. For rotations on the way down, start over with 25, 75, 12, 37, 6, 18, and 3, and then with 25, 75, 12, 37, 31, 43, and 28.
  4. Press Ascending to insert 10, 20, 30, and so on. A plain binary search tree would become one long chain, but this tree stays short and bushy. Step replays the most recent insertion one action at a time.

Deletion

Deletion starts like ordinary binary search tree deletion (Hour 15), including the use of the inorder successor when the node has two children. The trouble comes afterward. Removing a red node changes no black height, but removing a black node leaves every path through it one black node short, which breaks rule 4. The repair involves more cases than insertion, and its color changes and rotations can ripple back up the tree.

The book doesn't work through the deletion algorithm. Many implementations sidestep it with an isDeleted flag, as described in Hour 15. Deleting just marks the node, and the other operations skip marked nodes. The tree's shape never changes, so its balance is never disturbed. That is a sensible trade when deletions are rare, though the dead nodes still take up memory.

Efficiency of Red-Black Trees

Search, insertion, and deletion in a red-black tree all take O(log N) time, and the tree keeps that promise whatever order the data arrives in.

A search visits one node per level. A typical search takes about log₂N comparisons, and it can be shown that no search ever needs more than about 2×log₂N. The factor of 2 comes from the rules. All paths hold the same number of black nodes, and red nodes never come two in a row, so the longest possible path (alternating black and red) is at most twice as long as the shortest (all black).

Comparisons needed to find a key among N items (rounded up)
NPlain BST built from sorted keys (worst)Red-black tree, typicalRed-black tree, never more than
1,0001,0001020
10,00010,0001428
1,000,0001,000,0002040
1,000,000,0001,000,000,0003060

The search routine never looks at colors, so a red-black tree is exactly as fast to search as an ordinary tree of the same shape. The only storage cost is the color itself, one bit of information per node, usually kept in a bool.

Insertion and deletion are slower than in an ordinary tree by a constant factor, because of the flips and rotations. On average an insertion needs about one rotation. Both operations remain O(log N). Since most programs search far more often than they insert or delete, the overall penalty is small, and in return sorted or nearly sorted input can no longer turn the tree into a slow O(N) list.

Implementing the Insertion Process

The book doesn't list code for red-black insertion. It describes what the code needs, and with this hour's rules the list is short.

  • A color in every node. A bool isRed data member is enough.
  • The ordinary insertion routine from Hour 15 as a starting point.
  • A check at each node on the way down. A black node with two red children gets flipped, but the root stays black.
  • After a flip, a red-red check against the parent, repaired by one rotation (outside grandchild) or two (inside grandchild) plus the color switches.
  • At the bottom, the new node inserted as red, followed by the same check.

The rotations need X, P, G, and also G's parent, because the node that ends up on top must be hooked back in where G used to hang. You can track four pointers during the descent, or you can give each node a pointer to its parent.

The code never has to compute a black height. Rule 3 can be checked locally, by comparing a node with its parent, and if the flips and rotations are done correctly, rule 4 takes care of itself. The Workshop applet checks black heights only because a person pressing buttons can easily make a wrong move.

The two listings below are a compact sketch of our own, not from the book. They follow this hour's rules and use parent pointers. The RBTree class holds pRoot and declares these functions plus a one-line helper, isRedNode(p), which returns p != NULL && p->isRed so that a missing child counts as black. Searching works exactly as in Hour 15.

replaceChild() hangs the rising node where the old top used to hang. If the old top was the root, it updates pRoot, which is what happened when the rotation at 50 made 25 the root. In rotateRight(), pRiser is the left child of pTop. Its right subtree, the crossover subtree, moves across to become pTop's left subtree. Then pRiser takes pTop's place, and pTop becomes its right child. rotateLeft() is the mirror image, with Left and Right exchanged.

fixRedRed() handles every red-red conflict, whether X is a new node or one that a flip just turned red. G always turns red. If X and P hang on the same side, X is an outside grandchild, so P turns black and one rotation at G follows. Otherwise X turns black, a rotation at P lifts X into P's place, and the rotation at G lifts it again. The two bools pick the rotation directions, so the mirror-image cases need no extra code.

insert() is the ordinary descent with the flip test added. After a repair it simply continues down from the same node. That is safe, because the subtrees the search still needs are either below that node or were handed to P and G, which are now its children. The last line keeps the root black, which matters when the very first node goes in. Fed the keys 1 to 1,000 in ascending order, this code builds a tree only 16 levels deep, where a plain binary search tree would be 1,000 levels deep.

Other Balanced Trees

The oldest balanced tree is the AVL tree, named for Adelson-Velskii and Landis, who described it in 1962. Each node stores the difference between the heights of its left and right subtrees, and that difference may never be more than 1. After an insertion, the algorithm walks back up the insertion path, checking each node. Where the difference has reached 2, it rebalances with a single rotation or, when the path bends, a double rotation, much like this hour's outside and inside cases.

AVL tree. A binary search tree in which, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one.

Because an AVL tree is so tightly balanced, searches are fast. Insertion is a little slower than in a red-black tree, since it needs a pass down to insert and a pass back up to check, while top-down red-black insertion does all its work on the way down.

The other big family is the multiway tree, whose nodes can have more than two children. You'll meet the simplest one, the 2-3-4 tree, in Hour 19. Its larger relative, the B-tree, packs many keys into each node and is widely used for data stored on disk.

Summary

  • Top-down insertion repairs the tree during a single trip from the root to the insertion point, plus one small fix at the bottom.
  • On the way down, every black node with two red children gets a color flip. A flip never changes black heights; at the root, the root stays black and the whole tree's black height grows by one.
  • A new node is always red, so an insertion can break rule 3 but never rule 4.
  • X is the node that caused a violation, P its parent, and G its grandparent. X is an outside grandchild if it is on the same side of P as P is of G, and an inside grandchild otherwise.
  • If P is black, nothing needs doing. If P is red and X is outside, switch G and P and rotate once at G. If P is red and X is inside, switch G and X, rotate at P, then rotate at G.
  • The flips on the way down guarantee that P never has a red sibling at the bottom, so those three cases are the only ones.
  • A flip can create a red-red conflict halfway down. It is repaired at once with the same moves before the search continues.
  • Deletion is considerably more complicated, and many programs avoid it by marking nodes as deleted.
  • Search, insertion, and deletion are all O(log N). Searching costs the same as in an ordinary tree of the same shape, and an insertion needs about one rotation on average.

Q&A

Why does the algorithm always insert the new node as red?
A red node adds no black node to any path, so rule 4 can't break. At worst rule 3 breaks, which is a local problem between X and its parent that one or two rotations can fix. A new black node would add a black node to some paths and not others, upsetting rule 4 across the tree.
Is a red-black tree perfectly balanced?
No. Some paths may be longer than others, but never more than twice as long. That is enough to guarantee O(log N) operations, and it is much cheaper to maintain than perfect balance.
How does an AVL tree differ from a red-black tree?
An AVL tree stores a height difference in each node instead of a color, and it insists that the two subtrees of every node differ in height by at most one. It is more tightly balanced, so searches can be slightly faster, but each insertion needs a pass down and a pass back up.

Quiz

  1. In the insertion algorithm, what are X, P, and G, and when is X an outside grandchild?

    Answer

    X is the node that caused a rule violation (a new node or a node whose color was just flipped), P is its parent, and G is its grandparent. X is an outside grandchild when it is on the same side of P as P is of G, so both are left children or both are right children.

  2. You have just inserted a red node, and its parent is black. What must you do?

    Answer

    Nothing. A red child of a black node breaks no rule, and a red node doesn't change any black height.

  3. The new node X is red, its parent P is red, and X is an outside grandchild of G. How do you fix the tree?

    Answer

    Switch the color of G, switch the color of P, and rotate with G at the top in the direction that raises X (a right rotation if X and P are left children).

  4. How does the fix change when X is an inside grandchild?

    Answer

    Switch the colors of G and X instead of G and P. Rotate with P at the top to raise X, which straightens the line, and then rotate with G at the top to raise X again. Two rotations are needed.

  5. Why does the algorithm perform color flips on the way down?

    Answer

    So that when the search reaches the insertion point, the new node's parent can't have a red sibling. That rules out the hard case and leaves only the three simple possibilities for the repair at the bottom.

  6. What is the Big O efficiency of searching a red-black tree, and how does it compare with searching an ordinary binary search tree of the same shape?

    Answer

    O(log N), with about log₂N comparisons normally and never more than about 2×log₂N. It is exactly as fast as searching an ordinary tree of the same shape, because the search ignores the colors.

Part IV · Trees

Hour 19 2-3-4 Trees

A 2-3-4 tree lets each node hold up to three keys and have up to four children. That extra room lets the tree stay perfectly balanced with nothing more than an occasional node split, which makes it much easier to follow than a red-black tree.

In this hour you'll learn

  • What a multiway tree is, and why the 2-3-4 tree is worth studying
  • How data items and children are arranged in a 2-3-4 node
  • How to search a 2-3-4 tree and where new items go
  • How nodes split, including the root, and why the leaves always stay level
  • How to watch searches, insertions, and splits in the Tree234 Workshop applet

Introduction to 2-3-4 Trees

Every tree you've met so far has been a binary tree, in which each node holds one data item and has at most two children. A 2-3-4 tree is a multiway tree. Each of its nodes can hold up to three data items and can have up to four children.

Multiway tree. A tree whose nodes can have more than two children. A 2-3-4 tree is a multiway tree of order 4, meaning four is the most children a node can have.

The 2-3-4 tree earns its place in the book for three reasons. It is a balanced tree, like the red-black tree, but it is easier to understand and to program, because it never needs a rotation. It has a surprising relationship with red-black trees, which Hour 20 reveals. And it is the simplest member of the B-tree family, the multiway trees used for storing data on disk.

What's in a Name?

The 2, 3, and 4 count the links to children a node can have. A node holding one data item always has two children, and it is called a 2-node. A node with two data items has three children (a 3-node), and a node with three data items has four children (a 4-node). In short, a non-leaf node always has exactly one more child than it has data items.

Leaves are the exception, since they have no children at all. A leaf can hold one, two, or three items, but it can't be empty, and no node in a 2-3-4 tree may be empty. Unlike a binary tree, where a node can have a single child, a non-leaf 2-3-4 node never has just one child link.

One more property gives the tree its strength. All the leaves are always on the same level, the bottom one, so a 2-3-4 tree is always perfectly balanced in height. You'll soon see how insertion manages to keep it that way.

2-3-4 Tree Organization

Inside a node, the data items are kept in ascending order of their keys, from left to right, in positions numbered 0, 1, and 2. The child links are numbered 0 to 3, and each child covers a range of keys.

  • Child 0 holds keys smaller than key 0.
  • Child 1 holds keys between key 0 and key 1.
  • Child 2 holds keys between key 1 and key 2.
  • Child 3 holds keys larger than key 2.

A node with fewer items simply uses fewer child links, so a 2-node uses only children 0 and 1. This is the binary search tree rule stretched to fit bigger nodes. A binary node splits the keys below it into two ranges, and a 4-node splits them into four. As in the book, assume that no two items have the same key.

Searching for a Data Item

Searching works much as it does in a binary search tree. Start at the root. If the key you want isn't one of the node's items, pick the child whose range contains it and move there. Repeat until you find the key, or until you reach a leaf that doesn't hold it, in which case the key isn't in the tree.

Try finding 64 in the tree below. The root holds 50, and 64 is larger, so the search follows child 1. That node holds 60 and 70, and 64 lies between them, so the search follows that node's child 1. The leaf there holds 62, 64, and 66, and the search is over.

Each node visited may take up to three comparisons instead of one, but the tree has fewer levels to pass through. Hour 20 weighs that trade.

Inserting a New Data Item

New data items are always inserted in leaves, on the bottom row of the tree. Putting one into an interior node would give that node an extra item without an extra child, which would break the one-more-child rule.

To insert, you follow the same path a search for the new key would take. If the leaf at the end of the path isn't full, the job is easy. The new item goes into its proper place in key order, and any larger items in the node shift one position to the right to make room. If the search meets a full node anywhere on its way down, that node must be split first, as the next section explains.

Node Splits

A full node holds three items. Call them A, B, and C, in key order. If the node isn't a leaf, it also has four children. The book uses a top-down method, which splits a full node as soon as the insertion's search meets it, before going any further. A split takes five steps.

  1. Create a new, empty node. It becomes a sibling of the node being split, placed to its right.
  2. Move item C into the new node.
  3. Move item B into the parent of the node being split.
  4. Leave item A where it is.
  5. Disconnect the two rightmost children from the node being split and connect them to the new node.

Afterward the old node holds only A and the new node holds only C, with B in the parent between them, marking the boundary between their ranges. The parent's links to children farther right each shift one place to make room for the new sibling. Every key is still in its correct place, and no leaf has changed its depth.

Here is an example. The root holds 50, its left child holds 30, and its right child holds 60, 70, and 80. You want to insert 99. The search goes right from 50 and meets the full node, so it splits that node. 60 (item A) stays, 70 (item B) moves up into the parent beside 50, and 80 (item C) moves into a new node on the right. Then the search continues. Since 99 is larger than 70, it goes to the new node, which has room, and settles in beside 80.

In that example the full node was a leaf, so there were no children to move. When a full interior node splits, its four children are shared out. The two left children stay with A. The two right children move to the new node, as its children 0 and 1. Their ranges still fit, because every key in them is larger than B, one child's keys are smaller than C, and the other's are larger.

Splitting the Root

When the root itself is full at the start of an insertion, there is no parent to receive item B, so the split works a little differently.

  • A new node is created to be the new root, and it becomes the parent of the node being split.
  • A second new node is created as the sibling of the node being split.
  • Item C moves into the new sibling, and item B moves into the new root.
  • Item A stays where it is.
  • The two rightmost children of the old root move to the new sibling.

The tree is now one level taller, and its root holds just one item, B. After the split, the insertion carries on down from the new root as usual.

Splitting the root is the only way a 2-3-4 tree ever gains a level, and the new level appears at the top. An ordinary binary search tree grows downward, one new leaf at a time, so its branches can end up at very different depths. A 2-3-4 tree grows upward from the root. When a new level appears, every leaf moves one level further from the root at the same moment, and that is why all the leaves always stay on one level.

Splitting on the Way Down

Because an insertion splits every full node it meets on the way down, the parent of a node being split is never full. If it had been full, it would have been split a moment earlier. So there is always room in the parent for item B, a split never spreads upward, and the insertion never needs to back up the tree.

To see all the pieces working together, build a tree from nothing by inserting 60, 30, 80, 40, 20, 50, 70, 90, 10, 55, 95, and 45, in that order. The table traces each step, and the figures after it show the tree at five points along the way.

Building a 2-3-4 tree one insertion at a time
InsertWhat happensLevels
60, 30, 80They go into the root, which is also the only leaf. It is now full: 30, 60, 80.1
40The root is full, so it splits. 60 moves up into a new root, 30 stays, and 80 goes to a new sibling. Then 40 joins 30.2
20Joins the left leaf, which becomes full: 20, 30, 40.2
50The search meets the full leaf 20, 30, 40 and splits it. 30 moves up beside 60, 20 stays, and 40 goes to a new leaf. Then 50 joins 40.2
70, 90Both join the right leaf, which becomes full: 70, 80, 90.2
10Joins 20 in the leftmost leaf.2
55Joins 40 and 50, filling that leaf.2
95The search meets the full leaf 70, 80, 90 and splits it. 80 moves up, which fills the root (30, 60, 80), and 90 goes to a new leaf. Then 95 joins 90.2
45The root is full, so it splits first, and 60 moves up into a new root. Farther down, the search meets the full leaf 40, 50, 55 and splits it too, sending 50 up beside 30. Then 45 joins 40.3

Notice how the last insertion needed two splits, and each happened as the search reached a full node. When the leaf 40, 50, 55 split, its parent was the old root, which the root split had just cut down to the single item 30, so there was plenty of room for 50.

The Tree234 Workshop Applet

The Tree234 Workshop applet draws a 2-3-4 tree on the screen and lets you search it and add to it. You type keys into its Number box and work it with four buttons: Fill, Find, Ins, and Zoom.

The Fill Button

Fill creates a new tree. Enter the number of data items you want in the Number box, and Fill builds a tree holding that many.

The Find Button

Type a key into the Number box and press Find again and again. Each press moves a red arrow one node farther along the search path, starting at the root, until it reaches the node that holds the key or a leaf that doesn't.

The Ins Button

Ins inserts the key in the Number box. Repeated presses take you through the insertion step by step. You see the arrow move down, every full node on the path split as the arrow reaches it, and finally the new item drop into a leaf.

The Zoom Button

A 2-3-4 tree fans out fast, and a large one won't fit on the screen with all its keys showing. In its normal view, the applet shows the top levels of the tree with their keys. Zoom switches to a zoomed-out view of the whole tree, up to four levels, in which each node is drawn as a small rectangle without its keys. Pressing Zoom again switches back.

Viewing Different Nodes

In the zoomed-out view you can click a node to see its subtree in detail. That way you can examine any part of a big tree, including the lower levels that don't fit in the normal view.

Experiments

The applet is at its most useful when you insert items one at a time and watch nodes fill and split. You'll see that every split pushes one item up a level, and that the tree stays balanced whatever order you insert in, even with keys in ascending order, the input that ruins an ordinary binary search tree. Keep inserting until the root splits and the tree gains a level, and notice that the new level appears at the top while the leaves stay together on the bottom row.

Here is a small thought experiment to go with it. A four-level tree made entirely of 2-nodes has 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes and so holds 15 items. The same four levels made entirely of 4-nodes have 1 + 4 + 16 + 64 = 85 nodes holding 255 items. So four levels can hold anywhere from 15 to 255 items, and the fuller the nodes, the shallower the tree needed for a given amount of data.

Try it. Our re-creation has a Key field and the buttons Fill, Find, and Ins. A log explains every split as it happens.

  1. Press Fill for a tree of random keys. Type one of its keys and press Find, and follow the path from the root. Then look for a key that isn't in the tree and see where the search gives up.
  2. Insert keys one at a time with Ins. Before each one, predict which leaf it will land in and whether any full node on the way will split. Check your guess against the log.
  3. Keep inserting until the root splits. The new level appears at the top, and every leaf stays on the bottom row.
  4. Leave the Show as red-black checkbox alone for now. Hour 20 explains what it shows.

Summary

  • A 2-3-4 tree is a multiway tree whose nodes hold up to three data items and have up to four children.
  • A non-leaf node always has one more child than it has items, making it a 2-node, 3-node, or 4-node. Leaves have no children, and no node may be empty.
  • Items in a node are kept in ascending order, and each child link covers the range of keys between its neighboring items.
  • Searching works like binary tree search, choosing at each node the child whose range contains the key.
  • New items are always inserted in leaves.
  • A full node is split as soon as an insertion meets it: A stays, B moves up to the parent, C moves to a new right sibling, and the two rightmost children go with C.
  • A full root splits into a new root holding B and two children, which makes the tree one level taller at the top.
  • Because the tree only grows at the top, all leaves stay on the same level, and because full nodes are split on the way down, a split never has to spread upward.

Q&A

Why must new items go into leaves?
A non-leaf node must have exactly one more child than it has items. Adding an item to an interior node would require an extra child as well, and there is nothing to put there. A leaf has no children to worry about, so it can take a new item whenever it has room.
Could one split set off a chain of splits all the way to the root?
Not with the top-down method used here. Every full node on the path is split before the search passes it, so the parent of a node being split always has room for item B. An approach that splits only when a leaf overflows could trigger such a chain, and it would have to climb back up the tree.
Is a 2-3-4 tree perfectly balanced?
In height, yes. Every leaf is on the same level. The nodes themselves can hold different numbers of items, though, so some subtrees may contain more data than others at the same depth.

Quiz

  1. What is the largest number of data items a 2-3-4 node can hold, and the largest number of children it can have?

    Answer

    Three data items and four children.

  2. A non-leaf node holds two data items. How many children does it have, and what is the general rule?

    Answer

    Three children. A non-leaf node always has one more child than it has data items.

  3. Where in the tree is a new data item always inserted?

    Answer

    In a leaf, on the bottom row of the tree.

  4. A full node holding items A, B, and C is split. What happens to each item, and to the node's children?

    Answer

    A stays in the node. B moves up into the parent. C moves into a new node created as the right-hand sibling. The two rightmost children are disconnected and become the new node's children.

  5. What happens when the root is full at the start of an insertion?

    Answer

    It is split using two new nodes: a new root, which receives B, and a new sibling, which receives C and the old root's two rightmost children. A stays in the old root. The tree becomes one level taller.

  6. Why do all the leaves of a 2-3-4 tree stay on the same level?

    Answer

    The tree gains height only when the root splits, which adds a level at the top and moves every leaf one level farther from the root at once. Other splits add nodes sideways, next to the node being split, without changing any depth.

Part IV · Trees

Hour 20 Implementing 2-3-4 Trees

This hour turns the 2-3-4 tree of Hour 19 into a working C++ program. Then it shows that 2-3-4 trees and red-black trees are two views of the same structure, and it weighs the two against each other for speed and storage.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How the DataItem, Node, and Tree234 classes of tree234.cpp work together
  • How the insert() and split() routines carry out the steps from Hour 19
  • How any 2-3-4 tree can be turned into an equivalent red-black tree
  • Why splitting a node and flipping colors are really the same operation
  • How 2-3-4 trees compare with red-black trees in speed and in memory use

Implementing a 2-3-4 Tree in C++

The book's program for this hour, tree234.cpp, is built from three classes. DataItem holds one data item. Node holds up to three items and links to up to four children. Tree234 holds the root and carries out searches, insertions, and splits. A main() function lets you show the tree, insert items, and search for them from the keyboard. The listings below are our own reconstruction in the book's style, and they keep the book's class and function names so you can match them with the original.

The DataItem Class

DataItem is about as simple as a class can be. It stores a single double called dData, which serves as the key. In a real program the object would carry a whole record, such as a name and an address, along with its key. displayItem() prints the item as a slash followed by the key, such as /27.

The Node Class

A Node stores pointers in two arrays. childArray has room for ORDER pointers to child nodes, and itemArray has room for ORDER-1 pointers to data items. With ORDER set to 4, that makes four child slots and three item slots. numItems records how many items are in use, and pParent points back to the node's parent (it is NULL for the root). Unused slots hold NULL.

The short member functions do the bookkeeping. connectChild() puts a child pointer into a given slot and, if the child exists, sets the child's pParent to point back at this node. disconnectChild() empties a slot and returns the pointer that was there, so the caller can attach that child somewhere else. isLeaf() checks whether childArray[0] is NULL, since any node with children has a child 0. isFull() checks whether all three item slots are in use. The rest are plain accessors.

findItem() compares the key with each item in use and returns that item's index, or −1 if the key isn't there. A node holds at most three items, so this never takes more than three comparisons.

insertItem() adds an item to a node that isn't full. It starts with the rightmost item in use and works left, sliding each item that is larger than the new key one slot to the right. When it reaches a smaller item, or runs off the left end, the gap it has opened is exactly where the new item belongs. It returns that position, which split() will need. This is the same shifting you saw in Hour 19 when 45 joined 40 and 50.

removeItem() takes the rightmost item, which is always the largest, out of the node and returns it. split() calls it twice, to lift out C and then B. displayNode() prints the items between slashes, as in /27/35/.

The Tree234 Class

Tree234 has a single data member, pRoot. Its constructor creates an empty node to serve as the root. That is the only empty node the tree ever contains, and only until the first item arrives.

find() starts at the root and asks each node whether it holds the key. If it does, find() returns the item's index within that node. If it doesn't and the node is a leaf, the search has failed, and find() returns −1. Otherwise getNextChild() picks the next node to visit.

getNextChild() counts the keys in the node that are smaller than the value, and that count is the number of the child to follow. A value smaller than every key leads to child 0, a value larger than all of them leads to the last child, and anything in between leads to the child whose range it falls in.

insert() walks down from the root. At each node it first asks whether the node is full. If so, it splits the node and climbs to the parent. After the split, the node it was standing on holds only A, and the new value might belong under C in the new sibling instead, so it lets the parent, which now holds B, choose the way again. If the node is a leaf, the loop ends. Otherwise getNextChild() takes the search one level down. Since every full node is split the moment it is reached, the leaf at the end always has room, and insertItem() puts the new item there.

split() carries out the five steps of Hour 19, though not in the same order.

  • The two calls to removeItem() lift C and then B off the right end of the node. A stays where it is (step 4).
  • disconnectChild(2) and disconnectChild(3) detach the two rightmost children. For a leaf these are just NULL.
  • A new node, pNewRight, is created (step 1). It receives C (step 2), and the two detached children become its children 0 and 1 (step 5).
  • If the node being split is the root, a new empty root is created and the old root is connected as its child 0. From here on, the parent is simply getParent().
  • B is inserted into the parent (step 3), and insertItem() reports the position where it landed. Every child link to the right of that position moves one slot right, and pNewRight is connected in the gap, just right of B.

Those last moves matter. Suppose the parent holds 40 and 80, and its middle child, holding 50, 60, and 70, splits. B (60) lands at position 1, between 40 and 80. The parent's child 2 (keys above 80) slides over to slot 3, and the new node holding 70 goes into slot 2, between 60 and 80, where its keys belong.

The tree234.cpp Program

The last pieces are the display routine and main(). displayTree() starts recDisplayTree() at the root, on level 0. recDisplayTree() prints a node's level, its child number within its parent, and its items, and then calls itself for each child, one level deeper. Because each node is printed before its children, the output follows a preorder traversal (Hour 16).

main() inserts five items and then waits for commands: s shows the tree, i inserts a value, and f finds one. You can trace the five insertions by hand. First 50, 40, and 60 fill the root, which is also a leaf. When 30 arrives the root is full, so it splits: 50 moves up into a new root, 40 stays, and 60 goes to a new node. Then 30 joins 40, and finally 70 joins 60.

Here is a short session. The first s shows that tree. Inserting 80 fills the right leaf, and inserting 90 then finds that leaf full and splits it: 70 moves up beside 50, 60 stays, and 80 goes to a new leaf, where 90 joins it.
