The program creates every node and item with new and never deletes any of them. That is harmless in a short demonstration, but a real program needs a destructor for Tree234 that visits every node, children first, deletes the node's items, and then deletes the node itself.

2-3-4 Trees and Red-Black Trees

A 2-3-4 tree and a red-black tree look completely different, yet they are equivalent. Any 2-3-4 tree can be turned into a red-black tree, any red-black tree can be turned back into a 2-3-4 tree, and the operations that keep the two balanced correspond as well. Historically, the 2-3-4 tree came first, and the red-black tree was developed from it. Rudolf Bayer introduced red-black trees in 1972, under the name symmetric binary B-trees.

Transformation from 2-3-4 to Red-Black

Three rules convert the nodes one at a time.

  1. Transform any 2-node into a black node.
  2. Transform any 3-node into a black parent P and a red child C. C can be either the left or the right child, so every 3-node has two possible red-black forms.
  3. Transform any 4-node into a black parent (the middle item) and two red children (the other two items).

In each case the node's own children, converted by the same rules, hang below the new nodes in key order. In the figures below, every child is a 2-node, so each becomes a single black node.

Convert every node of a 2-3-4 tree this way, and the result is always a legal red-black tree. Each 2-3-4 node becomes exactly one black node plus at most two red children, so no red node ever has a red child, and the root is black. Every level of the 2-3-4 tree contributes exactly one black node to any path through it. All 2-3-4 leaves are on the same level, so every path from the root to a null child passes through the same number of black nodes, and rule 4 holds. Going the other way is just as easy. Merge each black node with its red children, and you have the 2-3-4 nodes back.

Our re-creation of the Tree234 applet can show this conversion as you work. When its Show as red-black checkbox is ticked, it also draws the red-black tree that is equivalent to the 2-3-4 tree on screen.

Try it. Watch the two trees change together.

  1. Tick Show as red-black.
  2. The applet opens with the same tree that tree234.cpp builds, so inserting 80 and then 90 repeats the session shown earlier. Go on inserting keys one at a time with Ins, and check that each 2-node appears as a black node, each 3-node as a black node with one red child, and each 4-node as a black node with two red children.
  3. Whenever the log reports a split, look at the red-black drawing. The black parent with two red children has become a red node with two black children, which is a color flip.

Operational Equivalence

The match goes beyond shapes. The operations that keep each tree in balance correspond too.

Start with splits. In red-black form, a 4-node is a black parent with two red children, which is exactly the pattern a color flip looks for. Splitting a 4-node in the 2-3-4 tree is the same as flipping those colors in the red-black tree. After the flip, the parent is red, which means it now belongs with the node above it. It has moved up, just as item B moves up during a split. Its two children, now black, stand on their own as two separate 2-nodes, the A and C of the split.

Rotations have a counterpart as well. A 3-node has two red-black forms, with its red child on the left or on the right. A rotation, together with swapping the two nodes' colors, turns one form into the other, as in the two 3-node pictures above, while the 2-3-4 tree the drawing stands for doesn't change at all.

This explains the repairs of Hour 18. In Possibility 2 there, black 25 with red 12 and red 6 hanging in a line below it was really a single 2-3-4 node holding 6, 12, and 25, drawn lopsided. The rotation and the color switches redrew it in proper 4-node form, as black 12 with red children 6 and 25.

Efficiency of 2-3-4 Trees

With the equivalence in mind, the two trees are easy to compare. They are balanced in the same way, so the real questions are how fast each one runs and how much memory each one needs.

Speed

In a red-black tree, a search visits one node on each level, and a balanced binary tree has about log₂N levels. A 2-3-4 tree is shorter, because each node holds more data. If every node were full, it would have about log₄N levels, which is only half of log₂N. On the other hand, the search must compare the key with up to three items in each node instead of one.

Levels a search passes through (rounded)
NRed-black tree (about log₂N)2-3-4 tree with full nodes (about log₄N)
1,000105
1,000,0002010
1,000,000,0003015

The two effects roughly cancel. Searching a 2-3-4 tree is O(log N) and takes about as long as searching a red-black tree. Insertion is O(log N) as well, and the only restructuring it ever does is splitting nodes.

Storage Requirements

Every 2-3-4 node sets aside room for three data items and four child pointers, whether it uses them or not. Nodes are often far from full, so much of that space goes to waste. A 2-node uses only one of its three item slots and two of its four child pointers. A tree made up entirely of 2-nodes would leave two-thirds of its item slots and half of its child pointers empty.

How much of a 2-3-4 node is in use
Node typeItem slots usedChild pointers used (non-leaf)
2-node1 of 32 of 4
3-node2 of 33 of 4
4-node3 of 34 of 4

A red-black node, by contrast, holds exactly one item, two child pointers, and a color, and it uses all of them, apart from the null child pointers at the bottom that every binary tree has. So red-black trees make much better use of memory. The 2-3-4 tree's advantage is simplicity. It needs no rotations and no color cases, only splits, which makes it easier to program.

The 2-3-4 tree is also the simplest of the B-trees. B-trees whose nodes have hundreds of children are used when data is stored on disk. There, reading a node means reading a whole block from the disk, which takes far longer than comparing keys in memory. A very short, very bushy tree keeps the number of block reads small, and a few empty slots per node hardly matter.

Summary

  • The tree234.cpp program uses three classes: DataItem holds one key, Node holds up to three item pointers and four child pointers, and Tree234 holds the root and does the searching, inserting, and splitting.
  • Node::insertItem() slides larger items right to keep the keys in order and returns the new item's position. removeItem() takes out the largest item.
  • Tree234::insert() splits every full node on its way down, returns to the parent after each split to choose the path again, and finally inserts the new item in a leaf.
  • split() removes C and B, gives C and the two rightmost children to a new sibling, inserts B into the parent (a brand-new root if necessary), and shifts the parent's child links to make room.
  • Any 2-3-4 tree converts to a red-black tree. A 2-node becomes a black node, a 3-node a black parent with one red child on either side, and a 4-node a black parent with two red children.
  • Splitting a 4-node corresponds to a color flip, and switching a 3-node's red child from one side to the other corresponds to a rotation.
  • Searching takes about the same time, O(log N), in both trees. The 2-3-4 tree has fewer levels but more comparisons per node.
  • A 2-3-4 tree wastes memory in partly empty nodes, while a red-black tree uses memory efficiently. The 2-3-4 tree is easier to program, and its larger relatives, the B-trees, are the standard way to organize data on disk.

Q&A

Why does the Node class store pointers to DataItem objects rather than the objects themselves?
Items move around a lot in a 2-3-4 tree. They shift within a node during insertions and jump to other nodes during splits. Moving a pointer costs the same however large the record is, and an empty slot is easy to mark with NULL.
Which should I use, a 2-3-4 tree or a red-black tree?
For data in memory, they search equally fast. The red-black tree uses less memory, and the 2-3-4 tree is easier to understand and to program. For data on disk, the 2-3-4 tree's larger relative, the B-tree, is the usual choice.
How do I turn a red-black tree back into a 2-3-4 tree?
Merge each black node with its red children, if it has any, into a single node. A black node on its own becomes a 2-node, a black node with one red child becomes a 3-node, and a black node with two red children becomes a 4-node.

Quiz

  1. In the Node class, what do childArray and itemArray hold, and how many slots does each have?

    Answer

    childArray holds pointers to the node's children and has ORDER (4) slots. itemArray holds pointers to the node's data items and has ORDER-1 (3) slots.

  2. In split(), what happens to items B and C?

    Answer

    Both are removed from the node being split. C goes into a new node that becomes the right-hand sibling, along with the node's two rightmost children. B is inserted into the parent, which is a newly created root if the node being split was the root.

  3. What does a 3-node become in a red-black tree?

    Answer

    A black parent with one red child. The red child can be either the left or the right child, so there are two equivalent forms.

  4. Which red-black tree operation corresponds to splitting a 4-node in a 2-3-4 tree?

    Answer

    A color flip. The black parent with two red children becomes a red parent with two black children, and the red parent joins the node above, just as item B moves up in a split.

  5. Why can a 2-3-4 tree waste a lot of memory?

    Answer

    Every node reserves space for three items and four child pointers, but many nodes aren't full. A 2-node leaves two of its three item slots and two of its four child pointers empty.

  6. How does searching a 2-3-4 tree compare in speed with searching a red-black tree?

    Answer

    They are about the same, both O(log N). The 2-3-4 tree has fewer levels (as few as half as many), but each node may need up to three comparisons instead of one.

Part V · Hash Tables

Hour 21 Hash Tables

A hash table works out where an item must be and goes straight there, so insertion and searching take close to one step. This hour builds the idea from the ground up, deals with keys that collide, and ends with a working C++ table that uses linear probing.

In this hour you'll learn

  • Why hash tables are fast, and where they fall short
  • How a word becomes a number, and a number becomes an array index
  • What a collision is, and the two families of solutions
  • How linear probing inserts, finds and deletes items
  • Why clustering and a high load factor slow a table down
  • How the program hash.cpp works, and how to move a table into a bigger array

Most structures in this book find an item by searching for it, halving an ordered array or walking down a tree. A hash table skips the search. It feeds the key into a quick calculation that names the array cell where the item belongs. Insertion and searching therefore take close to O(1) time, the same few steps whether the table holds a hundred items or a million, and the code is much simpler than a balanced tree's.

The drawbacks are real, though. A hash table is built on an array, and an array is hard to enlarge once created. Some kinds of hash table slow down badly when the array gets too full, so you need a fair idea of how many items you will store. And there is no convenient way to visit the items in key order. If you don't need ordered traversal and can predict the size of your data, a hash table is very hard to beat.

Introduction to Hashing

Hashing means turning a key into an array index. Lafore starts with keys that already are indices, then moves to English words, where the conversion takes some thought.

Employee Numbers as Keys

Picture a small company with about 1,000 employees, numbered in order of hiring from 1 up to 1,000. The records of people who leave are kept on file, so no number is ever reused and the sequence has no gaps.

Store each record in the array cell whose index equals the employee number. Employee 72's record sits in cell 72, so fetching it is a single array access, databaseArray[72], with no searching at all. Adding a new hire is just as quick, because the record goes into the cell for the next unused number. Both operations are O(1).

This works only because the keys are unusually tidy. They are consecutive, they have no gaps, and the largest one is known, which fixes the size of the array. Real-world keys are rarely so well behaved.

A Dictionary

Now suppose you want a 50,000-word English dictionary in memory, with every word in its own cell of a 50,000-cell array, so that any word can be looked up in one step. Which cell does giraffe belong in? Before anything else, you need a rule that turns a word into a number.

Converting Words to Numbers

Computers already store letters as codes (in ASCII, a is 97 and z is 122), but a simpler code is handier here. Let a be 1, b be 2 and so on up to z at 26, with 0 for a blank. That gives 27 symbols, ignoring capital letters. There are two obvious ways to combine a word's codes into one number.

Add the digits. Adding the codes turns cats into c (3) + a (1) + t (20) + s (19) = 43, so cats would live in cell 43. The trouble is the range. If no word has more than 10 letters, no total can exceed 26 × 10 = 260 (for zzzzzzzzzz), so every word lands in cells 0 to 260. That crams 50,000 words into 261 cells, about 192 words per cell, which is far too crowded to be useful.

Multiply by powers. The opposite idea gives every word a number of its own, copying the way decimal numbers work. The number 7,546 means 7 × 10³ + 5 × 10² + 4 × 10¹ + 6 × 10⁰. Treat each letter as one digit of a base-27 number instead, and multiply it by a power of 27, as the table shows for cats.

Turning cats into a base-27 number
LetterCodePowerPower's valueCode × value
c327³19,68359,049
a127²729729
t2027¹27540
s1927⁰119
Total60,337

Now no two words share a number, since every different string of letters is a different base-27 number. The catch is size. The string zzzzzzzzzz works out to 27¹⁰ − 1, which is 205,891,132,094,648, more than 205 trillion. No memory can hold an array that big, and nearly all of its cells would be reserved for nonsense such as qxvkzjrwpt. Adding made the range far too small, and multiplying makes it absurdly large.

Hashing

The way out is to squeeze the huge range of base-27 numbers into a range that fits a reasonable array. For the dictionary, a good size is about twice the number of words, so 100,000 cells for 50,000 words.

The squeezing tool is the modulo operator, %, which gives the remainder after a division. To squeeze the numbers 0 to 199 into the range 0 to 9, write smallNumber = largeNumber % 10;. The remainder after dividing by 10 is always between 0 and 9, so 157 becomes 7 and 43 becomes 3. The size of the small range equals the divisor.

The dictionary does the same with arrayIndex = hugeNumber % arraySize;. The word table has the base-27 number 10,650,290, and 10,650,290 % 100,000 = 50,290, so table goes in cell 50,290. Even zzzzzzzzzz lands in cell 94,648. Only the 50,000 real words are ever hashed, so no cell is wasted on nonsense, and about half the cells stay empty as slack.

Hash function. A function that converts a number in a large range into a number in a small range, usually an index into an array. That array is called a hash table, and storing an item at the index the function produces is called hashing the item.

Collisions

Squeezing has a price. Countless huge numbers leave the same remainder, so two different words can hash to the same index. Lafore pictures inserting the word melioration and finding that its hash value is the very cell already holding cats. That is a collision. With vastly more possible words than cells, collisions cannot be prevented, only handled well. There are two broad approaches.

  • Open addressing. The array has plenty of empty cells, so put the item in some other empty cell. There are three standard ways to choose that cell: linear probing, quadratic probing and double hashing.
  • Separate chaining. Make every cell hold a linked list, and add each item to the list at its hash index, however many items that list already holds.

Linear probing fills the rest of this hour. Quadratic probing and double hashing follow in Hour 22, and separate chaining in Hour 23.

Linear Probing

In linear probing you step along the array one cell at a time, looking for a vacant cell. If a key hashes to cell 5,421 and that cell is taken, you try 5,422, then 5,423, and so on. Each look at a cell is called a probe, and since the probes march along in a straight line, the method is called linear probing. A search that runs past the last cell wraps around to cell 0 and carries on.

The Hash Workshop Applet

Lafore's Hash Workshop applet shows this in action. It starts with a 60-cell array partly filled with random keys from 0 to 999, and it hashes with key % arraySize, so the key 472 goes to cell 52 (472 is 7 × 60 + 52). A red arrow marks the cell being examined. The buttons are New (which asks for the table size, the number of items and whether duplicates are allowed), Fill, Ins, Find and Del.

Inserting. The arrow jumps to the key's hash index. If that cell is empty, the key goes there after one probe. Otherwise the arrow moves forward cell by cell to the first empty one, and the key goes there. The number of cells visited is the probe length.

Finding. Find follows the same path from the hash index until it meets the key or reaches an empty cell. An empty cell proves the key is absent, because the key's own insertion would have followed this same path and could never have gone past an empty cell.

Deleting. You cannot simply empty the cell. In the 7-cell tables below, the keys 15, 22 and 29 all hash to cell 1 (each leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 7), so they occupy cells 1, 2 and 3. If deleting 22 left cell 2 empty, a later search for 29 would stop at that hole and report 29 missing.

So a deleted item is replaced by a special marker, shown as Del in the applet and as a DataItem with key −1 in the C++ code. Insertion treats a marked cell as free and may reuse it. Find treats it as occupied and steps over it.

Markers have a cost. After many deletions the table is littered with them, and every search must walk past them, so probes lengthen even though fewer real items remain. Rehashing, described at the end of this hour, clears them out.

Our re-creation below works the same way. It shows each probe sequence and the current load factor, a measure of fullness explained shortly.

Try it. Watch linear probing in a small table.

  1. Type 23 in the size field and press New, then type 12 in the count field and press Fill. The load factor is 12/23, about 0.52.
  2. Take a key already in the table, add 23, and insert the result with Ins (if 40 sits in cell 17, insert 63). It collides with the original key and probes forward.
  3. Press Find for the same key and count the probes. Then look for a key that is not in the table and see where the search stops.
  4. Press Del on a key in the middle of a run of filled cells, then find a key further along that run. The search steps over the marker.
  5. Insert a key that hashes into that run and watch it reuse the marked cell.

Duplicates Allowed?

The applet lets you allow duplicate keys, but they complicate things. To report every copy of a key, Find would have to keep going past the first match to the end of the cluster, which slows every search, even for keys that have no copies. Deleting all copies of a key has the same problem. So hash tables usually forbid duplicates, typically by calling Find before each insertion and refusing a key that is already there. The insert() function later in this hour skips that check to stay short, leaving it to the caller.

Clustering

Keep filling the applet's table and the occupied cells bunch into runs called clusters. A key that hashes anywhere into a cluster must step along to its end, and then it takes the first empty cell beyond, making the cluster longer. So a cluster is a target that grows every time it catches a key.

Before 167 arrived, every key that hashed to any of cells 5 through 10 was headed for cell 10. That is 6 of the 23 possible home cells, so roughly one new key in four would have landed there. A lone empty cell such as 15, with an empty cell in front of it, only catches keys that hash to 15 itself, about one key in 23.

This effect is called primary clustering. Big clusters grow faster than small ones, and neighboring clusters merge into bigger ones. If an item lands in cell 4, the small cluster in cells 2 and 3 fuses with the big one into a single run from cell 2 to cell 10. Long clusters mean long probes, both for insertions and for searches that end in failure.

Load Factor

Load factor. The number of items in a hash table divided by the number of cells in its array. A load factor of 0.5 means the table is half full.

A table of 10,000 cells holding 6,667 items has a load factor of 0.6667 (in code, loadFactor = nItems / arraySize; computed in floating point). The clustering picture shows 11 items in 23 cells, a load factor of about 0.48.

With linear probing, clusters stay modest while the load factor is below about one-half. Past two-thirds they lengthen and merge, and probe lengths shoot up. So keep a linear-probing table no more than one-half to two-thirds full, which is why the dictionary got twice as many cells as words. Hour 22 supplies the exact numbers.

C++ Code for a Linear Probe Hash Table

The program hash.cpp puts these ideas into C++. It fills a hash table with random keys and then lets you show, insert, delete and find items from the keyboard. The table is a vector of pointers to DataItem objects, with NULL marking an empty cell.

Classes

A DataItem holds one int key, iData. A real record would carry more fields, but the key is all the hash table looks at. HashTable holds the vector, its size, and pNonItem, a pointer to the single item that marks deleted cells.

The constructor sets every cell to NULL and creates the marker with key −1, which is safe because real keys are never negative. Every deleted cell will point at this one shared marker, so a deletion never has to create anything. The hash function is the plain modulo from earlier in the hour. The other member functions are defined outside the class.

insert() hashes the key, then walks forward as long as the current cell holds a live item, meaning the cell is not NULL and its key is not −1. It stops at the first empty or deleted cell and stores the item there.

Nothing in this program checks for a full table. If every cell holds a live item, insert() circles the array forever. The search functions below stop only at a NULL cell, so once no empty cells remain (only items and markers), a search for a missing key circles forever too. A real program would count its items and refuse the insertion, or enlarge the table, long before that point.

find() moves forward from the hash index until it reaches a NULL cell, returning the item as soon as a key matches. A deleted cell holds pNonItem, which is not NULL, so the search steps past it, and since −1 never equals a real key, the marker is never mistaken for a match. remove() runs the same loop. On a match it puts pNonItem into the cell and returns the removed item, so the caller can use it or delete it.

displayTable() prints every cell on one line, showing the key, ** for an empty cell or −1 for a deleted one. main() asks for the table size and the number of starting items and inserts that many random keys. Each key is rand() % (keysPerCell * size) with keysPerCell set to 10, so about ten possible key values map to each cell. Then it loops on a menu, where s shows the table, i inserts, d deletes and f finds. Here is a short session with 13 cells and 8 starting items.

Table size: 13
Items to start with: 8
Command (s, i, d, f): s
Table: ** ** 41 94 108 ** 110 7 59 124 ** ** 38
Command (s, i, d, f): i
Key to insert: 33
Command (s, i, d, f): s
Table: ** ** 41 94 108 ** 110 7 59 124 33 ** 38
Command (s, i, d, f): d
Key to delete: 59
Command (s, i, d, f): s
Table: ** ** 41 94 108 ** 110 7 -1 124 33 ** 38
Command (s, i, d, f): f
Key to find: 124
Found 124

The random keys 7, 59 and 124 all hash to cell 7 (59 is 4 × 13 + 7, and 124 is 9 × 13 + 7), so they ended up side by side in cells 7, 8 and 9. The new key 33 also hashes to 7, so it probes cells 7, 8 and 9 and settles in cell 10. After 59 is deleted, cell 8 shows −1, and the search for 124 steps over it and succeeds.

Wraparound

The statement hashVal = (hashVal + 1) % arraySize; advances and wraps in one step. From any cell but the last, adding 1 gives a number below arraySize, which % leaves alone. From the last cell, arraySize − 1, adding 1 gives exactly arraySize, which % turns into 0. The book writes the same thing as two statements, an increment followed by hashVal %= arraySize;.

Expanding the Array

When a table gets too full, you can move its items into a bigger array. Copying each cell to the same index in the new array won't work, though. The hash function depends on the array size, so a key's proper cell changes with the size. In a 23-cell table the key 52 lives in cell 6 (52 % 23), while in a 47-cell table it belongs in cell 5 (52 % 47).

Instead you rehash, which means going through the old array and inserting every live item into the new one with insert(). Empty cells and markers are skipped, so rehashing also clears out old deletion markers. The new size is typically about double the old one, adjusted to a prime number, so 23 cells would become 47, the first prime after 46. Hour 22 explains why primes matter.

Rehashing costs O(N) time, since every item is inserted again, so it pays to choose a big enough array at the start. A vector's own ability to grow does not help, because growing leaves every item at its old index, which is now the wrong one.

The sketch below is our own illustration of rehashing, not a listing from the book. It is written as an extra HashTable member function, so declare void rehash(); in the class first.

Applied to the 13-cell table from the session above, the sketch builds a 29-cell array (26, 27 and 28 are not prime). Every key moves to key % 29, so 124 lands in cell 9 and 33 in cell 4, and the −1 marker disappears.

Summary

  • A hash table stores each item at an array index computed from its key by a hash function, so insertion and searching take close to O(1) time.
  • Hash tables are hard to expand, can slow down badly when too full, and cannot visit their items in key order.
  • A word can become a number by treating its letters as base-27 digits, and % arraySize squeezes that huge number into the array's range.
  • A collision happens when a key hashes to an occupied cell. Open addressing finds another cell in the array; separate chaining keeps a linked list at every cell.
  • Linear probing checks the following cells one by one, wrapping from the last cell to cell 0. Find follows the same path and gives up at an empty cell.
  • Deleted items are replaced by a marker (key −1 in the C++ code) that insertion may reuse and searches step over.
  • Duplicate keys slow searching and deleting, so they are usually forbidden.
  • Linear probing suffers from primary clustering, so keep its load factor below about one-half to two-thirds.
  • To enlarge a hash table, create a bigger array (about double, adjusted to a prime) and rehash every item into it.

Q&A

If hash tables are so fast, why bother with trees?
Because of what a hash table cannot do. It cannot list its items in key order without sorting them, it needs a good size estimate in advance, and an overfull open-addressing table slows to a crawl. A balanced tree keeps its items in order and grows smoothly, at the price of O(log N) access. Hour 24 weighs these choices.
Why must a linear-probing table always keep some empty cells?
Empty cells are what stop searches. The fuller the table, the longer the clusters and the probe sequences. With the code in this hour, a table with no empty cells at all makes insert(), or a search for a missing key, loop forever.
Can I avoid rehashing altogether?
Only if you know how much data is coming. Rehashing costs time in proportion to the number of items, so choose a generous array at the start and let rehashing be a rare event.

Quiz

  1. What does a hash function do?

    Answer

    It converts a key, or a number from a large range, into a number in a smaller range, usually an index into the hash table's array. The usual tool is key % arraySize.

  2. Using a = 1, b = 2 … z = 26, what number does cats get if you simply add its letter codes?

    Answer

    3 + 1 + 20 + 19 = 43.

  3. Why can't a word's base-27 number (letters multiplied by powers of 27) be used directly as an array index?

    Answer

    The range is far too large. Ten-letter words produce numbers up to 27¹⁰ − 1, over 205 trillion, so the array could not fit in memory, and nearly all its cells would belong to strings that are not words.

  4. What is primary clustering?

    Answer

    In linear probing, occupied cells bunch into runs. A key that hashes anywhere into a run must step to its end and lands just past it, making the run longer, so big clusters grow faster than small ones and probes get longer.

  5. Why is a deleted item replaced by a special marker instead of leaving its cell empty?

    Answer

    Searches stop at the first empty cell. An emptied cell inside a cluster would stop later searches early, making keys beyond it seem missing. The marker tells searches to keep going, while insertion may still reuse the cell.

  6. With linear probing, what is the highest load factor you should normally allow?

    Answer

    About one-half to two-thirds (0.5 to 0.67). Beyond that, probe lengths climb steeply.

Part V · Hash Tables

Hour 22 Quadratic Probing

Linear probing's clusters make a crowded table slow. This hour tries two smarter ways of choosing the next cell to probe, quadratic probing and double hashing, and then measures how each open-addressing method copes as the table fills.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How quadratic probing spreads its probes out, and the secondary clustering it still suffers from
  • How double hashing gives each key a step size of its own
  • The two rules every secondary hash function must obey
  • Why the table size should be a prime number
  • How the average number of probes depends on the load factor for each method

In Hour 21 you watched linear probing build clusters that grow faster the bigger they get. Both methods in this hour are still open addressing. Every item lives in the array itself, and a collision sends you looking for another cell. What changes is the order in which the cells are tried.

Quadratic Probing

Clusters form in linear probing because each probe checks the cell right next door. Once the table is fairly full, a key that hashes into a cluster must crawl through all of it and then makes it longer. Quadratic probing tries to stop clusters from forming by probing cells that are farther apart.

The Step Is the Square of the Step Number

With linear probing, if the hash index is x, the probes go to x + 1, x + 2, x + 3 and so on, one cell further each time. With quadratic probing the distance from x is the square of the step number, so the probes go to x + 1, x + 4, x + 9, x + 16, x + 25, which is x + 1², x + 2², x + 3² and onward. Each index is taken % arraySize, so the sequence wraps past the end of the array as before. In code, probe number i examines cell (x + i * i) % arraySize.

The first probes stay close to home, and then the jumps quickly get long. A key that hashes into a cluster escapes it after a few probes and settles somewhere far away, where it does not make the cluster any bigger.

With linear probing the same key would have walked through cells 3 to 8 and settled in cell 9, seven probes that also lengthen the cluster. Quadratic probing needs five and leaves the cluster alone. Had more probes been needed, the next ones would have been 3 + 25 = 28, which wraps to cell 5, and 3 + 36 = 39, which wraps to cell 16.

The HashDouble Applet with Quadratic Probes

Lafore's HashDouble applet looks like the Hash applet, but when you create a new table you can choose between quadratic probing and double hashing. With quadratic probes selected, you can watch each probe sequence start near the hash index and then leap across the array in ever longer jumps.

As the table nears capacity, the leaps multiply and the sequences get long. Sometimes the applet even reports that it cannot find an empty cell while empty cells plainly exist, because the probe sequence never visits them. The note after the exercise below, and the section on prime table sizes, explain how that can happen. Our re-creation puts both methods in one menu, so you can run the same keys through each and compare.

Try it. Follow the quadratic probe sequence.

  1. Choose Quadratic from the probing menu, type 23 in the size field and press New to get an empty table.
  2. Insert 3, 26, 49, 72 and 95, one at a time. All five hash to cell 3, and their probe sequences grow by one cell each time: 3; then 3, 4; then 3, 4, 7; then 3, 4, 7, 12; and finally 3, 4, 7, 12, 19.
  3. Press New again, type 20 in the count field and press Fill (a load factor of about 0.87). Insert a few more keys and see how far the sequences now leap.

The squares 1, 4, 9, 16 … taken % arraySize land on only some of the cells. With a prime size they reach about half of them (12 of the 23 cells in a 23-cell table), so quadratic probing is certain to find a free cell only while the table is less than half full. With a size such as 16 they reach just four cells, x, x + 1, x + 4 and x + 9, however long the sequence runs.

The Problem with Quadratic Probes

Quadratic probing cures primary clustering, but it has a milder problem of its own. The probe sequence depends only on the hash index, so every key that hashes to the same cell follows exactly the same path. Each newcomer must walk past all the cells its predecessors filled along that path.

Lafore's example uses a 59-cell table and the keys 184, 302, 420 and 538. Each is 7 more than a multiple of 59 (3 × 59 + 7, 5 × 59 + 7, 7 × 59 + 7 and 9 × 59 + 7), so all four hash to cell 7.

Four keys that hash to cell 7 in a 59-cell table, inserted with quadratic probing
KeyHash indexProbe sequenceProbes
184771
30277, 82
42077, 8, 113
53877, 8, 11, 164

Every extra key with the same hash index needs one more probe than the key before it. This is called secondary clustering. It is gentler than primary clustering, because keys with different hash indexes follow different paths, but it still wastes time. In practice quadratic probing is not used much, because double hashing does better.

Double Hashing

Secondary clustering happens because the probe sequence depends only on the hash index. The cure is to make the sequence depend on the key itself. Double hashing does this by hashing the key a second time, with a different hash function, and using the result as the step size. The step stays fixed throughout one key's probe sequence, but different keys, even keys that share a hash index, generally get different steps.

The secondary hash function must obey two rules.

  • It must differ from the primary hash function. If it were the same, keys that share a hash index would share a step as well, and secondary clustering would be back.
  • It must never return 0. A step of 0 would probe the same cell forever.

Experts have found that a function of the form stepSize = constant - (key % constant); works well, where constant is a prime number smaller than the array size. The book uses 5, giving stepSize = 5 - key % 5;. Since key % 5 lies between 0 and 4, the step lies between 1 and 5 and can never be 0.

Run the four secondary-clustering keys through this formula and they part company. In the 59-cell table, 184 gets a step of 1 (because 184 % 5 is 4), 302 a step of 3, 420 a step of 5 and 538 a step of 2. The first still lands in cell 7, and each of the others finds a free cell on its second probe (cells 10, 12 and 9). The four insertions take 7 probes in all, instead of 10.

Implementation

The program hashDouble.cpp keeps the DataItem class, the vector of pointers and the −1 marker from hash.cpp. The single hash function becomes two member functions.

In this version insert() takes the key as a separate argument alongside the item. Here are insert() and find(), again as members of HashTable.

The only change from linear probing is the size of each jump. Where hash.cpp added 1, these functions add stepSize, which hashFunc2() computes once per call. remove() changes in the same way. It starts at hashFunc1(key), advances by hashFunc2(key), and drops the pNonItem marker into the cell when it finds the key. Every operation on a key must use the same step, or find() would search along a different path from the one insert() took.

The book's main() for this program works with a 23-cell table, and Lafore traces what happens as 21 items go into it, one after another. The table below repeats that trace. For each item it gives the key, the hash value (key % 23), the step size (5 − key % 5) and the cells visited, the last of which is where the item ends up.

Most early items find an empty cell on the first probe. The first collision comes with item 8, where the key 24 hashes to cell 1, already holding 1, and its step of 1 takes it to cell 2. Items 10 and 16 repeat keys that are already present (16 and 1). The program does not forbid duplicates, so each copy simply probes onward to a cell of its own.

The last few rows show what a nearly full table does to probe lengths. Item 20 needs 8 probes and item 21 needs 11, and by then the load factor is 21/23, about 0.91. A search for a key that is absent fares even worse at that point. Looking for 48 (hash value 2, step 2) visits 22 cells before it meets the empty cell 21.

Table Size a Prime Number

Double hashing needs one more thing, a table whose size is a prime number. To see why, suppose the table has 15 cells (indices 0 to 14) and a key hashes to cell 0 with a step of 5, as 45 does (45 % 15 is 0, and 5 − 45 % 5 is 5). Its probes go 0, 5, 10, 0, 5, 10 and so on, round and round. Only three cells are ever examined. If those three are full, the insertion never finishes, even though the other 12 cells are empty.

If the size is prime, no step smaller than the size can divide it evenly, so a probe sequence visits every cell before it repeats. In a 13-cell table, a key such as 65 also hashes to cell 0 with a step of 5, but its sequence runs 0, 5, 10, 2, 7, 12, 4, 9, 1, 6, 11, 3, 8, covering all 13 cells. It finds a free cell as long as one exists.

The trap exists for any size that shares a factor with one of the possible steps, which is what the comment in hashFunc2() warns about. A prime larger than 5 rules it out. Quadratic probing runs a similar risk, since with a non-prime size its sequences can stay inside a handful of cells.

Try it. Compare double hashing with quadratic probing, then spring the non-prime trap.

  1. In the applet above, choose Double, type 23 in the size field and press New. Insert 3, 26, 49, 72 and 95 again. Their steps are 2, 4, 1, 3 and 5, so after the first key each one lands on its second probe, in cells 7, 4, 6 and 8.
  2. Count the probes. Double hashing needed 9 in all, against 15 for quadratic probing with the same keys.
  3. Now type 15 in the size field and press New (the applet warns that 15 is not prime). Insert 30, 5 and 10, which fill cells 0, 5 and 10, then insert 45. Its probes keep revisiting cells 0, 5 and 10 and never reach any of the 12 empty cells.

Efficiency of Open Addressing

With no collisions, inserting or finding an item takes a single probe, so both are O(1). With collisions, the time depends on how many probes are needed on average, and that depends on the load factor, L. The formulas below come from Donald Knuth's analysis. An insertion has to find an empty cell, so it costs about as much as an unsuccessful search.

Linear Probing

For linear probing, the average number of probes P is:

  • successful search: P = (1 + 1 / (1 − L)) / 2
  • unsuccessful search or insertion: P = (1 + 1 / (1 − L)²) / 2

At L = 1/2, a successful search averages 1.5 probes and an unsuccessful one 2.5. At L = 2/3 the figures are 2.0 and 5.0. Here 1 − L is 1/3, whose reciprocal is 3, so the formulas give (1 + 3) / 2 = 2 and (1 + 9) / 2 = 5. At L = 0.8 they reach 3.0 and 13.0, and at L = 0.9 they reach 5.5 and 50.5.

Misses and insertions suffer most, because the squared term explodes as L approaches 1. So keep a linear-probing table below two-thirds full, and preferably below half. The price is memory, since a lower load factor leaves more cells empty, so the choice is a trade between space and speed.

Quadratic Probing and Double Hashing

Quadratic probing and double hashing share a pair of formulas, where ln is the natural logarithm:

  • successful search: P = −ln(1 − L) / L
  • unsuccessful search or insertion: P = 1 / (1 − L)

At L = 0.5 these give 1.4 and 2.0 probes (−ln 0.5 is 0.693, and 0.693 / 0.5 is about 1.39). At L = 0.8 they give 2.0 and 5.0, still comfortable, while linear probing needs 13 probes for a miss at the same load. At L = 0.9 a miss costs 10 probes against linear probing's 50.5. These methods can therefore run with fuller tables, up to a load factor of about 0.8.

Average probes for open addressing at several load factors
Load factor LLinear, foundLinear, not foundQuadratic or double, foundQuadratic or double, not found
0.11.11.11.11.1
0.51.52.51.42.0
2/3 (about 0.67)2.05.01.63.0
0.83.013.02.05.0
0.95.550.52.610.0

Open addressing can never go beyond L = 1, when the array is completely full, and close to that point every method falls apart. At L = 0.99 an unsuccessful search averages about 100 probes with double hashing and about 5,000 with linear probing. Hour 23 introduces separate chaining, a method that degrades far more gently.

Summary

  • Quadratic probing tries the cells x + 1, x + 4, x + 9, x + 16 … from the hash index x, which breaks up primary clustering.
  • Every key with the same hash index follows the same quadratic probe sequence, so such keys pile up along it. This is secondary clustering.
  • Double hashing uses a second hash function to choose each key's step size, so keys that share a hash index usually follow different paths.
  • The secondary hash function must differ from the primary one and must never return 0. The form stepSize = constant - key % constant, with a prime constant smaller than the array size, works well.
  • Double hashing needs a prime table size. Otherwise some probe sequences cycle through only a few cells and may never find an empty one.
  • For linear probing, a successful search averages (1 + 1/(1 − L)) / 2 probes and an unsuccessful one (1 + 1/(1 − L)²) / 2. Keep L below 2/3, ideally below 1/2.
  • For quadratic probing and double hashing, the averages are −ln(1 − L) / L and 1 / (1 − L). A load factor up to about 0.8 is acceptable.
  • Open addressing cannot exceed a load factor of 1, and it performs terribly as it approaches that limit.

Q&A

If quadratic probing beats linear probing, why is it seldom used?
Because double hashing beats it too, with hardly any extra code. Double hashing removes secondary clustering as well as primary clustering.
Why not use one fixed step, say 7, for every key?
A fixed step is just linear probing with longer strides. Keys that collide still follow identical paths, and runs of occupied cells still build up along the stride. Double hashing works because the step depends on the key.
Does the constant in the step formula have to be 5?
No. Any prime smaller than the array size will do; 5 simply gives steps from 1 to 5. The table size must still be prime, so that every possible step can reach every cell.
How does deletion work with double hashing?
Just as with linear probing. The deleted item is replaced by the −1 marker, so searches keep following their probe sequences past it, and insertions may reuse the cell.

Quiz

  1. With quadratic probing, which cells are probed after a key hashes to index x?

    Answer

    x + 1, x + 4, x + 9, x + 16, x + 25 and so on (x plus the square of the step number), each taken % arraySize.

  2. What is secondary clustering?

    Answer

    With quadratic probing, all keys that hash to the same cell follow the same probe sequence, so each new key with that hash index must pass every cell the earlier ones filled and needs one probe more than the key before it.

  3. What is the usual form of the step-size function in double hashing?

    Answer

    stepSize = constant - (key % constant); where the constant is a prime smaller than the array size, for example 5 - key % 5, which gives steps from 1 to 5.

  4. What two rules must a secondary hash function follow?

    Answer

    It must not be the same as the primary hash function, and it must never output 0.

  5. Why should the table size be a prime number when you use double hashing?

    Answer

    If the size shares a factor with a step, that key's probe sequence cycles through only some of the cells (0, 5, 10, 0, 5, 10 … in a 15-cell table with a step of 5), so an insertion can loop forever even though empty cells exist. With a prime size, every step eventually visits every cell.

  6. With linear probing at a load factor of 2/3, how many probes does an unsuccessful search take on average?

    Answer

    (1 + 1/(1/3)²) / 2 = (1 + 9) / 2 = 5 probes.

Part V · Hash Tables

Hour 23 Separate Chaining

Separate chaining handles collisions by giving every cell of the array its own linked list, so items that collide simply share a list. This hour shows how chaining works and performs, when to choose it over open addressing, and what makes a good hash function.

In this hour you'll learn

  • How separate chaining stores colliding items in linked lists
  • How the HashChain applet and the hashChain.cpp program work
  • How chaining's speed depends on the load factor
  • When to choose separate chaining and when to choose open addressing
  • What makes a good hash function, including Horner's method for strings and folding for long numbers

Open addressing, the subject of the last two hours, answers a collision by hunting for another cell in the array. Separate chaining installs a linked list at every index of the hash table instead. A key is hashed to an index as usual, and the item is inserted into the list at that index. Other items that hash to the same index simply join the same list, so there is never any need to search the array for an empty cell.

Collisions no longer push items into other cells. They just make one list a little longer.

The HashChain Workshop Applet

Lafore's HashChain applet draws the array vertically, one index per row, with each index's list stretching to the right as a chain of small rectangles. Its buttons are New, Fill, Ins, Find and Del, as in the Hash applet. Ins hashes the key and adds the item to the list at that index. Find hashes the key to reach the right list and then searches along that list only.

Try it. Build a table of lists.

  1. Type 13 in the size field and press New, then type 20 in the count field and press Fill. Twenty items in 13 lists is a load factor of about 1.5, which open addressing could never reach.
  2. Look at the list lengths. Some cells are empty, many hold one or two items, and a few hold more.
  3. Insert a key and watch it join the list at its hash index. Then find a key in one of the longer lists and count the links examined.
  4. Delete a key. Its link simply disappears from the list, and no deleted marker is left behind.

Load Factors

The load factor behaves differently with chaining. Each cell can hold any number of items, so it is normal to put N or more items into an N-cell table, and the load factor can be 1 or more. In Lafore's rough picture of a table at L = 1, about a third of the cells are empty, a third hold one item, and a third hold two or more.

If keys fall into cells at random, the exact shares at L = 1 are about 37% empty, 37% with one item and 26% with two or more, close to Lafore's rough thirds.

Searching means hashing to the right cell and then walking its list. A successful search looks at about half the list on average, L/2 links, after the one step of hashing. So the lists should stay short. A load factor around 1 is typical, and much beyond 2 the lists start to slow things down.

Duplicates

Duplicates are allowed and cause no trouble. Every copy of a key hashes to the same cell, so all copies end up in the same list. Find returns the first copy it meets. To find or delete every copy, you search the whole of that one list, which is short anyway.

Deletion

Deletion is straightforward. Hash to the right cell and unlink the item from its list, as in any linked list (see Hour 8). There are no probe sequences to protect, so no deleted markers are needed, and deletions never slow down later searches.

Table Size

With chaining, a prime table size is not required the way it is for quadratic probing and double hashing, since there are no probe sequences that could cycle. A prime size is still a good idea. If many keys share a factor with the table size, they crowd into a few lists, as the section on hash functions shows.

Buckets

Instead of a linked list, each cell could hold a small array, called a bucket. Buckets share the usual weakness of arrays, a fixed capacity. Make them too big and most of the space is wasted; make them too small and some of them overflow. Linked lists grow exactly as needed, so they are the usual choice.

C++ Code for Separate Chaining

The program hashChain.cpp puts a sorted list from Hour 10 in every cell. Keeping each list sorted speeds up unsuccessful searches, because a search can stop as soon as it passes the place where the key would be. It does not speed up successful searches, which still go about halfway on average, and it makes insertion a little slower, since each new link must go in its proper place instead of at the front.

A Link holds one int key, iData, and a pointer to the next link, pNext, which the constructor sets to NULL. A SortedList keeps only pFirst, the pointer to its first link. The two member functions that matter most here are insert() and find().

insert() walks two pointers down the list, pPrevious one step behind pCurrent, until pCurrent reaches a key at least as large as the new one or runs off the end. The new link is spliced in between the two. If pPrevious is still NULL, the new link belongs at the front, so pFirst is changed instead.

find() walks the list while the keys are no larger than the one it wants, returning the link if it meets the key. As soon as it sees a larger key it gives up, because a sorted list cannot hold the key any further on. A search for 38 in the list 10, 31, 45, 52 stops at 45 after looking at three links. remove() walks the list the same way, with pPrevious trailing pCurrent, and when it finds the key it links pPrevious (or pFirst) past that link and deletes it.

The hash table is now a vector of SortedList pointers, and the constructor gives every cell its own empty list. After that, each operation is a single line that hashes the key and passes the work to the list at that index. displayTable() prints each index followed by its list.

As before, main() asks for the table size and the number of items, fills the table with random keys, and loops on a show, insert, delete and find menu. Here is the display for a 13-cell table holding 20 random keys between 0 and 129.

0. List (first-->last): 39 78
1. List (first-->last): 79
2. List (first-->last):
3. List (first-->last):
4. List (first-->last): 121
5. List (first-->last): 122
6. List (first-->last):
7. List (first-->last): 46 59
8. List (first-->last): 47 47 73 73
9. List (first-->last): 22 35 48
10. List (first-->last): 23 88
11. List (first-->last): 11 128
12. List (first-->last): 64 103

The load factor is 20/13, about 1.5. Three lists are empty, three hold a single item, and the longest, at index 8, holds four, including two pairs of duplicates (47 and 73) that chaining stores without any fuss.

Efficiency of Separate Chaining

Finding an item takes one step to hash the key and reach the right list, then a search of that list. With N items spread over arraySize lists, the average list holds N / arraySize items, which is exactly the load factor L. That makes the costs easy to state.

Searching

A successful search examines about half of its list, so it takes about 1 + L/2 probes. An unsuccessful search in an unsorted list must check every link, for 1 + L probes. In a sorted list a miss can stop partway, so it also averages about 1 + L/2.

Insertion

Inserting into an unsorted list takes a single step, since the new link goes straight to the front (unless you first search the list to reject duplicates). With sorted lists, as in hashChain.cpp, insertion must first find the right place, so it costs about 1 + L/2 probes, like a successful search.

Average probes for separate chaining
Load factor LSuccessful search (1 + L/2)Unsuccessful, unsorted lists (1 + L)Unsuccessful, sorted lists (1 + L/2)
0.51.251.51.25
11.521.5
2232
32.542.5

Compare that with open addressing. At L = 0.9, chaining needs about 1.45 probes for a hit and 1.9 for a miss, while linear probing needs 5.5 and 50.5. Chaining degrades gracefully as the load factor grows, and it can go on working at load factors that open addressing cannot reach at all.

Open Addressing Versus Separate Chaining

If you use open addressing, double hashing is generally the better choice over quadratic probing. The exception is when memory is plentiful and the data will not grow once the table is created. Then linear probing is the simplest to program, and at a load factor under 0.5 it costs little.

If you don't know how many items will be inserted, separate chaining is the safer choice. A rising load factor makes open addressing deteriorate sharply, but chaining only gradually. So when in doubt, use separate chaining. It does need a linked-list class, but adding more data than you expected will never bring it to a crawl.

Hash Functions

Every hash table depends on its hash function. A good one is quick to compute and spreads the keys evenly across the cells. How to achieve that depends on what the keys look like.

Quick Computation

The whole point of hashing is speed, so a slow hash function defeats the purpose. A function full of multiplications and divisions can take longer than the table lookup it serves. Bit operations can often stand in for arithmetic. Shifting a number left by one bit, for instance, multiplies it by 2.

Random Keys

A perfect hash function maps every key to a different cell. That is possible only when the keys are unusually well behaved, like the employee numbers of Hour 21, where the index is simply the key itself. In most applications there are far more possible keys than cells, and some collisions are inevitable.

When the keys are random, meaning every value is equally likely, index = key % arraySize; does a fine job. Every cell is equally likely to be chosen, so the keys spread out evenly.

Non-random Keys

Real keys are often far from random. Lafore's example is a car-part number such as 033-400-03-94-05-0-535, in which each group of digits has a meaning.

The fields of a car-part number
DigitsMeaningPossible valuesIn the example
0–2Supplier number1 to 999, currently up to 70033
3–5Category code100, 150, 200 … up to 850400
6–7Month introduced1 to 1203
8–9Year introduced00 to 9994
10–11Serial number1 to 9905
12Toxic risk flag0 or 10
13–15Checksumcomputed from the other fields535

The whole number, 0334000394050535, would be the key for hashing, and its digits are anything but random. The supplier number's first digit is always 0 for now, the category code is always a multiple of 50, and the month never goes above 12. The checksum adds nothing the other fields haven't already said; in the example it is simply their sum, 33 + 400 + 3 + 94 + 5 + 0 = 535. Lafore offers three guidelines for keys like these.

Don't use non-data. Squeeze out every part of the key that carries no new information, so that every bit counts. The checksum can be dropped, because it is computed from the other fields. Category codes that are always multiples of 50 can be divided by 50, which turns 100 through 850 into the small numbers 2 through 17.

Use all the data. Every part of the key that is real data should contribute to the hash value. If you hashed only the first few digits, for example, every part from the same supplier would collide.

Use a prime number for the modulo base. If many keys share a divisor with the array size, they bunch into a few cells. Keys that are all multiples of 10, placed in a table of 50 cells, can only land in cells 0, 10, 20, 30 and 40, leaving 45 cells unused. A prime array size shares no divisor with patterns like these, so it breaks them up. The two small tables below show the same effect.

Hashing Strings

Hour 21 turned a word into a number by treating its letters as the digits of a base-27 number, so cats became 3 × 27³ + 1 × 27² + 20 × 27¹ + 19 × 27⁰ = 60,337, which was then reduced with % arraySize. Computed that way, the method has two problems. Raising 27 to each power takes many multiplications, and longer words overflow an int. Already 27⁷ is more than 10 billion, far beyond the 2,147,483,647 that a 32-bit int can hold.

Horner's method gets rid of the powers by factoring out 27 over and over, so that 3 × 27³ + 1 × 27² + 20 × 27 + 19 becomes ((3 × 27 + 1) × 27 + 20) × 27 + 19. Starting from the leftmost letter, you multiply the running total by 27 and add the next letter's code. For cats that gives 3, then 3 × 27 + 1 = 82, then 82 × 27 + 20 = 2,234, then 2,234 × 27 + 19 = 60,337, the same answer without a single power.

The running total still grows until it overflows. The fix is to apply % at every step instead of only at the end. The final remainder comes out the same, because (A × 27 + B) % n always equals ((A % n) × 27 + B) % n. The running total then never gets much bigger than 27 times the array size.

hashFunc3("cats") with an array size of 13
LetterCodeCalculationhashVal
c3(0 × 27 + 3) % 13 = 3 % 133
a1(3 × 27 + 1) % 13 = 82 % 134
t20(4 × 27 + 20) % 13 = 128 % 1311
s19(11 × 27 + 19) % 13 = 316 % 134

The result, 4, matches 60,337 % 13, just as the identity promises. A common variation multiplies by 32 instead of 27. Every letter code is still smaller than the base, and multiplying by 32 is a shift left by 5 bits, which is quicker than a true multiplication.

Folding

Folding is a handy way to hash long numeric keys. Break the key into groups of digits and add the groups together. For a nine-digit Social Security number such as 123-45-6789 and an array of 1,000 cells, use groups of three digits. That gives 123 + 456 + 789 = 1,368, and 1,368 % 1,000 = 368. For an array of 100 cells, use two-digit groups instead, so 12 + 34 + 56 + 78 + 9 = 189, and 189 % 100 = 89.

The group size matches the number of digits in the array size, so the sum already lands near the right range and the modulo only trims it. If the array size is a prime such as 997 or 101, the modulo still does its job, giving 1,368 % 997 = 371 and 189 % 101 = 88.

Summary

  • In separate chaining, each cell of the hash table holds a linked list. Items that collide share a list, and no probing is needed.
  • The load factor can be 1 or more. About 1 is typical, and well above 2 the lists get slow.
  • Duplicates are easy, since every copy lands in the same list, and deletion simply unlinks an item with no marker left behind.
  • A prime table size is optional with chaining, though it still helps spread the keys. Small arrays called buckets could replace the lists, but lists grow as needed.
  • hashChain.cpp keeps each list sorted, so misses can stop early while insertions cost a little more.
  • A successful search takes about 1 + L/2 probes and an unsuccessful one 1 + L (about 1 + L/2 with sorted lists). Performance declines in a straight line as L grows.
  • Among open-addressing methods, double hashing is generally best, and linear probing suits only a fixed amount of data with plenty of memory. When in doubt, use separate chaining.
  • A good hash function is quick and spreads keys evenly. For non-random keys, drop non-data, use all the data, and use a prime modulo base.
  • Horner's method hashes strings without computing powers, and taking % at every step prevents overflow. Folding hashes long numbers by adding groups of digits.

Q&A

Why not always use separate chaining?
It needs a linked-list class, and every link carries a pointer as well as its data. If you know how much data is coming and can spare the memory, a double-hashing table is just as fast and simpler in structure.
Should the lists be sorted?
It depends on the mix of operations. Sorting helps unsuccessful searches and costs a little on insertion. With lists as short as they are at a load factor near 1, the difference is small either way.
Can the load factor go as high as 5 or 10?
The table still works, but every search then walks a list of 5 or 10 items, a small linear search. If the data grows that much, rehash into a bigger array.
Why multiply by 27 when hashing strings?
The code has 27 symbols, the blank plus 26 letters, so base 27 keeps different strings from producing the same number before the modulo is applied. Any larger base also works, and 32 is popular because multiplying by it is a quick shift.

Quiz

  1. In separate chaining, what does each cell of the hash table hold, and what load factor is typical?

    Answer

    A linked list (a sorted list in hashChain.cpp) of all the items that hash to that index. A load factor of about 1 is typical.

  2. At a load factor of 2, about how many probes does a successful search take?

    Answer

    1 + L/2 = 1 + 2/2 = 2 probes.

  3. When should you prefer separate chaining to open addressing?

    Answer

    When you don't know how many items will be inserted, or whenever you are in doubt. Its performance declines only gradually as the load factor rises, while open addressing deteriorates sharply.

  4. What three guidelines help when hashing non-random keys?

    Answer

    Don't use non-data (squeeze out parts such as checksums that add no information), use all the data (let every real field contribute), and use a prime number for the modulo base.

  5. What does Horner's method avoid, and how does hashFunc3() also avoid overflow?

    Answer

    It avoids computing powers of 27 by repeatedly multiplying the running total by 27 and adding the next letter. Applying % at every step keeps the running total small, so it never overflows.

  6. Folding the Social Security number 123-45-6789 into a 1,000-cell array gives which index?

    Answer

    123 + 456 + 789 = 1,368, and 1,368 % 1,000 = 368.

Part V · Hash Tables

Hour 24 When to Use What

The last hour adds no new structures. It steps back and turns the previous twenty-three hours into a way of choosing: which structure to store data in, which tool to reach for inside a program, and which sort to run.

In this hour you'll learn

  • The questions to ask before picking a data structure
  • When arrays, linked lists, trees and hash tables each make sense
  • How to choose between stacks, queues and priority queues
  • Which sort to use for small, large and nearly sorted data
  • Where to go after this book

By now you have seen a dozen ways to organize data and half a dozen ways to sort it. Each one was fast at some things and slow at others. Nothing is best at everything, so the useful skill is matching a structure to a job.

Before choosing, ask a few plain questions about your data. How many items will there be: dozens, thousands, millions? Do you know that number in advance? Which operations happen most: inserting, searching, deleting, or visiting everything in order? Could the keys arrive already sorted? And how much effort can you afford to spend writing and debugging the code? The answers usually point to one or two candidates.

Start with the simplest structure that could possibly work, usually an array. Measure. Move to something more complex only when the simple version is too slow for your real amount of data. Computers are fast, and for a few hundred items an O(N) search is often perfectly fine.

General-Purpose Data Structures

The general-purpose structures are the ones you use to store real-world records: personnel files, inventories, dictionaries, address books. There are four families: arrays, linked lists, trees and hash tables. Roughly speaking they get faster in that order, and also more complicated.

Speed and Algorithms

The table below collects the running times you met across the book. Remember what Big O hides: constants, memory use, and the cost of writing the code. An O(log N) tree beats an O(N) array only once N is big enough to matter, and a hash table that is nearly full can behave far worse than its O(1) promise.

General-purpose structures at a glance
StructureSearchInsertionDeletionVisit in key order
Unordered arrayO(N)O(1)O(N)Sort first
Ordered arrayO(log N)O(N)O(N)O(N)
Linked listO(N)O(1) at the frontO(N)Sort first
Sorted linked listO(N)O(N)O(N)O(N)
Binary search tree, random keysO(log N)O(log N)O(log N)O(N)
Binary search tree, sorted keys (worst case)O(N)O(N)O(N)O(N)
Balanced tree (red-black, 2-3-4)O(log N)O(log N)O(log N)O(N)
Hash tableO(1)O(1)O(1)Not supported

Arrays

Use an array when the amount of data is modest and you can predict how much there will be. Arrays are the simplest structure to write, they waste no memory on pointers, and they give instant access by index.

Choose the flavor by the operation that dominates. If you insert far more often than you search, an unordered array wins: each insertion is a single step at the end. If you search far more often than you insert, an ordered array wins: binary search finds any of a million items in about 20 comparisons (Hour 3). Deletion is slow in both, because the items above the hole must shift down.

The weak spot is size. An array is created with a fixed number of cells. Guess too low and it overflows; guess too high and memory sits idle. A vector can grow, but growing means copying every item into a bigger block, which is slow if it happens often.

Linked Lists

Reach for a linked list when you can't predict how many items you'll have, or when items are inserted and deleted constantly. A list grows one link at a time and never needs copying. Inserting or removing at the front is O(1), and removing a found item only changes pointers; nothing slides around.

The price is searching. There is no binary search in a list, because you can only reach an item by walking the chain from the start. That makes lists a poor fit for large amounts of data that must be searched often. A sorted list helps a little (a search can stop early), and a doubly linked list lets you walk backward and delete from either end (Hour 10).

Binary Search Trees

When arrays and lists prove too slow, a binary search tree is the next step. It finds, inserts and deletes in O(log N) time, and an inorder traversal hands you the keys in sorted order, which a hash table can't do. The minimum and maximum are a short walk down the left or right edge.

There is one catch, and it matters: the tree stays fast only if keys arrive in a fairly random order. Feed it sorted or reverse-sorted keys and it degenerates into a linked list, with O(N) operations (Hour 17). Use a plain binary search tree only when you're confident the input is random.

Balanced Trees

Red-black trees and 2-3-4 trees guarantee O(log N) no matter what order the keys arrive in. They are the safe choice for large amounts of data that must stay in order. Their drawback is complexity: the insertion and especially the deletion code is long and easy to get wrong. If a well-tested library version exists, use it.

In today's C++ Standard Library, std::map and std::set are almost always implemented as red-black trees, so you get the guarantees of Hours 17 and 18 without writing a line of rotation code. std::unordered_map and std::unordered_set, added in C++11, are hash tables with separate chaining.

Hash Tables

A hash table is the fastest way to store and retrieve items by key: insertion, search and deletion all take close to constant time. It is the natural choice for a spelling checker's dictionary, a compiler's table of variable names, or any lookup where you know the key and don't care about order.

Keep its limits in mind. It can't list items in key order or find the smallest one without examining everything. Performance depends on a good hash function and on the load factor. With open addressing the table must not get too full (keep linear probing under about half, double hashing under about two-thirds), so you need a decent estimate of the size, and growing the table means rehashing every item. Separate chaining is far more forgiving: its performance degrades only gradually as the load factor rises (Hour 23). When in doubt, chain.

Everything above assumed the data fits in memory. When it lives on disk, the expensive step is reading a block, and the winners change: B-trees (the big cousins of the 2-3-4 tree from Hour 20) and hashing into disk blocks both keep the number of disk reads tiny.

Special-Purpose Data Structures

Stacks, queues and priority queues are not usually where a program stores its main data. They are tools the program uses while it works: to remember where it was, to line up jobs, to pick the most urgent task next. Each deliberately restricts access to one item at a time, which is exactly what makes them simple and fast (Hours 6 and 7).

  • Stack (last in, first out): when the most recent item must be handled first. Matching delimiters, reversing sequences, undo histories, backtracking through a maze, and the way function calls themselves are managed.
  • Queue (first in, first out): when items must be served in arrival order. Print jobs, keyboard buffers, messages between parts of a program, and simulations of people or cars waiting in line.
  • Priority queue: when the most important item must come out first regardless of arrival order. Task scheduling by priority, and simulations that always process the earliest next event.

Each of these is an abstract data type (Hour 9): you choose the interface first and the implementation second. Use an array underneath when you know the maximum size, since it's simple and fast; use a linked list when the size is unpredictable.

Special-purpose structures
StructureImplementationInsertionDeletionComment
StackArray or linked listO(1) pushO(1) popRemoves the most recently inserted item
QueueCircular array or double-ended listO(1) at the rearO(1) at the frontRemoves the oldest item
Priority queueOrdered arrayO(N)O(1)Removes the item with the smallest key
Priority queueHeap (beyond this book)O(log N)O(log N)Better when there are many items

Sorting

The same advice applies to sorting: begin simple. For a small number of items, or data that is already nearly in order, the insertion sort is hard to beat. It is short, it sorts in place, it is stable, and on almost-sorted data it runs in close to O(N) time (Hour 5). The bubble sort is even simpler but roughly twice as slow, so it's rarely worth choosing.

When the insertion sort becomes too slow, move to quicksort, usually the fastest general-purpose sort for data in memory. Use the median-of-three pivot so that sorted or reverse-sorted input doesn't push it into its O(N²) worst case, and hand small partitions to an insertion sort (Hour 14).

Mergesort is the choice when you need a guarantee: it is O(N log N) every time, and it is stable. It pays for that with a second array as large as the first. It also shines when the data doesn't fit in memory: merging long sorted runs from disk is the classic way to sort huge files.

The sorts in this book
SortAverageWorstExtra memoryStable
Bubble sortO(N²)O(N²)NoYes
Insertion sortO(N²)O(N²)NoYes
MergesortO(N log N)O(N log N)A second array of N itemsYes
QuicksortO(N log N)O(N²), rare with median-of-threeNo (just the recursion)No

Sorting isn't always needed at all. If you only ever want the smallest item, a priority queue does less work than a full sort. If you need fast lookups but never sorted output, a hash table skips the question entirely.

Onward

This book gives you a working foundation, not the whole field. Several important topics lie just past its edge, and you're now ready for them:

  • Heaps, a tree-shaped structure stored in an array that makes priority queues O(log N) for both insertion and removal, and gives a sort of its own: heapsort.
  • Graphs, which model networks such as roads, airline routes and web links, along with the algorithms that search them, find shortest paths and build minimum spanning trees.
  • Other sorts, such as Shellsort and radix sort, and a deeper look at sorting files too big for memory.
  • Other balanced trees, such as the AVL tree mentioned in Hour 18, and B-trees for databases on disk.

Lafore's larger book on data structures (written with Java) covers heaps and graphs in the same hands-on style, and Appendix C points to the classic references. Whatever you read next, the habits from these 24 hours carry over: draw the structure, trace the pointers by hand, count the steps, and ask what happens as N grows.

Summary

  • Choosing a structure starts with questions: how much data, whether the size is known, which operations dominate, and whether keys might arrive sorted.
  • Try the simplest structure first and move up only when measurements say it's too slow.
  • Arrays suit small, predictable data; ordered arrays favor searching, unordered arrays favor insertion.
  • Linked lists suit unpredictable sizes and frequent insertion and deletion, but search slowly.
  • Binary search trees give O(log N) operations and sorted traversal, but only with randomly ordered keys; balanced trees guarantee O(log N).
  • Hash tables are the fastest for lookups by key but can't give ordered output; separate chaining handles growth most gracefully.
  • Stacks, queues and priority queues are programmer's tools with restricted access, built on arrays or linked lists.
  • Sort small or nearly sorted data with insertion sort, large data with quicksort, and use mergesort when you need guaranteed time, stability or external sorting.

Q&A

Is Big O all I need to compare two structures?
No. Big O describes how the time grows for large N. For small N, the constants it ignores often dominate, so a "slower" array can beat a "faster" tree. Memory use, how hard the code is to write correctly, and how often each operation really happens all matter too.
If libraries already provide these structures, why learn how they work?
Because choosing well requires knowing the costs inside. A library map and a library hash table look almost identical to use, but one keeps keys in order in O(log N) time and the other finds them in O(1) without order. Knowing why helps you pick the right one, predict its behavior on your data, and build a custom structure when nothing off the shelf fits.
What should I do when the data is too big for memory?
Design around disk reads, which are thousands of times slower than memory access. B-trees keep each node the size of a disk block so that a search touches only a few blocks, hashing can send each key straight to the block that holds it, and mergesort can sort a huge file by merging sorted runs.

Quiz

  1. You'll store about 200 records, the number hardly changes, and lookups by key vastly outnumber insertions. Which structure fits best?

    Answer

    An ordered array searched with binary search. The data is small and predictable, and the rare insertions can afford to shift items.

  2. Give two reasons not to use a hash table for everything, even though it's the fastest.

    Answer

    It can't visit items in key order or find the minimum quickly, and it needs a reasonable size estimate and a good hash function; with open addressing its performance collapses as it fills up.

  3. The keys you must store will arrive already sorted. Why is a plain binary search tree a bad idea, and what should you use?

    Answer

    Sorted input makes every new node a child of the previous one, so the tree becomes a linked list with O(N) operations. Use a balanced tree such as a red-black tree.

  4. Which sort is best for data that is already almost in order?

    Answer

    The insertion sort: each item moves only a short distance, so it runs in nearly O(N) time.

  5. Name one advantage of quicksort over mergesort, and one of mergesort over quicksort.

    Answer

    Quicksort sorts in place and is usually faster in practice. Mergesort guarantees O(N log N), is stable, and works well for data on disk.

  6. You need a stack and know it will never hold more than 100 items. Array or linked list?

    Answer

    An array: it's simpler and faster, with no pointer overhead. A linked list is the better choice only when the maximum size is unknown.

Appendix B: How to Run the Workshop Applets and Sample Programs

The Workshop Applets

The book's CD carried the Workshop applets as Java applets: small programs that ran inside a Java-enabled web browser, or in the appletviewer utility that came with Sun's Java Development Kit. Each one lived in its own folder with an HTML page that loaded it. You opened that page, and the applet's buttons, bars and trees appeared.

Web browsers have since dropped support for Java applets entirely, so the originals won't start in a modern browser. That is why every hour of this companion has a Workshop panel that re-creates the matching applet in JavaScript, with the same buttons wherever possible. The table shows where each one lives.

A few panels have no counterpart on the CD. They turn examples from the text into something you can play with: the guess-a-number game and the Big O growth table (Hour 3), delimiter matching (Hour 6), one interface with two implementations (Hour 9), and the triangle and anagram tracers (Hour 11).

If you have the original CD and want to see the real applets, you need an old Java setup: the appletviewer tool shipped with the JDK up to Java 10 and was removed in Java 11. Install an older JDK (Java 8 is the usual choice) and run appletviewer on an applet's HTML file.

The Sample Programs

The book's C++ examples are console programs: they print to a text window and some read keystrokes or numbers from it. They use Standard C++ (the string and vector classes and new-style headers such as <iostream>), so any modern compiler builds them. The listings in this companion are written the same way.

  1. Save a program in a file ending in .cpp, for example bubbleSort.cpp.
  2. With GCC or Clang, compile from a terminal: g++ -std=c++17 -Wall bubbleSort.cpp -o bubbleSort, then run ./bubbleSort (on Windows, bubbleSort.exe).
  3. With Visual Studio, create an empty C++ console project, add the file, and press Ctrl+F5 so the console window stays open when the program ends.

Programs that show a menu (such as the tree and hash table programs) wait for input: type the letter for a command and press Enter. Run them in a real terminal rather than an editor's output pane, which may not accept keyboard input.

Appendix C: Further Reading

The book closes with suggestions in four areas. Here's what each area is for, and books that are widely recommended in it.

Data Structures and Algorithms

The natural next step: more structures (heaps, graphs, B-trees), more sorts, and the mathematics of why algorithms cost what they do.

Object-Oriented Programming Languages

A solid grip on C++ itself makes every listing easier: classes, pointers, memory management, templates, and the Standard Library that now provides most of these structures ready-made.

Object-Oriented Design and Software Engineering

How to go from a problem to a set of classes, and how real programs are planned, built, tested and maintained over years.

Programming Style

How to write code that other people (including you, six months later) can read, trust and change.

Well-known titles in each area, suggested here rather than copied from the book's list. Algorithms: Donald Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming (Volumes 1 and 3); Robert Sedgewick, Algorithms in C++; Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms; Robert Lafore, Data Structures and Algorithms in Java, which adds heaps and graphs in this same style. Languages: Bjarne Stroustrup, The C++ Programming Language; Robert Lafore, Object-Oriented Programming in C++. Design: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, Design Patterns; Frederick Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month. Style: Kernighan and Plauger, The Elements of Programming Style; Jon Bentley, Programming Pearls; Steve McConnell, Code Complete.

About this companion. It follows the book's published table of contents hour by hour and retells its examples. The explanations and the C++ listings are written fresh, keeping the book's class and function names so you can follow along in a printed copy. The Workshop panels re-create the behavior of Lafore's Java applets, which today's browsers no longer run. Quiz answers sit under each question; the book collects them in Appendix A.
